Biography: Tamar Guimarães is a Brazilian artist who works with film, sound, and installation. Her practice is based on historical research and frequently incorporates photographs, texts, documents, and found objects. By reprocessing these materials, she creates narratives that move between documentary, essay, and fiction. Her work investigates how social relations of race, class, and labor are manifested in different cultural forms, from architecture to religious literature and dance. Recent solo exhibitions include SOAP at Fortes D'Aloia and Gabriel, Sao Paulo (2023), Video Room: Tamar Guimaraes at MASP, Sao Paulo (2022), El tejido hablado at Zarigueya/Alabado Contemporaneo, Quito (2019), Black Box at the Baltimore Museum of Art (2017), La Incorrupta at Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofia, Madrid (2016), and The Florists From Beyond the Grave at SKMU Sorlandets Kunstmuseum, Kristiansand (2015). She has also participated in group exhibitions including Illiberal Arts at Haus der Kulturen der Welt, Berlin (2021), Nine Lives at the Renaissance Society, Chicago (2020), Le jour des esprits est notre nuit at CRAC Alsace, France, Blackout at the International Film Festival Rotterdam and Kunsthal Rotterdam (2019), and Afinidades Eletivas at the 33rd Sao Paulo Biennial (2018). Her works are included in major public collections such as CIFO - Cisneros Fontanals Art Foundation, Miami, FRAC Auvergne, Clermont-Ferrand, Guangdong Museum, Guangzhou, Instituto Inhotim, Brumadinho, Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofia, Madrid, the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, and Tate Modern, London.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in São Paulo (Brazil) and in Berlin (Germany)
Biography: Clara Ianni is a Brazilian artist whose work explores the relationship between art and politics through video, sculpture, installation, and text. Her practice investigates historical narratives, collective memory, and the social structures that shape political experience. She holds a BFA in Visual Arts from the University of Sao Paulo and has developed projects that examine connections between Brazil and other regions, including the legacy of colonialism. Her exhibitions include Utopia/Distopia - Part I at MAAT, Lisbon (2017), Talking to Action / Hablar y Actuar in Los Angeles (2017), the Jakarta Biennale (2015), the 31st Sao Paulo Biennial (2014), the Yebisu Festival in Tokyo (2015), MDE15 in Medellin and Bogota (2015), the 19th Panorama VideoBrasil, the 33rd Panorama de Arte Brasileira at the Museum of Modern Art of Sao Paulo (2013), and the 12th Istanbul Biennial (2011). She has participated in residencies including AIR Laboratory in Warsaw (2017), HIWAR - Conversations in Amman (2013), Bolsa Pampulha at the Museu da Pampulha in Belo Horizonte (2011), and Casa Tomada in Sao Paulo (2010). Ianni is also curator of the program The Future of Memory - Memory and Forgetfulness in Latin America, organized with the Goethe Institute. In addition, she worked as an assistant to curator Regis Michel at the Louvre Museum and as part of the curatorial team of the 7th Berlin Biennale alongside Artur Zmijewski, Joanna Warsza, and Voina.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in São Paulo (Brazil)
Biography: Lucia Koch was born in Porto Alegre, Brazil, in 1966. She lives and works in São Paulo. Employing photographs, video, and architectural interventions and installations, her work brings attention to often-overlooked aspects of environments. In order to alter the spaces in which she works, Koch uses scrims, fabric, and other means to block and redirect light. Light and air become the materials with which the artist works, prioritizing atmosphere over color to transform a space into an architectural place. For the work Conversion at the 2013 Sharjah Biennial, Koch constructed colored filters over a sun-filled courtyard. In addition to such large-scale interventions, she has also created photographs of small models of building interiors, made of cardboard boxes, which dramatize spatial distortion in the images.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Rio de Janeiro (Brazil)
Biography: Maria Laet (born 1982 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil) is a Brazilian artist whose work explores the relationship between the body and the natural world through performance, video, drawing, and installation. Using materials such as sand, gauze, soil, and ink, she investigates permeability, visibility, and ephemerality through carefully executed and meditative actions. Her practice is driven by questions about the boundaries between the body and the world, often treating surfaces as spaces of encounter and exchange rather than separation. Since the mid-2000s, Laet has developed works that examine the body's interaction with natural environments, drawing inspiration from artists such as Ana Mendieta and Lygia Clark. Her works frequently employ fragile and porous materials to emphasize impermanence and transformation as fundamental aspects of everyday life. In the video performance Notes on the Limit of the Sea, she sews a white thread across the sand at the shoreline, allowing the movement of the tide to gradually erase her actions. In Caminho, a monotype from the portfolio The Valise, she records the trace of her body's movement and weight on paper, creating a path without landscape or fixed reference. Closely connected to the history of Brazilian art, her practice engages with the legacy of Neo-Concrete artists and the Grupo Frente while placing meditative action and attentive observation at its center. Rather than focusing primarily on sensory participation, her works emphasize silence, presence, and the continuous exchange between the human body and its surroundings.

Judith Lauand (1922-2022) was a Brazilian painter and printmaker and the only female member of Grupo Ruptura, the pioneering concrete art movement based in Sao Paulo. Born in Pontal, Sao Paulo, she studied fine arts at the Escola de Belas Artes in Araraquara, where she received a traditional artistic education in painting and printmaking. After graduating in the mid-1950s, she worked as a teacher while producing expressionist figurative paintings. In 1953, she moved to Sao Paulo, and the following year, while working as a gallery monitor at the Sao Paulo Art Biennial, she became connected with artists of Grupo Ruptura and soon joined the group. Her work became rooted in geometric abstraction and the analytical principles of concrete art that emerged in Brazil during the 1950s. Beginning in the 1960s, she expanded her practice by incorporating non-traditional materials such as paper clips and other objects, creating textured and uneven surfaces. Lauand maintained an independent position within the movement, notably continuing to sign her paintings on the front, contrary to the theoretical preferences of many of her contemporaries. Throughout her career, she worked across a wide range of media including painting, printmaking, collage, embroidery, sculpture, woodcut, and tapestry. She turned one hundred years old in 2022 and remained an important figure in the history of Brazilian modern and concrete art until her death in Sao Paulo later that year.

Cinthia Marcelle (born 1974 in Belo Horizonte, Brazil) is a Brazilian multimedia artist working with photography, video, and installation. She studied at the Federal University of Minas Gerais and lives and works in Sao Paulo. Her practice is characterized by a concise visual language that draws inspiration from everyday objects, places, and social interactions. One of her early recognized works, Capa Morada (2003), created with South African artist Jean Meeran, consisted of photographs in which she blended into urban landscapes through the use of a color-matched cape. In works such as Education by Stone, she transformed ordinary materials into large-scale installations that examine social structures and collective behavior. Marcelle has presented solo exhibitions at institutions including MoMA PS1 and the Secession. She has also participated in major international exhibitions such as the Venice Biennale, the Berlin Biennale, the Istanbul Biennial, the Sharjah Biennial, and the New Museum Triennial. In 2017, she received an Honorable Mention for her presentation at the Brazilian Pavilion of the 57th Venice Biennale. She is also the recipient of the Future Generation Prize (2010) and the Bolsa Pampulha (2003-2004).

Tiago Mata Machado (born 1973, Brazil) is a Brazilian artist and filmmaker whose work has been presented internationally through exhibitions, screenings, and collaborative projects. His practice frequently engages with moving images, narrative structures, and contemporary social and political questions. In recent years, his work has been featured in exhibitions including Faire Corps at FRAC Bretagne in Rennes, Under Pressure Above Water at ARTER in Istanbul, and Sounds of Babel at the Taiwan Contemporary Culture Lab in Taipei. In 2022, he presented Obscura Luz (Obscure Light) at Galeria Luisa Strina in Sao Paulo. He has collaborated extensively with Cinthia Marcelle, including the exhibition Cinthia Marcelle and Tiago Mata Machado at Galeria Vermelho in Sao Paulo in 2021 and Divine Violence at the Logan Center, University of Chicago, in 2017. Earlier exhibitions include In The Land of the Blind The One Eyed Man Loses Sight at Dittrich and Schlechtriem in Berlin and Eri Mielta: Nykytaiteen Toisinajattelijoita at Kiasma Museum of Contemporary Art in Helsinki in 2015.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in São Paulo (Brazil)
Biography: Ana Mazzei (born 1979 in Sao Paulo, Brazil) is a Brazilian artist who lives and works in Sao Paulo. Her practice combines organic and figurative forms with a precise geometric sensibility, often engaging with the constructive legacy of Brazilian Concretist and Neo-Concretist movements. Through colorful wooden sculptures displayed individually or in groups, she creates open-ended narratives that draw on theater, literature, mythology, and personal references without revealing their sources directly. Her works construct intimate territories in which different stories and symbols intersect, reflecting on contemporary life and its complexities. In 2024, she presented the solo exhibition Garden Scene at Martins and Montero in Sao Paulo. In 2023, she held the solo exhibition Love Scene, Crime Scene at gb agency in Paris. Recent exhibitions include Vai, vai, saudade at Museo Madre in Naples, The Disagreement: A Theater of Statements at Neuer Kunstverein Wien, Uma cadeira e uma cadeira e uma cadeira at Galeria Luisa Strina, and The Bridge Project at Galpao Cru in Sao Paulo. She has also participated in the 37th Panorama of Brazilian Art, the 14th Cuenca Biennial, Histórias Feministas at MASP, Glasgow International, and the 32nd Sao Paulo Biennial. Mazzei has been an artist-in-residence at Cite Internationale des Arts in Paris, Gasworks in London, CAC Noisy-le-Sec, and Sculpture Studios in Glasgow.

Morgan-Snell (1920-2007) was a Brazilian artist born in Sao Paulo who was largely self-taught, developing her artistic skills through constant observation and drawing from an early age. After World War II, she spent extended periods in Europe, studying the works of major masters in French and Italian museums. In 1943, she painted portraits of Brazilian dignitaries, and in 1946 major exhibitions of her work were held at the Barcinsky Gallery in Rio de Janeiro and the Copacabana Palace Hotel. She moved to Paris in 1948, where she continued to build an international reputation and received seventeen awards during her career. Her work entered important public collections, including the Musee National d'Art Moderne de Paris and the Musee d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris. In 1958, the French State commissioned her monumental mural The Snatchers of the Sea for the General Post Office of Les Sables d'Olonne, and in 1960 she was commissioned to create two large murals for the Church of the Trinity in Paris. From the 1950s onward, she exhibited extensively in France and internationally, including in Switzerland, Sweden, the United States, Canada, Germany, Poland, Russia, and Brazil. In 1975, she was invited by the Brazilian Ministry of Culture and Foreign Affairs to present exhibitions at the National Museum of Rio de Janeiro and the Assis Chateaubriand Museum in Sao Paulo. Her work was also featured in a retrospective at UNESCO in Paris in 1977, and she participated in numerous international exhibitions and museum presentations throughout her career. She received thirty-three medals and several major French artistic prizes and was named Woman of the Year for Plastic Arts in Brazil in 1975 before dedicating herself to charitable activities in Brazil and France from 1978 onward.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Belo Horizonte (Brazil)
Biography: Rivane Neuenschwander (born 1967 in Belo Horizonte, Brazil) is a Brazilian artist whose work explores language, nature, geography, time, and social interaction through installations, films, photographs, and participatory projects. She is known for using fragile and everyday materials such as garlic peels, ants, dried flowers, soap bubbles, dust, water. During the 1990s, her practice focused on mapping and ephemeral materials familiar to everyday life in Brazil, while her later works increasingly addressed politics, sexuality, and subjectivity. She graduated from the Federal University of Minas Gerais in 1993 and completed an MFA at the Royal College of Art in London in 1998, later traveling extensively throughout Europe. Neuenschwander has exhibited internationally for more than two decades and was shortlisted for the Hugo Boss Prize in 2004 and awarded the Yanghyun Prize in 2013. In 2010, the New Museum in New York presented the survey exhibition A Day Like Any Other, which subsequently traveled to institutions in the United States and Ireland. She has participated in major international exhibitions including the Istanbul Biennial, the Sao Paulo Biennial, the Venice Biennale, and the Carnegie International. More recent presentations have included projects at MoMA, the Tanya Bonakdar Gallery, the Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, and public art initiatives organized by Inhotim in Belo Horizonte. Her works continue to combine material experimentation and audience participation while reflecting on contemporary social and political realities.

Heloisa Novaes (born 1953 in Brazil) is a Brazilian artist whose works have appeared at public auction primarily in the drawing and watercolor category. The earliest recorded auction of her work was La petite ravaudeuse de temps (texte d'Irene Frain), presented at Tajan in 2000. The most recent recorded sale was Algumas cores vindo de mansinho / Sans titre, presented in 2026. Her works have been offered at public auction fifteen times, with most sales taking place in France. According to available auction records, one of her works is scheduled to be offered at auction in the near future.

Birth / death: 1927, Rio de Janeiro (Brazil) - 2004, Rio de Janeiro (Brazil)
Biography: Lygia Pape (1927-2004) was a Brazilian visual artist, sculptor, printmaker, and filmmaker who played a central role in both the Concrete and Neo-Concrete movements in Brazil. Born in Nova Friburgo, she studied philosophy at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro and later received artistic training under Fayga Ostrower at the Museum of Modern Art in Rio de Janeiro. In the 1950s, she became known for her Tecelares series of woodcuts, which combined geometric abstraction with references to weaving and indigenous Brazilian culture, marking a transition from Concrete to Neo-Concrete art. In 1952, she joined Grupo Frente alongside artists including Helio Oiticica, Ivan Serpa, and Aluisio Carvao, and in 1959 became a signatory of the Neo-Concrete Manifesto. During this period, she created key works such as Livro da Criacao (Book of Creation), which encouraged viewers to actively engage with the artwork through handling and interpretation. Her practice increasingly focused on the relationship between the body, perception, and space, resulting in participatory and multisensory works such as O Ovo and the Tteias series. From the 1960s onward, she produced films, installations, and projects that often addressed political and social issues, including criticism of the Brazilian dictatorship. Between 1972 and 1985, she taught semiotics and fine arts in Rio de Janeiro while continuing her artistic research into urban space and social experience. She received a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1981, and her work is held in major collections including the Museum of Modern Art, Tate, and Museo Reina Sofia.

Marilena Pelosi (born 26 February 1957 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil) began painting during her adolescence after experiencing a difficult and neglected childhood. At the age of twenty, she left Brazil and spent many years traveling through Europe, the Americas, and India before eventually settling in France. Following her separation from her husband in the late 1990s, she experienced a period of profound loneliness and depression, finding refuge in artistic creation as a way to confront personal suffering and inner struggles. Pelosi creates her drawings using simple materials such as ballpoint pen, felt-tip pen, and Indian ink on paper or tracing paper. Her works reveal a labyrinthine universe populated by intertwined human figures connected by strings, chains, or cords. Victims and executioners coexist within scenes where blood, water, and exaggerated tongues appear as recurring motifs. Water often functions as a symbol of purification and redemption within her imagery. Balancing cynicism, love, nightmare, exorcism, and childhood play, her work deliberately embraces a polymorphic and constantly shifting visual language. Based in France, her work has been exhibited at Le Pluriel des Singuliers in Aix-en-Provence, Galerie Alain Dettinger in Lyon, the Festival d'Art Singulier in Roquevaire, and Galerie Beatrice Soulie in Paris.

Marina Perez Simao (born 1980 in Brazil) is an artist whose work is centered on the human figure and is distinguished by the important role of drawing in her practice. In 2009, she was awarded the first Prix des Partenaires of the Musee d'Art Moderne de Saint-Etienne Metropole, a prize created to support a young artist living and working in France through a museum exhibition and publication. The jury recognized the technical maturity of her work, the coherence of her artistic development, the authenticity of her visual language, and the depth of her narratives. Her delicate drawings, executed on a variety of papers, depict female figures emerging from an imaginary world where fairy tales, family memories, and intimate everyday experiences intersect. Her work is characterized by great sensitivity, expressed through transparent layers of paper, soft and sensual colors, blurred contours, and an intentional sense of incompletion. Drawing from diverse influences connected to her personal background and artistic formation, she creates poetic and introspective images that explore memory, identity, and imagination. The award provided her with the opportunity to present a first solo museum exhibition and publish her work to a wider audience. At the time of receiving the prize, she presented a selection of her most recent works, then still in production.

Elizabeth de Portzamparc is a French-Brazilian architect born in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Influenced from an early age by art and architecture, she developed a particular interest in urbanism while studying anthropology, urban sociology, and regional planning in France. During the late 1970s, she conducted pioneering research on neighborhoods, local life, and territorial relationships, placing these concepts at the center of urban planning policies. She later taught at French architecture schools and contributed to research projects for the French Ministry of Environment and Quality of Life as well as the Ministry of Equipment. In 1986, she founded and directed the Mostra Gallery in Paris, where she worked closely with artists, designers, and architects while exploring the specificities of different creative disciplines. In 1987, she established her own architectural practice, which has since developed projects across architecture, urban planning, design, and museography. Among her notable projects are the Information Center of the French National Assembly, the museography of the Korean National Museum, the Museum of Brittany in Rennes, and the stations and urban furniture of the Bordeaux tramway network. Her work is characterized by a focus on public space, urban identity, transparency, and the relationship between architecture and everyday life. She has also contributed to research on sustainable, mixed-use, and affordable housing, including projects designed for homeless and vulnerable populations.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in São Paulo (Brazil)
Biography: Leticia Ramos (born 1976 in Brazil) is an artist trained as a filmmaker who has focused on the history, processes, and evolution of photography and film techniques since the beginning of her career in the early 2000s. Her research-based practice explores the material, historical, and conceptual dimensions of image-making and the ways images shape our perception of reality. For each project, Ramos develops custom devices and image-capturing machines that allow her to produce visual narratives beyond the possibilities of conventional cameras and cinematic languages. Her work incorporates experimental film emulsions, homemade pinhole cameras, microfilming systems, and X-ray machines, using these tools to connect scientific inquiry with fictional storytelling. Through these self-designed methods, she investigates relationships between historical events, scientific experiments, natural phenomena, and sociopolitical processes. More recently, her research has focused on environmental issues and climate-related disasters. Drawing on speculative fiction, mysticism, and science fiction, she creates works that blur the boundaries between fact and imagination. She lives and works between Sao Paulo, Brazil, and Lisbon, Portugal.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Rio de Janeiro (Brazil)
Biography: Rosangela Renno Gomes (born 1962 in Belo Horizonte, Brazil) is a Brazilian artist who lives and works in Rio de Janeiro. Her practice is based on photographic images drawn from public and private archives, which she uses to question the nature of images and their symbolic value. Through photographs, installations, and objects, she appropriates anonymous photographs and negatives found in flea markets, family albums, newspapers, and archives, giving them new meanings and contexts. Her interest in discarded images and collecting has been central to the development of her artistic methods. Renno focuses on what she describes as the 'little stories of the downtrodden and the vanquished', exploring overlooked or suppressed episodes of history. She is particularly interested in vernacular photography, identification photographs, and portraits, which she considers among the most neglected categories of images. Rather than producing new photographs, she works exclusively with existing ones, reusing and reinterpreting them. Her approach has been influenced by the ideas of Vilém Flusser and Andreas Muller-Pohle, particularly concepts related to the preservation and recycling of images. Through this process, Renno investigates memory, history, visibility, and the cultural value of photographic archives.

Paula Siebra (born 1998 in Fortaleza, Brazil) is a Brazilian artist who lives and works in Fortaleza. Working from notebooks, drawings, and memories, she develops paintings through the gradual accumulation of domestic, material, and vernacular images. Her canvases often begin with terracotta, ochre, or neutral-toned grounds, onto which she builds thin layers that soften contours, reduce contrast, and create subtle atmospheres. Recurring motifs include rivers, hills, clay jars, lace, wooden ex-votos, sun-bleached facades, gloves, suitcases, and tableware, drawn from everyday life, memory, and dreams. Her visual vocabulary emerged from her experience in Ceara, where she absorbed elements of daily life, local craft traditions, natural forms, and the geometry of modest architecture. Through careful observation and familiarity with her surroundings, she develops imagery that extends beyond regional references. Meaning in her work emerges through the quiet relationship between forms rather than through direct narrative. Her paintings often depict landscapes, interiors, and domestic scenes marked by stillness and suspension. When figures appear, they are usually observed from a distance, reinforcing a sense of intimacy, reflection, and private time.

Tarsila do Amaral (1886-1973) was a Brazilian painter, draftswoman, and translator who became one of the leading figures of Brazilian modernism. Born in Capivari, Sao Paulo, into a wealthy family of coffee farmers and landowners, she received support to pursue artistic studies at a time when higher education for women was uncommon in Brazil. As a teenager, she traveled to Spain, where she began drawing and painting works inspired by the art she encountered there. She later studied painting in Sao Paulo with Pedro Alexandrino and continued her artistic education at the Academie Julian in Paris between 1920 and 1923. Tarsila became a central member of the Grupo dos Cinco alongside Anita Malfatti, Menotti Del Picchia, Mario de Andrade, and Oswald de Andrade, contributing significantly to the development of modern art in Brazil. She is particularly associated with the search for a distinctly Brazilian artistic language that combined modernist experimentation with national identity. Her painting Abaporu inspired Oswald de Andrade's Manifesto Antropofago and played a key role in the formation of the Antropofagia movement of 1928-1929. Through her work, she helped shape a modern Brazilian aesthetic that remains influential in Latin American art history.

Ana Maria Tavares (born 1958 in Belo Horizonte, Brazil) is a Brazilian artist whose work explores the intersection of art, architecture, and design. She studied at the School of the Fundacao Armando Alvares Penteado, receiving a Bachelor of Arts in 1982, and later earned an MFA from the Art Institute of Chicago in 1986. After returning to Brazil, she completed a PhD in art at the University of Sao Paulo in 2000, where she continued as a professor. Tavares was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2001 and was the Ida Ely Rubin Artist-in-Residence at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2007. Her multimedia practice critically examines modernism, which she describes as an ideological construction with unexpected effects. In 2013-2014, the Frist Center for the Visual Arts in Nashville presented her solo exhibition Deviating Utopias Opens, which reflected on the legacy of Oscar Niemeyer and the relationship between modernist architecture and contemporary urban life. In 2014, she presented Euryale Amazonica at Sicardi Gallery, a project inspired by the Victoria amazonica water lily. Her 2018 solo exhibition Rotacoes Infinitas was held at Galeria Vermelho in Sao Paulo, and in 2023 she presented Sortir du silence: au-dela de la modernite at Galleria Continua in Paris. Through installations and multimedia works, Tavares investigates the social, cultural, and spatial implications of modernist thought and architecture.

Biography:
Joao Walter Toscano (1933-2011) was a Brazilian architect born in Itu, Sao Paulo. Throughout his career, he designed numerous projects between the 1960s and 1990s, including the Aguas da Prata spa complex, the Centro Empresarial do Aco, the Terminal Princesa Isabel, and the Largo 13 de Maio station, now Santo Amaro Station on Line 9 of the Sao Paulo metropolitan rail network. Several of his projects became landmarks of steel architecture in Brazil. His work contributed significantly to the development of modern architectural and urban infrastructure projects in Sao Paulo and other regions of the country.

Odilea Helena Setti Toscano (1934-2015) was a Brazilian architect, professor, and visual artist born in Sao Bernardo do Campo. Married to architect Joao Toscano, she became widely known for her public artworks integrated into transportation spaces in Sao Paulo. Her works are installed at Santo Amaro Station of the CPTM network and at four Sao Paulo Metro stations: Santana, Sao Bento, Paraiso, and Jabaquara. She is recognized as the artist with the largest number of works in the contemporary art collection of the Sao Paulo public transportation system. Alongside her architectural and teaching activities, she developed a significant artistic practice focused on public space.

Massayoshi Kamimura (born 1941 in Duartina, Brazil) is a Brazilian architect. He was born in Duartina and has lived and worked in Sao Paulo. His professional career is associated with architectural practice in Brazil, particularly in Sao Paulo, where he developed his activities as an architect.

Julio Roberto Katinsky is a Brazilian designer, architect, urban planner, and Professor Emeritus at the Faculty of Architecture and Urbanism of the University of Sao Paulo (FAU-USP). As a recent graduate, he joined the design team of L'Atelier, founded by Jorge Zalszupin, during a period when Brazilian furniture design was becoming closely linked to the development of modern architecture. Between 1959 and 1960, he created some of his best-known furniture designs, including the Andorinha table, a low armchair made of metal and leather, a stool combining rosewood, leather, and metal, and the Sputnik lamp. Educated at FAU-USP between 1952 and 1957, Katinsky belonged to the pioneering generation that sought to develop a distinct local technical and design language in Brazil. He participated in the cultural environment fostered by MASP and attended a decorative arts course taught by Lina Bo Bardi in 1955. Beyond design practice, he contributed significantly to architectural theory, research, and education. In 1962, he helped establish industrial design as part of the architecture curriculum at FAU-USP and later expanded the History of Technology course to include the study of technological development in Brazil.

Abrahao Velvu Sanovicz (1933-1999) was a Brazilian architect, designer, and artist who graduated from FAU-USP in 1958 and was associated with the Escola Paulista, one of the most influential generations of Sao Paulo architecture. He designed and built residential, cultural, educational, service, and infrastructure projects throughout his career. As a young student, he attended the School of Crafts at the Museum of Modern Art of Sao Paulo and completed an internship in Milan at the office of designer Marcello Nizzoli. In addition to architecture, he produced works in fine arts, particularly drawing and printmaking, and was active in graphic and product design. His multidisciplinary practice connected architecture, visual arts, and design, reflecting the broader cultural context of Brazilian modernism. His career and contributions have been documented through the Brazilian Architecture series created by the Lina Bo and P. M. Bardi Institute in partnership with Romano Guerra Editora, which highlights architects whose work contributed significantly to Brazilian architectural culture.

Cybele Varela (born 1943 in Petropolis, Brazil) is a Brazilian mixed-media artist whose practice encompasses painting, photography, video, and sculpture. She studied visual arts at the Museum of Modern Art in Rio de Janeiro between 1962 and 1966. Varela began her career as a painter and sculptor and received the Young Contemporary Art Prize from the Museum of Contemporary Art of the University of Sao Paulo in 1967 for her triptych Of All That Could Have Been, But That Wasn't. The same year, she participated for the first time in the Sao Paulo Biennial. In 1968, she received a scholarship from the French government to study at the Ecole du Louvre in Paris and later worked at the Cite Internationale des Arts between 1971 and 1972. She continued her studies at the Ecole Pratique des Hautes Etudes from 1976 to 1978. During the 1980s, while living in Geneva, her work focused on themes drawn from nature, while in the 1990s she developed a more figurative approach incorporating photography, digital printing, and video. Since 2000, her work has moved toward pop surrealism. In 1997, one of her paintings was donated by the Brazilian government to the United Nations.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Lisbonne (Portugal) and in Paris (France)
Biography: Ana Vaz (born 1986 in Brazil) is an artist and filmmaker whose work explores cinema as a medium of the visible and invisible, questioning its capacity to shape perceptions of humanity and its relationship to non-human and spectral forms of life. Born in the Brazilian Midwest, a region marked by the legacy of Brasilia and the histories buried beneath its modernist project, Vaz has developed a filmography that investigates memory, colonization, territory, and ecological interconnections. Her practice extends beyond filmmaking to include writing, critical pedagogy, installations, and collective walks. Through these different forms, she examines the boundaries between history, mythology, and lived experience. One of her research projects, ANHNANGUERA, is a script for a transhistorical fiction inspired by the history of colonization in the Brazilian Far West, her place of origin and a recurring subject in her work. The project draws on Paulo Bertran's book History of the Earth and Humanity in the Central Plateau, which interweaves geological, pre-modern, and modern temporalities. It also incorporates archival research from the Institutum Historicum Societatis Iesu in Rome, an institution connected to the Jesuit evangelization of Brazil. Through this cosmopolitical western, Vaz continues her exploration of the intersections between history, landscape, spirituality, and the lasting effects of colonialism.

Decio Tozzi (born 1936 in Sao Paulo, Brazil) is a Brazilian architect associated with the ideas of the Paulista School, whose work emphasizes architecture as a tool for social transformation. His practice is characterized by a strong attention to landscape, functionality, and the relationship between architecture and society. Light, space, and materiality are central elements of his architectural language, with concrete, glass, and steel playing a fundamental role in the creation of expressive spatial environments. Through the careful manipulation of natural light and texture, Tozzi develops projects that balance aesthetic refinement with intellectual rigor. His work reflects a critical understanding of design and a commitment to the integration of buildings within the urban fabric. The aesthetic quality of his architecture emerges from a synthesis of formal invention, technical precision, and social awareness. Throughout his career, he has explored the dynamic relationship between architecture, the city, and collective life. He is regarded as one of the important figures of Brazilian architecture.

Karla Albuquerque (born 1962 in Pocos de Caldas, Brazil) is a Brazilian architect. She has lived and worked in Sao Paulo, where she has developed her professional practice. Her career is associated with architecture and urban design in Brazil, contributing to the contemporary architectural landscape through her work and projects.

Maria Thereza Alves (born 1961 in São Paulo, Brazil) is a Brazilian-born artist, activist, writer, filmmaker, and researcher whose multidisciplinary practice examines the lasting effects of colonialism, migration, environmental change, and social injustice. As a child, she moved with her family to New York City to escape Brazil`s military dictatorship, an experience that deeply influenced her political and artistic outlook. She studied architecture at Cooper Union, graduating in 1985, and has since developed an internationally recognized career that combines artistic production with social and environmental activism. At the age of seventeen, she addressed the United Nations Human Rights Committee in Geneva on human rights violations against Indigenous peoples in Brazil, demonstrating an early commitment to political engagement. In 1987, she co-founded the Green Party of São Paulo, further strengthening her involvement in environmental and social causes. Her most celebrated long-term project, *Seeds of Change*, investigates the intertwined histories of colonial trade, slavery, migration, and global commerce through the study of plant seeds transported across continents in the ballast of colonial ships. Through research-based installations, videos, writings, and public interventions, Alves reveals hidden ecological and historical narratives that connect human and environmental histories. Her work has been presented at major international exhibitions, including Documenta 13, Manifesta 12, the Sharjah Biennial, and the Sydney Biennale, establishing her as an important voice in contemporary art. In 2016, she received the Vera List Center Prize for Art and Politics in recognition of her influential contributions to socially engaged artistic practice. Living and working in Berlin, Alves continues to create projects that challenge dominant historical narratives while advocating for environmental awareness, Indigenous rights, and social justice.

Jimmie Durham (1940-2021) was an American sculptor, essayist, and poet whose work combined visual art, political activism, and critical writing. During the 1960s and 1970s, he was active in the civil rights movements of African Americans and Native Americans and served on the Central Council of the American Indian Movement. After studying and working in Europe, including a period in Geneva, he returned to the United States in 1973 and became involved with the International Indian Treaty Council, advocating for Indigenous rights at an international level. In the early 1980s, after moving to New York City, he focused increasingly on visual art, creating sculptures and installations that challenged conventional historical and cultural narratives. His work often explored themes of identity, language, colonialism, architecture, monumentality, and power. After living in Mexico during the late 1980s and early 1990s, he relocated to Europe, where he settled first in Berlin and later in Naples. Throughout his career, he exhibited internationally at major institutions and events including the Whitney Biennial, Documenta, the Venice Biennale, and the Gwangju Biennale. He received numerous awards, including the Gunther Peill Prize in 2003, the Robert Rauschenberg Award in 2017, and the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale in 2019. His multidisciplinary practice, spanning sculpture, performance, video, poetry, and essays, established him as a significant figure in contemporary art.

Angéle Etoundi Essamba (born 1962 in Douala, Cameroon) is a Cameroonian photographer who lives and works in Amsterdam. Best known for her black-and-white photography, she focuses primarily on representations of African women, challenging gender stereotypes and giving visibility and voice to her subjects. Raised in Yaounde within a large extended family, she moved to Paris as a child and later settled in the Netherlands, where she studied photography at the Dutch School for Professional Photography. Her artistic practice is shaped by her experiences in both Africa and Europe and combines personal history, cultural identity, and social awareness. Through her photographs, she explores questions of femininity, dignity, self-representation, and intercultural dialogue. Her first exhibition took place in Amsterdam in 1985, and since then her work has been presented in more than 200 exhibitions worldwide. In 1996, her series White Line received the Prix Special Afrique at the Festival des Trois Continents in Nantes. She has participated in major international events including the Havana Biennial, the Venice Biennale, and the Johannesburg Biennale. In 2009, she founded Essamba Home, an organization dedicated to mentoring and supporting vulnerable girls in Cameroon. Her work continues to be exhibited internationally, including major monographic exhibitions such as Daughters of a Life at the Museum Funf Kontinente in Munich in 2018.

Gracia Barrios Rivadeneira (1927-2020) was a Chilean painter and recipient of the 2011 National Prize for Plastic Arts. The daughter of writer Eduardo Barrios and pianist Carmen Rivadeneira, she developed an early interest in art and studied at the School of Fine Arts of the University of Chile between 1944 and 1949. She later taught at the same institution from 1953 until 1973, contributing to the education of a new generation of artists. During the 1960s, she became a member of Grupo Signo, an influential collective that challenged traditional post-impressionist painting and promoted new artistic approaches. Following the 1973 Chilean coup d'etat, Barrios went into exile in France with her family, remaining abroad for nearly a decade before returning to Chile. Her work evolved from figurative painting toward what she described as 'informal realism', focusing on human experience through monumental forms and expressive compositions. Themes such as war, poverty, exile, and the human condition were central to her artistic practice. In addition to oil and acrylic paint, she experimented with materials such as earth and clay to enrich the physical presence of her works. Her paintings were exhibited internationally and are held in collections in Chile and Europe. In 2011, she received Chile's National Prize for Plastic Arts in recognition of a career dedicated to exploring the relationship between individuals and their historical and existential realities.

Carolina Bassi Acuna, known as Carolina Bassi (1966-1997), was a Chilean artist born in Santiago, Chile. Her artistic career developed during the final decades of the twentieth century, and she is recognized as part of the contemporary Chilean art scene of her generation. Although her life was cut short in 1997, her work remains associated with the cultural and artistic developments that emerged in Chile during a period of significant social and political transformation. Her practice contributed to the visibility of contemporary Chilean artistic expression and reflects the creative concerns of her time.

Marta Colvin Andrade (1907-1995) was a Chilean sculptor born in Chillan, Chile. Following the devastating Chillan earthquake of 1939, she moved to Santiago, where she studied at the School of Arts and began a distinguished artistic career. In 1943, she became an assistant professor in the sculpture workshop led by Julio A. Vasquez and Lorenzo Dominguez, and in 1950 she was appointed professor. Seeking further artistic development, she studied at the Academie de la Grande Chaumiere in Paris in 1948 under renowned sculptors Ossian Zadkine and Henry Laurens. She subsequently lived in France for more than thirty years, expanding her international presence and artistic practice. Colvin gained worldwide recognition for her monumental sculptural work and her distinctive approach to form and abstraction. In 1965, she participated in the first Sao Paulo Biennale, further establishing her international reputation. Her contributions to art were honored with Chile's National Art Prize in 1970. Throughout her career, she became one of the most important figures in modern Chilean sculpture. She died in Santiago in 1995.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Saint-Ouen (Seine-Saint-Denis, France) since 1964
Biography: Irene Dominguez is a Chilean artist who studied art at the Catholic University and the University of Chile in Santiago between 1954 and 1961. In 1957, she received a scholarship for advanced studies in ceramics in Madrid, Spain. After arriving in Paris in 1964, she met influential figures including Wilfredo Lam, Lou Laurin, Ghérasim Luca, and Micheline Catty, who helped introduce her to the Parisian artistic milieu. From 1976 to 1980, she was a resident at the Cite des Arts in Paris, where she eventually settled and continues to live. Throughout her career, she has exhibited extensively across Europe and Latin America, presenting solo and group exhibitions in France, Chile, Italy, Sweden, Denmark, Switzerland, Germany, Argentina, and Cuba. Her exhibitions have been held at institutions and galleries including the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes in Santiago, the Chilean Embassy in Paris, the UNESCO headquarters, the Institut Cervantes in Paris, and numerous galleries in Santiago, Paris, Vina del Mar, Concepcion, and elsewhere. She has collaborated and exhibited with artists such as Lou Laurin Lam, Pilar Dominguez, and Guy de Gontaut. In 2003, she received the First Prize at the Salon Saint Ouen in Paris. Her long international career reflects a sustained engagement with painting, ceramics, printmaking, and cultural exchange between Chile and Europe.

Paz Errazuriz (born 1944 in Santiago, Chile) is a Chilean photographer known for documenting marginalized communities, including sex workers, psychiatric patients, circus performers, and others living outside the center of social power. She began her photographic practice during the military dictatorship in Chile while working as a primary school teacher, using photography as a way to reveal realities often ignored by society. Her work focuses on individuals and groups who have historically been excluded, subordinated, or rendered invisible. In 1981, she co-founded the Association of Independent Photographers (AFI), an organization created to support artists, provide legal assistance, and facilitate collective exhibitions during a politically repressive period. Alongside her photographic projects, she collaborated with the magazine Apsi and various press agencies. Throughout her career, she has used photography as a tool for social observation and human engagement, emphasizing the dignity and presence of people living on the margins. Her images challenge viewers to confront subjects that are often overlooked and to reconsider dominant social narratives. She remains one of the most important figures in contemporary Chilean photography.

Emma Malig (born 1960 in Santiago, Chile) is a Chilean painter, printmaker, and visual artist who has lived and worked in Paris since 1993. She began studying at the School of Art of the University of Chile in 1979 but left in 1981 to travel through Europe, eventually settling in Paris where she attended open workshops at the Ecole Nationale Superieure des Beaux Arts and later became a regular student under the guidance of Vladimir Velickovic. She received a scholarship from the Paris School of Fine Arts to specialize in lithography at the Kunstlerhaus Bethanien in Berlin and later spent five years in Kyoto, Japan, where she exhibited her work and studied traditional Japanese paper-making and painting techniques. Throughout her career, she has received numerous distinctions, including the First Prize of the Fondation Cegedim in France in 1994, the First Prize at the Salon d'Art Contemporain of the Museum of Natural History in Paris in 2001, and the Prix Coffin pour l'Art Contemporain in 2002. Her work has been featured in solo exhibitions across France, Chile, Japan, South Korea, and Italy, including presentations at the Museo de Arte Contemporaneo and the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes in Santiago. In 2005, filmmaker Patricio Guzman invited her to contribute her work to the film Salvador Allende. Her artworks are held in public and private collections in Chile, France, Belgium, Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom, including the Fonds National d'Art Contemporain and the Musee d'Art Moderne de Paris. Her practice reflects an international trajectory shaped by experiences in Europe, Latin America, and Asia.

Juana Muller (1911-1952) was a Chilean sculptor born in Santiago to German immigrant parents. She studied sculpture between 1930 and 1933 at the School of Fine Arts of Santiago under Julio Antonio Vasquez and Lorenzo Dominguez. In 1937, she received a scholarship that enabled her to move to Paris, where she joined the studio of Ossip Zadkine at the Academie de la Grande Chaumiere and attended the Academie Ranson. During this period, she met the painter Jean Le Moal, whom she later married in 1944. In 1939, she encountered Constantin Brancusi and subsequently worked in his studio on the Impasse Ronsin, becoming closely connected to the Parisian avant-garde. Muller also played an important role in introducing fellow Chilean sculptors to artistic circles in Paris, notably Lily Garafulic. After World War II, her work evolved from figurative sculpture toward abstraction, and she became associated with the New School of Paris. Her sculptures were exhibited at prominent venues including Galerie Jeanne Bucher, the Salon de Mai, and the Salon de la Jeune Sculpture. In 1952, she participated in a group exhibition at Galerie MAI alongside Etienne Martin, Francois Stahly, and Marie-Therese Pinto. She died in Paris in 1952 at the age of 41.

Rocio Olivares (born 1990 in Santiago, Chile) is a multidisciplinary artist whose practice examines the unequal distribution of power, information, and resources within the context of globalization. She earned her BFA from the Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Chile and later completed an MFA at Columbia University in New York. Through her work, she investigates systems of political, economic, and cultural control, exploring how global structures shape contemporary life. Her projects have been exhibited internationally at institutions and venues including The Drawing Center, the Museum of the Moving Image, The Jewish Museum, Sean Kelly Gallery, and the Elizabeth Foundation for the Arts in New York, as well as MuseumsQuartier in Vienna and Dilalica in Barcelona. In Chile, her work has been presented at the Museo de Artes Visuales, the Museo de Arte Contemporaneo, and Galeria Bicentenario. Olivares was a resident at the Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture in 2018 and participated in the Whitney Independent Study Program from 2018 to 2019. She is the recipient of the Fulbright Scholarship and the Becas Chile Scholarship. She currently lives and works in Santiago, Chile.

Marie-Therese Pinto (1894-1980) was a Chilean sculptor who developed an international career between Europe and Latin America. Born in Santiago into the prominent Pinto family, she spent part of her childhood in Germany while her father served as Chilean ambassador and later continued her artistic formation in Italy under the guidance of sculptor Rebeca Matte Bello. She began her sculptural career in Italy before settling in Paris in 1934, where she studied with Constantin Brancusi and Henri Laurens and exhibited at the Salon des Tuileries. In 1940, she moved to Mexico with her husband Gilbert Medioni, becoming part of the Surrealist exile community and incorporating influences from Surrealism and Pre-Columbian art into her work. Together with Medioni, she published Art in Ancient Mexico in 1941, a book that introduced Diego Rivera's collection of Pre-Columbian sculptures and influenced a generation of Chilean sculptors. After returning to Paris following World War II, she joined the New School of Paris and exhibited regularly in France and internationally. Between 1950 and 1960, she participated in the Salon de la Jeune Sculpture and, in 1951, was selected to represent France at the first Sao Paulo Art Biennial. Her sculptures were later exhibited at the Chilean National Museum of Fine Arts and at Galerie MAI in Paris alongside prominent modern sculptors including Juana Muller. Throughout her career, Pinto maintained strong artistic connections between Europe and Latin America, contributing to the development of modern sculpture in both regions. She died in Paris in 1980.

Lotty Rosenfeld (1943-2020) was a Chilean interdisciplinary artist whose work emerged during the period of the Chilean military dictatorship and became a powerful form of political and social resistance. Associated with the neo-avant-garde movement Escena de Avanzada, she used performance, video, and public interventions to question systems of power, authority, and control. In 1979, together with Raul Zurita, Diamela Eltit, Fernando Balcells, and Juan Castillo, she co-founded CADA (Colectivo de Acciones de Arte), a collective that challenged the Pinochet regime through artistic actions in public space. Rejecting traditional art institutions and the commercial art market, Rosenfeld turned the streets into sites of critical engagement and political reflection. She is best known for her iconic intervention Una Milla de Cruces sobre el Pavimento (A Mile of Crosses on the Pavement), first realized in Santiago in 1979, in which she transformed road markings into crosses using white tape. By altering traffic lines, she disrupted everyday visual codes and symbolically challenged the mechanisms of social control imposed by the dictatorship. Her work explored how political power shapes public space and marginalizes individuals, while opening possibilities for collective resistance and alternative meanings. Rosenfeld's performances, video installations, and multimedia projects were exhibited throughout Latin America and internationally in Europe, Japan, and Australia. She remains one of the most influential figures in contemporary Chilean art and political performance.

Carolina Andrea Saquel Martínez was born in Concepción (Chile) in 1970. She earned a Bachelor’s degree in Arts from the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile and a Master’s degree in Arts from the University of Paris VII. From 2000 to 2003, she was professor instructor of the course on Methodology of Research, School of Arts, Universidad Católica of Santiago, Chile. Her artistic practice deals mostly with installations, graphic art, photography and, above all, video. She participated in several solo and group shows, including various editions of the Video and Electronic Art Biennial held at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Santiago, Chile (1999, 2001, 2003 e 2007); Handle with care at the MAC in Santiago (2007); La catástrofe es amarilla (Catastrophe is Yellow) at Espai 13 of the Fundació Joan Mirò, Barcelona (2007).

Vivian Scheihing is a Chilean artist who studied Fine Arts at the University of Chile in Santiago before earning an MA in Fine Art (Painting) from the Royal College of Art in London. Between 1971 and 1973, she worked as an assistant at the School of Fine Arts of the University of Chile under Jose Balmes and Francisco Brugnoli. Since the 1970s, she has developed an international career marked by exhibitions, murals, artist books, and collaborations across Europe and the Americas. Her work has been presented in numerous solo exhibitions in Chile, France, Germany, Sweden, Tunisia, Switzerland, Canada, Norway, and the United States, including exhibitions at the National Museum of Fine Arts in Santiago, the Instituto Cervantes in Bremen, and the Maison de l'Amerique Latine in Paris. She has also participated in major mural projects in Chile, France, and the United Kingdom and has completed artist residencies at the Cite Internationale des Arts and Confluences in Paris. Scheihing has received several distinctions, including the John Milton Scholarship, the Balford Foundation Award, the Amstruther Award, and the Industrial Award in the United Kingdom. In recent years, she has expanded her practice through the creation of limited-edition artist books inspired by literary works and poetry. Her artworks are held in important public and private collections, including the Arts Council Collection and Hayward Gallery in London, the Fonds National d'Art Contemporain in France, the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes and Museo de Arte Contemporaneo in Chile, Stanford University, and the Bibliotheque Nationale de France. She continues to live and work internationally, maintaining a practice that connects painting, printmaking, publishing, and literary collaboration.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Berlin (Germany) and in New York (New York, United States)
Biography: Johanna Unzueta (born 1974 in Chile) is a Chilean artist whose practice moves fluidly between drawing, sculpture, and installation, challenging conventional distinctions between two- and three-dimensional forms. Working with found objects, natural materials, and pigments derived from plants and vegetables, she creates works that are deeply connected to the environment while evoking a reflective and dreamlike dimension. Her art is characterized by carefully crafted woven surfaces that emphasize both the labor involved in their making and the fragility of materials subject to transformation over time. Through an approach that combines precision, craftsmanship, and experimentation, Unzueta explores themes of memory, time, materiality, and human connection to the natural world. Born in Chile, she moved to New York in 2000 and later established her practice in Berlin. Her work has been acquired by major international institutions, including the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York and Tate in London. In 2020, significant presentations of her work were organized at Modern Art Oxford and Talbot Rice Gallery in Edinburgh. Unzueta continues to develop a body of work that links contemporary concerns with historical traditions of making, creating objects that connect the present to the past through beauty, care, and material exploration.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in New York (New York, United States)
Biography: Cecilia Vicuna (born 1948 in Santiago, Chile) is a Chilean poet, visual artist, performer, and activist whose work explores themes of language, memory, exile, ecological destruction, feminism, and Indigenous knowledge. She studied fine arts at the University of Chile, where she received her MFA in 1971, and later continued her education at the Slade School of Fine Art in London with a British Council Award. Following the 1973 military coup in Chile, she remained in exile in London, where she became deeply involved in political activism and co-founded Artists for Democracy. In 1967, she founded Tribu No, an experimental collective that developed artistic actions and performances in Chile. Her multidisciplinary practice is especially known for quipus, precarios, palabrarmas, and works made from fragile natural materials that connect art, ecology, spirituality, and feminist thought. After periods in London and Bogota, where she researched Indigenous cultures and created stage designs, she settled in New York while maintaining strong ties to Chile. Over several decades, her work has been exhibited internationally at institutions including MoMA, the Guggenheim Museum, Tate Modern, and Documenta. In 2019, she received the Premio Velazquez de Artes Plasticas, Spain's highest visual arts award, recognizing her achievements as an artist, poet, and activist. She is also the author of more than twenty books of poetry and visual art, translated into numerous languages. Today, Vicuna is regarded as one of the most influential Latin American artists of her generation, known for connecting art, environmental awareness, social justice, and ancestral knowledge.

Ingrid Wildi Merino (born 1963 in Santiago, Chile) is a Chilean-born Swiss video artist, curator, and educator whose work explores themes of migration, identity, memory, language, and cultural exchange. Born to a Swiss father and a Chilean mother, she moved to Switzerland in 1981, settling in the Canton of Aargau. Between 1994 and 1997, she studied at the Zurich University of the Arts and later completed a postgraduate diploma at the Ecole Superieure des Beaux-Arts in Geneva, where she studied under Sylvie Defraoui, Dominique Gonzalez-Foerster, and Ursula Biemann. Alongside her artistic practice, she taught at the Geneva University of Art and Design from 2005 to 2016 and at the University of Alcala in Spain. Her work has been exhibited internationally, beginning with solo exhibitions at the Aargauer Kunsthaus and the Centre d'Art Contemporain Geneve in 2004. In 2005, she represented Switzerland in the Swiss Artists Pavilion at the 51st Venice Biennale, and in 2009 she participated in the 7th Mercosul Biennial in Porto Alegre, Brazil. Her artworks are included in important public collections such as the Aargauer Kunsthaus, Kunsthaus Zurich, and the Fonds Municipal d'Art Contemporain de la Ville de Geneve. She received the Manor Cultural Prize for the Canton of Aargau in 2004 and the prestigious Prix Meret Oppenheim in 2009. Wildi Merino currently lives and works in Santiago, Chile.

Lorena Zilleruelo (born 1974 in Chile) is a Chilean artist who has lived in France since the age of eighteen and is currently based in Paris. She studied scenography and theatrical costume design before continuing her artistic education at the Ecoles des Beaux-Arts of Grenoble and Paris-Cergy. Her multidisciplinary practice encompasses video, installation, and other contemporary forms of expression, often exploring themes of memory, migration, identity, and collective history. Through her work, she investigates personal and cultural narratives, creating projects that connect individual experiences with broader social and historical contexts. Her recent exhibitions and screenings include Jeu d'images: Infinies Resistances at the Cinema Etoile in La Courneuve in 2009, Perdu/Gagne at the Festival Photos & Legendes in Paris in 2008, and Home? Figures de Migrations at the Galerie Villa des Tourelles in Nanterre. In 2007, she presented Memoria de los libros, exhumacion de una historia at the Consejo Nacional de la Cultura y las Artes in Valparaiso and at Galeria Concreta, Matucana 100 in Santiago, Chile. Her work reflects an ongoing interest in displacement, remembrance, and the ways stories are preserved and transmitted across generations and territories.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Beijing (China) and in Guangzhou (China)
Biography: Cao Fei, born 1978 in Guangzhou province living in Beijing, was a wanderer between the worlds, while her father had the privilege earlier when she was young to work in Hong Kong. This confronts and influenced her withe Western pop-culture. Today Cao Fei is renowned as one of the most popular and influential Chinese artists. She is the face of the new generation of artists. 2016 she exhibited at MoMA PS1 New York, at Secession Vienna 2015, at Contemporary Art Center of South Australis 2014, at Tate Modern Londond 2013, at Surrey Art Gallery Vancouver 2012, at The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art Kansas City 2011, Institute of Modern Art Brisbane 2009. 2010 she was finalist for the Hugo Boss Prize at Guggenheim Foundation New York.

Chen Lingyang was born in Zhejiang Province in 1975, and she studied in the Affliated High School of China Academy of Art, Hangzhou, and Central Academy of Fine Arts, Beijing. She now lives in Beijing. Chen Lingyang mainly works with installation and photography, and her works usually explore the beauty of female bodies and their intrinsic meanings. In one of her major photography works, “Twelve Flower Months”, what audience see through the traditional Chinese mirrors are no longer the 'beautiful' faces and bodies we are accustomed to, but the female sex organs in menstruation. The traditional poetic Chinese concept of twelve flower months provides a metaphor for the female physiological truth of menstruation through the twelve months of the year. With the traditional Chinese forms of ancient mirrors and garden windows, gentle and sober disposal of light and color around the sexual organs, directness of menstrual blood and stimulation, Chen Lingyang breaks the tradition in a seemingly traditional way and destroys the 'femininity' with a seemingly 'feminine' approach. The direct selection of the female topic, the attention to both 'truth' and 'beauty' of female bodies, and the utilization of Chinese traditions and feminine form are all skillfully and consciously presented.

Cui Xiuwen (1967-2018) was a Chinese contemporary artist known for her work in painting, photography, and video, exploring themes of identity, femininity, social norms, and the role of women in contemporary China. Born in Harbin, she studied at the Fine Arts School of Northeast Normal University before earning a Master of Fine Arts from the Central Academy of Fine Arts in Beijing in 1996. Throughout her career, she developed a multidisciplinary practice that combined traditional Chinese visual references with contemporary conceptual approaches. She gained international recognition with works such as Ladies' Room (2000), a video installation that documented the private experiences of women in a Beijing karaoke club and was later censored from the first Guangzhou Triennial. Her celebrated photographic series Existential Emptiness explored adolescence, loneliness, and mortality through images of a schoolgirl and her life-sized doll in vast landscapes. In works such as the Angel series and One Day in 2004, she addressed issues of female representation, sexuality, social expectations, and cultural memory. Cui frequently incorporated motifs inspired by traditional Chinese scroll painting while questioning contemporary realities through staged and digitally manipulated imagery. Her work was exhibited internationally at institutions including Tate Modern, Centre Pompidou, MoMA PS1, Today Art Museum, and the National Museum of China. She received numerous awards and became one of the most influential female artists of her generation in China. Her works are held in major collections including Tate Modern and the Brooklyn Museum.

Fan Tchunpi (1898-1986), also known as Fang Junbi, was a pioneering Chinese artist who combined traditional Chinese brush-and-ink painting with Western artistic techniques. Born into a wealthy family in Fuzhou, she moved to France in 1912 and studied at the Académie Julian and the École des Beaux-Arts in Bordeaux, graduating in 1920. She became the first Chinese woman admitted to exhibit at the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts and the first Chinese female artist to participate in the Salon Société des Artistes Françaises. After returning to China, she became associated with the Lingnan School, contributing to the renewal of Chinese painting through the integration of Western perspective, light, and naturalism. Influenced by French Impressionism and artists such as Paul-Albert Besnard, her work balanced European formal innovations with Chinese cultural traditions. She published books on her painting and worked closely with the renowned painter Qi Baishi between 1943 and 1949. Following the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949, she went into exile, living in Paris, later Boston, and finally Geneva, where she spent her last years. Her career was marked by international recognition and numerous exhibitions. Today she is regarded as one of the most important and prolific Chinese artists of the twentieth century.

Hao Jingban (born 1985 in Taiyuan, China) is a video artist who lives and works in Beijing. Her practice combines documentary observation and staged reconstruction, focusing on contemporary Chinese society. She is particularly interested in Beijing's dance halls, which she views as revealing sites of the social transformations associated with the emergence of the People's Republic of China. Through slow, often static and long-duration shots, she documents these spaces and the people who inhabit them. Her works combine close-up interviews, recordings of spontaneous situations, and reconstructed scenes that reproduce the visual codes of dance halls. By moving between observation and fiction, she explores social and cultural change through narratives shaped by memory, performance, and everyday life.

Kan Xuan was born in 1972 in Xuan Cheng, Anhui Province, China. Lives and works in Beijing and Amsterdam. Kan Xuan's video and installation works often incorporate static objects and enduring landscapes. She is interested in exploring the relationship between individuals' subjectivity and the external world, how these relationships form and dissolve, and if art making can provide ways to make new ones. Simple yet incisive, intelligent yet sensorial, her artistic language seeks the tension and balance between narratives and poetics. Kan applies a sincere and inquisitive self to her practice, whether by examining the prosaic details of quotidian life or engaging complex historical topics, she spends long periods of time with her subjects, an approach that lends her work a unique and focused tempo against the ever-accelerating, overwhelming rush of contemporary life.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in London (United Kingdom)
Biography: Firenze Lai (born 1984 in Hong Kong) is a painter who lives and works in London. Her work explores the social, political, and spatial conditions that shape individual and collective consciousness, often focusing on the relationship between internal and external realities. Through anonymous figures and ambiguous settings, she examines themes of identity, human behavior, movement through space, and self-awareness. Growing up in Hong Kong's dense urban environment strongly influenced her interest in physical and psychological space. After studying at the Hong Kong Art School from 2004 to 2006, she worked while painting at night and began painting full-time in 2011. Her paintings often depict solitary figures or groups as metaphors for broader social and psychological conditions, emphasizing the tension between individuality and collectivity. Using a restrained palette and expressive brushwork, she creates dreamlike scenes that blur the boundaries between reality, memory, and the unconscious. More recent works also address displacement, digital culture, and the search for orientation in a rapidly changing world. Her work has been exhibited internationally, including at M+, Centre Pompidou, Ikon Gallery, the 57th Venice Biennale, and the New Museum.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Fontainebleau (Seine-et-Marne, France) since 2024
Biography: Li Shuang (born 1957 in Beijing, China) is a contemporary Chinese artist whose work reflects her personal and artistic journey shaped by the Cultural Revolution. Raised in a family of intellectuals, she was strongly influenced by her grandfather, a dealer in antiques, books, and artworks. During the Cultural Revolution, her family suffered persecution, and her father was arrested, an experience that deeply affected her and inspired her commitment to drawing. After graduating from high school in 1976, she was sent to the rural outskirts of Beijing, where she worked in agriculture for three years while continuing to practice art. Due to her family background, she was unable to attend a professional art school despite her ambitions. Her artistic talent was later recognized, leading to her acceptance into the China National Youth Theater as a stage designer. She became known for her contributions to the institution and later gained international recognition. During China's period of reform and opening up, her name became widely known in France and other European countries. Her life and work are often associated with the 'Li Shuang Incident', which was regarded by Western observers as an important moment in the emergence of contemporary Chinese artistic expression.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Rouen (Seine-Maritime, France) since 2017
Biography: Li Xia, also known as Lilou Oh Yeah (born 1991 in Chongqing, China), is an artist and illustrator based in Rouen, France. Working primarily in oil painting and watercolor, her practice explores ephemeral moments and everyday objects through carefully composed planes of flat color and subtle brushwork. Her works combine representational and imaginary spaces, reflecting a sensitive attention to ordinary and fleeting aspects of daily life. She studied at Sichuan Fine Arts Institute (BFA, 2014), ESADHaR in Le Havre-Rouen (MFA, 2020), and Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne (MFA, 2021). Li has exhibited internationally at institutions and galleries including the LONG Museum, Minsheng Art Museum, and Bananafish Gallery in Shanghai, Yi Gallery in New York, Kate MacGarry Gallery in London, Villa des Arts in Paris, and Rola Bola in Rouen. She lives and works in Rouen, France.

Pan Yuliang (1895-1977), born Chen Xiuqing and also known as Zhang Yuliang, was one of the first Chinese women to receive formal training in oil painting and life drawing and is regarded as a pioneer of modern Chinese art. She studied in Shanghai, Lyon, Paris, and Rome, and later taught at the École des Beaux Arts. Her work developed a distinctive style that combined European modernist techniques with traditional Chinese pictorial sensibilities. Pan is remembered as the first woman in China to paint in a Western style and as an artist who explored the tensions between East and West, tradition and modernity, and gender expectations. She frequently depicted the female nude, an unusual and controversial subject at the time, using it to present women as active subjects rather than passive objects. Her work challenged the male-dominated art world and has been interpreted as an assertion of female agency and subjectivity. Pan exhibited internationally across Europe, the United States, and Japan, receiving several awards throughout her career. After her death, a large part of her oeuvre was transferred to China and is now held by the National Art Museum of China in Beijing and the Anhui Museum in Hefei. Her paintings, sculptures, and prints are also preserved in the collection of the Musée Cernuschi in Paris.

Ma Qiusha was born in 1982 in Beijing, China. She received her BA in Digital Media Art from the Central Academy of Fine Arts (China) in 2005 and her MFA in Electronic Integrated Arts from Alfred University (U.S.) in 2008. She currently lives and works in Beijing. Ma employs multiple media such as photography, video, installation, and drawing to explore the life experience under sociocultural transformations. Often in an intimate visual language, her work addresses the themes between individuals and the collective, and private spaces and public spheres. Drawing on an anthropological perspective, her research on individuals, families, and intergenerational relationships raises questions of appearance and disappearance, and of the truth or mistruth of history.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Vanves (Hauts-de-Seine, France)
Biography: Zhen Shi is a Chinese visual artist who lives and works between Paris and Beijing. Her practice includes photography, artist’s books, and video. Her work has been presented in exhibitions and festivals in China and France, including the Lianzhou Foto Festival, Guangdong, China (2015), Art Book in China – abc/f Art Book Fair, Shanghai, China (2016), and Les Rencontres d’Arles, France (2016).
