Artist: SONG HUAI-KUEI known as MADAME SONG
Biography: Song Huai-Kuei (1937-2006), also known as Madame Song, was a Chinese artist, actor, fashion icon, socialite, and businesswoman. She studied at the Central Academy of Fine Arts in Beijing, where she met Bulgarian tapestry artist Marin Varbanov, whom she married in 1956 in what was considered the first mixed marriage in the People's Republic of China. In 1959, the couple moved to Sofia, Bulgaria, where they worked as artists. Song met fashion designer Pierre Cardin in Paris in 1979 and later became his representative in Beijing, helping introduce international fashion and lifestyle culture to China during the 1980s. She returned to Beijing in 1980 to work full-time for Cardin and played a key role in opening Maxim's de Paris restaurant in the city, serving as its manager for two decades. In 1987, she appeared in the film The Last Emperor, portraying the mother of Pu Yi. She had two children, Boryana and Phénix Varbanov.

Evelyn Taocheng Wang (born 1981 in Chengdu, China) is a Chinese contemporary artist whose practice spans painting, performance, calligraphy, and fashion. She studied Chinese classical literature, calligraphy, and landscape painting at Nanjing Normal University after an early education that included Soviet Realism, the Russian avant-garde, and European modernism. In 2007, she moved to Germany for an artist residency and later studied at Städelschule under Willem de Rooij before completing a residency at De Ateliers in Amsterdam. Since 2012, she has lived in the Netherlands. Wang’s work explores how language, custom, and culture shape identity, often addressing themes of immigration, belonging, gender, class, and self-representation. Her practice also draws on literary references, including feminist authors, and frequently combines Chinese artistic traditions with contemporary approaches. In 2024, she presented the series Do Not Agree with Agnes Martin All the Time at the 60th Venice Biennale, reinterpreting motifs associated with Agnes Martin alongside elements of classical Chinese painting. In 2025, she received the Wolfgang Hahn Prize and presented new works at Museum Ludwig inspired by Martin’s geometric paintings.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Bastia (Haute-Corse, France) and in Paris (France)
Biography: Yuyan Wang (born 1989 in Qingdao, China) is a Chinese artist working across video, performance, and installation. She studied at the China Academy of Art, graduating in 2012, and later at the École des Beaux-Arts de Paris, where she graduated in 2016 with jury honors. She also studied at Le Fresnoy – Studio National des Arts Contemporains. Her multimedia projects often take immersive forms and draw inspiration from horror films, wellness culture, self-help pseudo-sciences, and everyday life. Through subtle shifts of existing forms, Wang examines contemporary systems that seek to produce optimistic states, using processes of abstraction to deconstruct and reconsider them. She lives and works between France and China.

Xiao Zhuang (1932-2026), born Zhuang Dongying, was a Chinese photographer and photo editor known for documenting everyday life in China between the 1950s and 1970s. She began her career in 1950 as a photographer for the Lu Shui Newspaper of the People's Liberation Army and became a photojournalist for Xinhua News Daily in 1952. From 1980, she served as chief editor of the photography department at Jiangsu Publishing Company and worked for Light and Photography magazine. After retiring in 1994, she became a consultant to the Chinese Photographers Association of Jiangsu Province. Her photographs are considered important visual records of Mao-era China and valuable resources for Chinese studies. Xiao participated in major exhibitions including Photography from China 1934-2008 in Houston (2008), Historical Retrospective Part I at 798 Photo Gallery (2011), and Grain to Pixel: A Story of Photography in China (2015). She also published photographic books, including The Red Albums: Photographic Notes of Xiao Zhuang, which gathers images made between the 1950s and 1970s. She died on 4 January 2026.

Xing Danwen (born 1967 in Xi'an, China) is a Chinese contemporary artist and photographer whose practice includes photography, video, mixed media, and installation. She studied painting at the Xi'an Academy of Fine Arts and later earned a BFA in oil painting from the Central Academy of Fine Arts in Beijing. In the late 1980s, she turned to photography and became one of the few Chinese artists of her generation to use the medium as a form of contemporary art. During the early 1990s, she documented the Beijing East Village performance art movement. In 1998, she moved to New York with support from the Asian Cultural Council and completed an MFA at the School of Visual Arts between 1998 and 2001. Her work explores themes of cultural dislocation, globalization, tradition, environmental issues, urban development, and the relationship between fiction and reality. Notable projects include disConnexion (2002-2003), a series examining electronic waste exported from the United States to China, Urban Fiction (from 2004), which combines architectural models with staged domestic scenes, and Wall House (2007), focused on Beijing's urban transformation. Her work has been exhibited internationally, including at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and Harvard University.

Yang Guangnan (b. 1980, Hebei, China) graduated from the Sculpture Department of the China Academy of Art with B.A in 2006, and the Sculpture Department of Central Academy of Fine Arts with M.A in 2009. She currently lives and works in Beijing. Taking the traditional language of sculpture as her starting point, Yang Guangnan gradually expands her artistic medium to installation and video. She investigates and elaborates upon personal experience in the everyday life, developing artworks that are charged with an emotional strength. Actively dealing with an individual’ s living condition, identity, affects and temporal experience, the artworks are seemingly spontaneous and casual; also present and pervading in the artworks however, is a distinct, delicate, sharp, unyielding and resilient consciousness, that renders Yang’ s practice utterly and patently singular.

Yao Qingmei (also known as Qingmei Yao, born 1982 in Zhejiang, China) is an artist based in Paris whose practice centers on performance, video, and installation. Her work incorporates scenography, costumes, texts, lectures, games, sound poetry, and contemporary choreography. By intervening in specific spaces, she challenges established rules, explores symbols of everyday life, and examines how bodies gain or lose power within social and cultural frameworks. Through displacement, metaphor, and allegory, her projects address political and social issues, combining critical inquiry with elements of humor and lightness. She studied at the École Nationale Supérieure d'Art de Limoges and graduated in 2013 from the École Nationale Supérieure d’Art de Villa Arson in Nice with a DNSEP degree in Fine Arts. Yao received the Jury Special Award at the Salon de Montrouge in 2014, the inaugural Porsche Young Chinese Artist of the Year Award in 2017, the Jeune Création Prize in Paris in 2018, and the Asian Cultural Council New York Fellowship in 2022. Her work has been presented at institutions including Palais de Tokyo, West Bund Museum, Centre Pompidou, Whitechapel Gallery, Haus der Kunst, the Shanghai Biennale, UCCA Beijing, and Para Site Hong Kong. Her works are held in collections such as the Centre Pompidou Collection, the Fonds Municipal d'Art Contemporain de la Ville de Paris, the Guangdong Museum of Art, Taikang Space, and Kadist Art Foundation.

Shen Yuan (born 1959 in Xianyou, Fujian, China) is a Chinese-born French artist. She graduated from the China Academy of Art in 1982 and became associated with the Xiamen Dada group, an experimental collective known for its radical avant-garde practices in southern China. Following the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests, she moved to Paris with her husband, artist Huang Yong Ping. Shen Yuan’s work often reflects on Chinese cultural and political realities, with a particular focus on feminism, gender roles, labor, social inequality, and conflict. Her artistic practice frequently involves site-specific research and collaboration with local communities, including children and workers. She has participated in numerous international exhibitions, including Art and China after 1989: Theater of the World at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum and Hong Kong Foot at Tang Contemporary Art in Hong Kong. She lives and works in Paris, France.

Yi Zhou (born 1978 in Shanghai, China) is a Chinese film director, writer, producer, and multimedia artist. At the age of nine, she moved to Rome and later studied at the American University of Paris and the London School of Economics. She began her artistic career in Paris, where her first major exhibition was presented at the Jérôme de Noirmont Gallery in 2002. Her work combines film, video, sculpture, animation, and multimedia installations. Notable projects include Paradise, installed in Florence in 2006, and a public art commission for Place Vendôme in Paris in 2008. In 2010, she returned to China and founded YiZhouStudio in Shanghai and Hong Kong. Her work has been exhibited internationally, including a solo presentation at the 54th Venice Biennale in 2011 and exhibitions in Beijing, Vladivostok, Paris, and Rome. Alongside her artistic practice, she has collaborated with fashion and luxury brands and developed projects across film, design, and digital media. In 2024, she released her first documentary feature film, In Between Stars and Scars: Masters of Cinema. She is also involved in philanthropic initiatives in collaboration with international organizations, including the United Nations.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Taïpei (Chine (Taiwan)) and in Paris (France)
Biography: Charwei Tsai (born 1980 in Taipei, Taiwan) is a Taiwanese multidisciplinary artist who lives and works in Taipei. She attended Taipei American School in Taipei and Stevenson School in Pebble Beach, California. She graduated from Rhode Island School of Design in 2002 with a degree in Industrial Design and completed a postgraduate research program at the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris in 2010. In 2002, she moved to New York City, where she worked part-time at Printed Matter and volunteered at Tibet House. From 2004 to 2006, she worked as an assistant in Chinese artist Cai Guo-Qiang's studio in New York. She was also influenced by the earthworks series of artist Robert Smithson. Tsai has worked as an artist in Taipei, Paris, and Ho Chi Minh City. In 2005, she founded the art journal Lovely Daze. Her work has been widely exhibited in international museums, galleries, biennials, and art fairs.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Taïpei (Chine (Taiwan)) and in Tokyo (Japon)
Biography: Wang Yahui (1973 - 2023) born in Taipei and held a master`s degree in arts and technology from the Taipei National University of the Arts in 2004. She works across mediums, from video to installation, photography to painting. Using mediums of image, her practice centers on the peripheral vision of the viewer, and the overlap of the reality and the image, proposing questions about virtual / real, interior / exterior, the essence of image, and the viewing experience. Her motif revolves around the Eastern natural philosophy and the relationship between human-beings and the world. She is genuinely interested in the incorporation of Eastern thought into present world in her examination of contemporary living.  Her work of image does not concern creating or delineating a certain landscape; instead, it concerns how a landscape is essentially constructed in the moving image. She had held residencies at Location One (New York, 2006), Cité des Arts (Paris, 2007), and the Helsinki International Artist Programme (Helsinki, 2010). Her work had also been exhibited at the the Yebisu International Festival for Art & Alternative Visions in Tokyo Photographic Art Museum (2023); the Hors Pistes Film Festival at the Centre Pompidou, Paris, France (2008); the Shanghai Biennale (2006); and the Taipei Biennial (2002 and 2023). She had received “Asian Cultural Council (ACC) / Yageo Tech Art Award, Taiwan; Loop Award, Best Gallery Work and Presentation, Barcelona, Spain and the Taipei Arts Award, Taipei, Taiwan.

A. Stella (born 1958) lives and works in Saint-Étienne. For around twenty years, the artist has focused on the articulation of two elements, notions, or complementary processes operating simultaneously to create mechanisms of perception. Five complementary units, described as “double forms,” structure this research. Across different periods, developments have been based on these five units, which include the “géogrammes” and “planogrammes,” expressed through paintings and paper structures. New formulations followed, including “pligramme,” “optigramme,” “planoptic,” and “pliptyque,” leading in 2019 to the installation “Bibliogramme.” In 2020, A. Stella began a project dedicated to isolating this unit and concentrating research on its mechanism of perception, focusing on the formal relationship between the vertical interlocking of two forms and their horizontal linguistic extension through a complementary form. This research is entirely dedicated to the space of painting.

Haris Epaminonda (born 1980 in Nicosia, Cyprus) is an artist living and working in Berlin. Her work has been presented in solo and group exhibitions at institutions including The Museum of Modern Art, Aspen Art Museum, The New Museum, Schirn Kunsthalle Frankfurt, Tate Modern, Secession, Modern Art Oxford, Le Plateau (FRAC Île-de-France), Kunsthaus Zürich, KW Institute for Contemporary Art, Point Centre for Contemporary Art, Martin-Gropius-Bau, Kunstmuseum St. Gallen, Hammer Museum, Querini Stampalia, Site Gallery, Malmö Konsthall, The Renaissance Society, Neuer Berliner Kunstverein, Hamburger Bahnhof, Badischer Kunstverein, Museo Madre, and the Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis. She has also participated in major international exhibitions including Documenta 13, Manifesta, the Berlin Biennale, São Paulo Biennale, Sharjah Biennale, Athens Biennale, Pune Biennale, and the Venice Biennale. In 2019, she was awarded the Silver Lion for Promising Young Participant at the Venice Biennale.

Lakeridou Youlika, born in Cyprus around 1940, is a painter and engraver. She settled in Paris and studied at the École des Beaux-Arts and the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales. She received silver and gold medals at the Salon des Artistes Français in 1971 and 1977, respectively. She has had numerous solo exhibitions in galleries and museums, including the Galerie Liliane François in Paris, the National Gallery of Greece in Athens, and the National Gallery of Cyprus in Limassol. The artist's works have gone up for sale at public auction 17 times, mostly in the Painting category. The oldest auction recorded on our site is for the artwork Santorini presented in 2008 at Psatharis Auctions (Painting) and the most recent is for the artwork Sea front presented in 2026 (Painting).

Lia Lapithi (born 1963 in Nicosia, Cyprus) is a Greek Cypriot artist specializing in multimedia and visual art. She studied Art and Environmental Design at the University of California Santa Cruz, followed by an MPhil at Lancaster University. After returning to Cyprus in 1984, she continued her studies, obtaining a Master's degree in Architecture from the Kent Institute of Art and Design in 1991 and a Master's degree in Art Education from the University of Wales in 1994. Based in Nicosia, her practice initially focused on landscape and still-life painting through the use of technology and later on medical art, before expanding to address environmental and political issues, including collective memory, nationalist historiography, and the Cyprus dispute. In 2006, she founded the first Cypriot feminist art group, Washing-Up Ladies. Her work has been exhibited internationally, including in Athens, Alexandria, Paris, Vienna, and Istanbul, and is represented in a number of permanent museum collections. In 2023, she participated in the Cyprus Pavilion at the 18th Venice Biennale of Architecture with the project *From Khirokitia to Mars*, which explored social sustainability, cultural heritage, and space exploration.

Eleni Nicodemou (b.1955 in Alona, Cyprus). She lives and works in Nicosia. She studied Economics Sciences in Athens and she also studied painting and engraving at the Ecole Nationale Superieure des Beaux-Arts, Paris. In 1981-84 the artist stayed and worked at the Cité Internationale des Arts, won Scholarships from the French Government in 1981-83 and 1987-88; Leventis Foundation, 1985-86; EOMEX,1980. In 1986 she received the 1st Prize, Matisse Competition, French Embassy, Nicosia. She presented her work at Glosia Gallery, Nicosia (2012 and 2010), Gallery 2016, Hauterive, Neuchatel, Switzerland (1997), Alexandria Biennale (1994), Gallery Y Grego, Lisbon, Portugal (1990), International Engraving Biennale / 2nd Biennale of Young artists from Europe and the Mediterranean, Thessaloniki(1986), International Biennale of Graphic Arts, Ljubljana (1987 and 1985) and 6th Gravure Biennale, Mulhouse (1984).

Olga de Amaral (born 1932 in Bogotá, Cundinamarca, Colombia) is a Colombian textile and visual artist known for large-scale abstract works made with fibers and covered in gold and silver leaf. She was one of the few artists from South America to achieve international recognition in fiber art during the 1960s and 1970s. Born Olga Ceballos Velez, she grew up in a family with five sisters and two brothers. In 1951–1952, she earned a degree in Architectural Design from the Colegio Mayor de Cundinamarca in Bogotá. In 1954, she moved to New York City to study English at Columbia University and subsequently studied fiber art at the Cranbrook Academy of Art in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, from 1954 to 1955, where she met Jim Amaral. Returning to Colombia in 1955, she began producing commissioned decorative textiles for architects. Jim Amaral visited Colombia in 1956, and they married in 1957, settling in Bogotá, where they raised two children and established a workshop for handwoven textiles. In 1965, de Amaral founded and taught at the Textile Department of the University of Los Andes in Bogotá. Between 1966 and 1967, the family lived in New York, where she met Eileen Vanderbilt of the World Crafts Council and became the organization's Colombian representative. She lives and works in Bogotá, Colombia.

Milena Bonilla's (Bogotá, Colombia, 1975) work dives into political complexities among humans, language and living entities in order to trace and map the cracks that those interactions have left in silence through the sedimentation of predetermined logics and beliefs. The artist uses a variety of media in her production including installations, video, performance, drawing, text, public interventions and photography. She lives and works in Amsterdam, The Netherlands.

Her work has been shown and performed in different international venues including Museo d’Arte Contemporanea MACRO, Rome; Kadist Paris and San Francisco; Rijksakademie van beeldende kunsten, Amsterdam; The Mistake Room, Los Angeles Ca.; Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam; Ar/Ge Kunst, Bolzano;  The Jewish Museum, New York; MAMM, Medellín; Spring Workshop in Hong Kong; CA2M Madrid; MNBA, Buenos Aires; The Photographer’s Gallery and the International Institute of Visual Arts in London; Witte de With in Rotterdam; Framer Framed, Amsterdam; Konstall C, Stockholm; Marrakech and Shangai Biennial’s parallel projects, and the 12th Istanbul, 10th Havana and 3rd Bucharest Biennials.

In 2019 Milena Bonilla was a recipient of The Work Award Proven Talent, given by the Mondriaan Fonds in The Netherlands. At Framer Framed she participated in two group exhibitions HERE/NOW, Current Visions from Colombia (2019) and Elsewheres Within Here (2019). Milena Bonilla is Core Tutor of the two year Master Program Planetary Poetics (2023-2024) at Sandberg, the postgraduate programme of the Gerrit Rietveld Academie Amsterdam.

Milena Bonilla’s contribution to the exhibition HERE/NOW, Current Visions from Colombia consisted of the work, Money (2012), a collection of 260 frottages of coins from various countries with depictions of plants and animals. The Money series calls attention to the iconographic use of plants and animals in nation-building — think of our national birds and flowers. The landscape of a region is poetically intertwined with our conception of it, from plains of farmland and rolling hills to stretches of desert sands or dense jungle. While we employ these symbols to capture the essence of our country’s spirit, we often fail to care for these environments and their native flora and fauna as they exist in the natural world and within our borders. Milena Bonilla thus points to the dissonance, at a societal level, between the idealisation of nature and its exploitative commodification through economic and representational systems.

Clemencia Echeverri (born 1950 in Salamina, Caldas, Colombia) lives and works in Bogotá. She studied Visual Communication at the Universidad Pontificia Bolivariana and Fine Arts at the Universidad de Antioquia, later completing a Master's degree in Visual Arts and studies in Contemporary Art History and Theory at Chelsea College of Arts in London. She taught undergraduate and graduate art courses for 27 years at the Universidad de Antioquia and the Universidad Nacional de Colombia. Initially focused on painting and sculpture, since the 1990s her practice has explored violence, memory, and the forces of nature in Colombia through drawing, video, photography, sound, and installation.

Her projects often combine field research, social engagement, and technology. In 2019–2020, the Museo de Arte Miguel Urrutia in Bogotá presented LIMINAL/Clemencia Echeverri, a retrospective of the previous twenty years of her work curated by María Margarita Malagón. During the same period, she presented Duelos at Fragmentos, Espacio de Arte y Memoria as part of the Premio a la Creación of the Museo Nacional de Colombia. Her work has been presented internationally in events and exhibitions including the Sydney Biennale, Shanghai Biennale, Les Rencontres de la Photographie in Arles, the Liverpool Biennial, and exhibitions in New York, Madrid, Paris, and Toulouse. Publications on her work include Sin Respuesta, La Imagen Ardiente, Trepidaciones, and contributions to several books on contemporary Colombian and Latin American art.

Maria Elvira Escallon (born 1954 in London) is a Colombian visual artist who lives and works in Bogotá. She studied Psychology before pursuing art studies through independent workshops and academic institutions, later completing a Master's degree in Art and Architectural Theory and History at the Universidad Nacional de Colombia. Active since 1980, she has participated in numerous solo and group exhibitions and received her first individual creation grant from Colcultura in 1993. Since 2000, her work has gained increasing international visibility.

Escallón’s practice is characterized by long-term and process-based investigations. Her work explores themes of memory, forgetting, ruin, decay, abandonment, and the social and political consequences of economic conditions and armed conflict. She is also interested in the relationships and tensions between nature, representations of nature, and culture. Often working through site-specific interventions, she incorporates field research and interviews as integral components of her artistic process. She currently teaches at the Pontificia Universidad Javeriana in Bogotá.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Paris (France) and in Bogota (Colombia)
Biography:
Adriana Garcia Galan (born 1977 in Neiva, Colombia) is a Colombian visual artist, video maker, composer, and educator who lives and works between Bogotá and Paris. She studied Fine Arts at the Universidad de los Andes, completed postgraduate studies at the École Nationale des Beaux-Arts de Lyon, and participated in the La Seine research program at the École Nationale Supérieure des Beaux-Arts de Paris. Her multidisciplinary practice spans video, sound art, performance, installation, and experimental music, often exploring the relationships between sound, language, the body, and social experience. She was a resident at Le Pavillon, Palais de Tokyo (2005–2006), and her work is held in public collections including the Centre Pompidou, the FNAC, and the FRAC Champagne-Ardenne in France. 

Alongside her artistic practice, García Galán has developed an extensive career as a composer for film, animation, theater, and audiovisual projects, receiving recognition including a Macondo Award for Best Original Song for *Virus Tropical* (2018) and nominations for her film scores. Her work has been exhibited internationally in venues and events such as the Centre Pompidou, Palais de Tokyo, Art Paris, LAXART, the Istanbul Biennial, and numerous exhibitions across Europe, Latin America, North America, and Asia. Since 2024, she has served as Director of the Arts Program at the Faculty of Creation of Universidad del Rosario in Bogotá, where she also teaches. She is an active member of MUCINE and the Colombian Academy of Cinematographic Arts and Sciences, and was a jury member of the Annecy International Animation Film Festival in 2024.

Beatriz González (1932–2026) was a Colombian painter, sculptor, curator, critic, and art historian, widely regarded as one of the most influential figures in Latin American contemporary art. Born in Bucaramanga, she studied fine arts at the Universidad de los Andes under art critic Marta Traba and painter Joan Antonio Roda. Although frequently associated with Pop Art, González rejected the label, developing a distinctive visual language that combined references to popular culture, mass media, political imagery, and everyday Colombian life. Her work often transformed newspaper photographs, historical paintings, and political portraits into brightly colored, ironic compositions that examined class, power, and national identity.

Growing up during the period of political violence known as *La Violencia* profoundly shaped her artistic vision. Her breakthrough came in 1965 with *The Suicides of Sisga*, a painting based on a newspaper photograph that won a special prize at the Salon of Colombian Artists. During the 1970s she became known for painting images onto domestic furniture, appropriating both Renaissance masterpieces and contemporary media imagery. After the 1985 Palace of Justice siege, her work took a darker turn, focusing on death, political conflict, forced disappearances, and collective memory. Through six decades of artistic production, González created a powerful visual record of Colombian society while maintaining a critical yet deeply human perspective on its tragedies and contradictions.

Her work has been exhibited internationally and is considered foundational to modern Colombian art. In 2019, the Pérez Art Museum Miami presented the first major retrospective of her work in the United States, featuring nearly 150 artworks spanning her career. González also participated in major international exhibitions, including BIENALSUR in 2023. Recognized for her influence on generations of artists and for her engagement with themes of memory, violence, and representation, she remains one of the most important figures in Latin American art history. She died on 9 January 2026 at the age of 93.

Laura Huertas Millan (born 1983 in Bogotá, Colombia) is a Colombian-born French artist and filmmaker whose practice bridges cinema, visual art, and anthropology. Based in Paris, where she completed a PhD focused on ethnographic fictions, she has developed a distinctive body of work that combines documentary research with speculative and experimental storytelling. Her films explore themes of colonial history, cultural representation, memory, landscape, and the construction of the “Other,” often challenging conventional ethnographic narratives.

Working within the genre of ethnofiction, Huertas Millán blends anthropological inquiry with cinematic invention to examine the legacies of imperialism and the ways non-Western identities have been represented and objectified. Her films have been screened at major international festivals including IFFR, FIDMarseille, Cinéma du Réel, Berlinale Forum Expanded, and the Locarno Film Festival. In parallel, her work has been widely exhibited in museums and contemporary art institutions across Europe and the Americas. Through a practice that moves fluidly between art and cinema, she has established herself as a leading voice in contemporary experimental film and moving-image art.

Lives / Works: Lives in Bogota (Colombia) and in Cali (Colombia)
Biography:
Verónica Lehner (born 1980 in Cali, Colombia) is a Colombian artist who lives and works in Berlin. She studied Fine Arts at the Universidad de los Andes in Bogotá and later completed a Master's degree in Spatial Strategies at the Weißensee Kunsthochschule in Berlin. Her practice spans installation, video, photography, performance, and interventions in public space, often exploring the relationship between urban environments, social interaction, and spatial perception. Through site-specific projects and collaborative actions, she investigates how everyday spaces can be reimagined and activated through artistic intervention.

Lehner has presented her work in exhibitions and public projects in Colombia, Germany, Poland, and Japan. Selected projects include public-space interventions in Berlin, Potsdam, and Skoki, as well as exhibitions such as *Dump Art/Kunst von der Halde*, *Site Exploration*, and *échale salsita!* in Berlin. Alongside her artistic practice, she has worked as an educator, teaching sculpture, spatial strategies, art, and aesthetics in Colombia. Her work reflects an ongoing engagement with urban space as a site of encounter, participation, and transformation.

Rosario Lopez (born 1970 in Bogotá, Colombia) is a Colombian artist and educator who lives and works in Bogotá. She studied Visual Arts at the Universidad de los Andes and later earned a Master's degree in Sculpture from Chelsea College of Art and Design in London. Since 1999, she has been a professor of sculpture at the Universidad Nacional de Colombia, where she also served as Academic Coordinator of the Master's Program in Visual Arts from 2004 to 2006. Her practice is rooted in sculpture, photography, and the observation of urban space, often examining the relationships between architecture, public environments, and everyday visual experience.

López gained recognition with *Esquinas gordas* (Fat Corners), a project inspired by overlooked architectural details in Bogotá that she interpreted as a vernacular, post-minimalist form of sculpture. Developed through photographic documentation of the city, the work explored the intersection of geometric abstraction and urban reality, revealing unexpected aesthetic possibilities within the built environment. In 2000, *Esquinas gordas* received First Prize at the 7th Bogotá Art Biennial. Through her artistic and academic work, López has continued to investigate how sculpture can emerge from ordinary encounters with space, architecture, and the city itself.

Susana Mejia (born 1978 in Medellín, Colombia) is a Colombian artist whose practice explores the relationships between nature, craft, ecology, and material knowledge. She studied Fine Arts at The Art Institute of Boston, where she developed a strong interest in painting and color, before shifting her focus toward collaborative and socially engaged projects. Early in her career, she organized weaving workshops for women in prison in Medellín, preserving the fique-fiber textiles produced through these initiatives and incorporating ideas of labor, memory, and collective making into her artistic research.

Mejía's work is deeply informed by her long-term engagement with the Amazon region and its ecological knowledge systems. Fascinated by natural pigments and traditional dyeing techniques, she developed *Color Amazonia*, a seven-year interdisciplinary project carried out in collaboration with artists, anthropologists, botanists, photographers, and filmmakers. Through this research, she identified and documented plants used as sources of pigment by Amazonian communities, highlighting the cultural and environmental significance of color. Her work has been presented in solo exhibitions such as *El Paraíso Perdido* in Medellín and in international exhibitions including *Humboldt: Traspasar el mito* (Quito, 2019), *Proyecto Arte Vivo* (Bogotá, 2019), and *Cosmogonies, au gré des éléments* at MAMAC in Nice, France.

Ana Mercedes Hoyos (29 September 1942 - 5 September 2014) was a Colombian painter, sculptor and a pioneer in modern art in the country. In her half-century of artistic works, she garnered over seventeen awards of national and international recognition. Beginning her career in a Pop Art style which moved towards abstract, her trajectory moved toward cubism and realism as she explored light, color, sensuality and the bounty of her surroundings. Her reinterpretations of master painters led her to an exploration of Colombian multiculturalism, and her later works focused on Afro-Colombian and mestizo heritage within the Colombian landscape. Her works can be found in the permanent collections of the Fuji Art Museum in Tokyo; the Ibercaja Collection in Zaragoza, Spain; the Museum of Modern Art in Mexico City; the Nassau County Museum of Art of Roslyn Harbor, New York, as well as Juan Antonio Roda and museums in other Latin American cities. Her collection of archival materials on San Basilio de Palenque were donated to the United Nations University in Tokyo and the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture.

Julieth Morales (born 1992 in Silvia, Cauca, Colombia) is a Colombian artist whose practice centers on performance, collective action, and the intersections of gender, territory, and Indigenous identity. Working from her own body as a primary medium, she examines the social and political structures that shape contemporary life, particularly the persistence of colonial and heteropatriarchal systems. Her work is informed by theories of performativity, drawing on the idea that gender is produced through repeated actions and social constructions rather than fixed identities.

Morales increasingly develops collaborative projects with members of her community, challenging the modern notion of the artist as an isolated creator and instead conceiving artistic practice as a platform built through relationships and collective experience. Through performance and participatory actions, she explores forms of resistance, belonging, and the ongoing struggle for territorial and cultural self-determination. Her work has been presented in solo exhibitions including *Srape Pøtø Tul-yu, El último círculo* at Museo La Tertulia, Cali (2019), and *Namui nu pirꝋ. [Our Territory]* at MAMBO, Museo de Arte Moderno de Bogotá (2025).

Her work has also been featured in international group exhibitions such as *Invisibles* at FRAC Bretagne, Rennes (2025), *Trópico sin tópico: Amazonas* at CentroCentro, Madrid (2025), and *Curatorial Studies: Dancing Forward, Looking Backward* at Kunsthal Gent (2023). Through a practice that intertwines performance, activism, and community engagement, Morales investigates how personal and collective histories can become tools for social transformation.

Libia Posada (born 1959 in Medellin, Colombia) is a Colombian multidisciplinary artist, physician, and surgeon whose practice operates at the intersection of art, medicine, politics, and society. Trained at the Universidad de Antioquia, she has developed a body of work that examines the human body not merely as a biological entity but as a site where individual and collective histories, social realities, and political structures converge. Drawing on medical materials, imagery, and systems of classification, she creates critical reflections on themes such as life and death, gender-based violence, mental health, displacement, and the tensions between scientific, empirical, and ancestral forms of knowledge.

Posada's projects range from installations and photographic series to community-based collaborations, often involving women and other specific social groups. Characteristic of her work is the construction of clinical or scientific environments within exhibition spaces, where the apparent neutrality and authority of medicine are questioned through experiences that evoke vulnerability, memory, and human fragility. Through works such as *Evidencia Clínica*, *Retratos*, *Hierbas de Sal y Tierra*, and *Signos Cardinales*, she reveals how bodies carry the marks of broader historical, cultural, and political conditions.

Her work has been exhibited extensively in Colombia and internationally, including at the Museum of Modern Art of Medellín, the National Museum of Colombia, Musée Les Abattoirs in Toulouse, the Wellcome Trust in London, the Havana Biennial, FOTOESPAÑA, and the Cartagena Biennial. In 2021, her work was presented at the Palais de Tokyo in Paris under the curatorship of Adélaïde Blanc. Her works are held in major public collections, including the Museo Nacional de Colombia, the Banco de la República Art Collection, and the Museo de Antioquia. She lives and works in Medellín.

Sofía Reyes is an ultra-contemporary artist. Sofía Reyes is a colombian female artist born in Bogotá (CO) in 1982. Sofía Reyes's artistic practice revolves around her personal experiences and perceptions of the world, focusing on intimacy, connection with others, and the search for otherness. She expresses these themes through brave and honest gestures, working across various mediums such as performance, exhibition, and reader formats. Reyes's stylistic approach is characterized by a deep exploration of the inner life of the spirit and the impact of digital technologies on contemporary society.

Sofía Reyes’s first verified exhibition was Un Lugar Y El Tiempo at Espacio Odeon in Bogota in 2016, and the most recent exhibition was La Bienal Internacional de Arte y Ciudad 2025 – BOG25 at La Bienal Internacional de Arte y Ciudad in Bogota in 2025. Sofía Reyes is most frequently exhibited in Colombia, but also had exhibitions in Mexico, Spain and elsewhere. Reyes has at least two solo shows and 16 group shows over the last 9 years (for more information, see exhibitions). Reyes has also been in no less than one art fair and in one biennial. A notable show was The Good Life – Works from the Bank of the Republic collection at MAMM - Museo de Arte Moderno Medellin in Medellín in 2023. Other notable exhibitions were at La Casa Encendida in Madrid and Museo de Arte Moderno de Bogotá (MAMBO) in Bogota. Sofía Reyes has been exhibited with Ana María Millán and Milena Bonilla.

Sofía Reyes is ranked among the Top 100,000 globally, and among the Top 1,000 in Colombia. Reyes’s best rank was in 2025, with the most dramatic change in 2017. For a complete illustration of the artist’s career since 2016, please see the career chart on the analytics page.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Kinshasa (Democratic Republic of the Congo)
Biography:
Gosette Lubondo (born 1993 in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo) is a Congolese photographer whose work explores memory, history, and the traces left by abandoned spaces. She studied Communication and Visual Arts at the Académie des Beaux-Arts in Kinshasa, where she developed a practice centered on staged photography and narrative reconstruction. Drawing on personal and collective histories, Lubondo creates images that blur the boundaries between documentation and fiction, transforming forgotten sites into spaces of imagination and remembrance.

She is best known for her ongoing series *Imaginary Trip*, initiated in 2016, in which she photographs abandoned locations overtaken by nature and reactivates them through carefully constructed scenes. Rather than simply documenting these places, the project seeks to preserve their memory while reflecting on their social and historical significance in the present. In 2018, during a residency at the Musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac in Paris, she developed *Imaginary Trip II*, expanding her exploration of absence, memory, and the afterlives of institutional spaces. Her work has gained international recognition and is included in the collection of the Musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac.

Alisa Andrasek (born 1972 in Croatia) is a Croatian architect, designer, researcher, and innovator working at the intersection of architecture, computer science, artificial intelligence, and emerging technologies. Inspired by biological systems and their capacity for adaptation and evolution, she develops experimental design methodologies that draw on the processes of growth found in nature rather than on its direct imitation. In 2001, she founded Biothing, a transdisciplinary design laboratory exploring the relationships between ecology, digital technologies, architecture, and art. Through collaborations with scientists, engineers, and researchers, Andrasek has pioneered computational and generative approaches to sustainable design.

Her work investigates how algorithms, genetic models, robotics, and artificial intelligence can generate new architectural forms and systems capable of responding to environmental conditions. Among her notable projects is *Bloom* (2012), a large-scale interactive installation created with José Sánchez and composed of thousands of modular elements assembled by the public. The project received international recognition after winning the Wonder Series competition organized for the London 2012 Olympic Games. Andrasek is also a partner of Bloom Games and co-founder of AI Build, a company focused on AI-driven robotic construction. Her work has been exhibited internationally, including at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the New Museum in New York, the FRAC Centre-Val de Loire, the Beijing Biennale, and the Sydney Biennale. She currently serves as Professor of Design Innovation at RMIT University in Melbourne.

José Sánchez is an architect, game designer, media artist, and researcher whose work explores the relationship between architecture, participation, digital platforms, and interactive technologies. Based in New York, he is the founder of Plethora Project, a research studio dedicated to developing new forms of architectural knowledge through games, simulations, and collaborative systems. His practice investigates how digital media can democratize design processes and enable broader public engagement with ecological and urban issues.

Sánchez is widely known as the creator of the video games *Block’hood* and *Common’hood*, which use gameplay to explore architecture, resource management, and community building. He is the author of *Architecture for the Commons: Participatory Systems in the Age of Platforms* (2020), a major contribution to contemporary discussions on participatory design. Together with Alisa Andrasek, he co-created *Bloom* (2012), an interactive modular installation that allowed visitors to collectively build evolving architectural structures. In addition to his artistic and research practice, Sánchez has taught at institutions including the Architectural Association, The Bartlett School of Architecture, the University of Southern California, and the University of Michigan. He is currently Associate Professor at Cornell Tech in New York, where he directs the Game Assemblies Lab and researches collaborative forms of simulation and interactive media.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in London (United Kingdom) and in New York (New York, United States)
Biography:
Alisa Andrasek (born 1972 in Croatia) is a Croatian architect, designer, researcher, and innovator whose work explores the convergence of architecture, computer science, artificial intelligence, robotics, and ecological design. Inspired by the adaptive processes of living systems, she develops computational methodologies that draw on biological growth, emergence, and self-organization to generate new architectural forms. In 2001, she founded Biothing, a transdisciplinary design laboratory dedicated to investigating the intersections of nature, digital technologies, architecture, and art through collaborations with scientists, engineers, and researchers.

Her practice focuses on generative design systems, algorithmic modeling, and advanced fabrication technologies, seeking sustainable architectural solutions informed by the dynamics of natural environments. Through projects ranging from installations and experimental furniture to large-scale architectural research, Andrasek has contributed to the development of computational design as a creative and ecological discipline. Among her notable works is *Bloom* (2012), an interactive modular installation developed through algorithmic principles and public participation, which gained international recognition during the London Olympic cultural program.

Alongside her design practice, Andrasek has played an important role in architectural education and research. She has directed advanced design programs at University College London, led the Wonderlab research platform, and later became Professor of Design Innovation at RMIT University in Melbourne. She is also co-founder of AI Build, a company focused on AI-driven robotic construction technologies. Her work has been exhibited internationally at institutions and events including the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the New Museum in New York, the FRAC Centre-Val de Loire, the Beijing Biennale, and the Sydney Biennale. She lives and works in Melbourne, Australia.

Jagoda Buić (1930–2022) was a Croatian visual artist renowned for her monumental textile installations, tapestries, and sculptural works that transformed fiber art into a major form of contemporary artistic expression. Born in Split, she studied at the Academy of Fine Arts and the University of Zagreb before graduating in interior architecture, scenography, textile, and costume design from the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna in 1953. She later pursued studies in film set design at Cinecittà in Rome and costume history in Venice, experiences that profoundly influenced her understanding of space, materiality, and theatricality.

Beginning her career as a costume and stage designer, Buić worked on more than 120 productions for opera, ballet, theatre, and film across Europe. International recognition came in 1965 when her first textile installation was presented at the Lausanne Biennial of Textile Art and acquired by the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam. She subsequently developed a distinctive artistic language based on monumental structures made from wool, hemp, ropes, and woven fibers, creating immersive environments that challenged traditional definitions of tapestry and sculpture. Alongside Magdalena Abakanowicz, she is regarded as one of the pioneers who redefined textile art within contemporary practice during the 1960s and 1970s.

From the 1980s onward, Buić expanded her work to include metal sculptures and installations, while in later years she experimented with collage and mixed-media compositions incorporating paper, cardboard, and textile elements. Her works have been exhibited internationally and were included in the landmark exhibition *Women in Abstraction* at the Centre Pompidou in 2021. Throughout her career she received numerous distinctions, including the Grand Prize at the São Paulo Art Biennial, the Herder Prize, and the Vladimir Nazor Lifetime Achievement Award. She died in Venice in 2022.

Hana Miletic (born 1982 in Zagreb, Croatia) is a Croatian artist living and working in Brussels whose practice investigates the social, political, and economic traces embedded in everyday urban environments. Originally trained in photography at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp, where she graduated in 2009, she developed a multidisciplinary approach that combines photography, weaving, installation, performance, publishing, and collective workshops. Her work examines acts of repair, maintenance, and resilience as material expressions of broader social and political transformations.

Photography often serves as the starting point for Miletić’s artistic process. Through attentive observation of streets, buildings, vehicles, and improvised repairs, she creates a visual archive of overlooked details that reveal both vulnerability and resistance within contemporary society. These photographic records are subsequently translated into other forms, most notably woven textiles and installations, allowing the artist to reinterpret fragments of reality through labor-intensive and tactile processes.

Since 2018, her ongoing series *Softwares* has explored the relationship between mechanical production and manual craftsmanship through Jacquard weaving, a technology historically linked to the origins of computer programming. By introducing hand-made variations into industrial weaving processes, Miletić highlights forms of care, repair, and collective knowledge. Her work has been exhibited internationally, including solo exhibitions at WIELS in Brussels, Apoteka in Vodnjan, LambdaLambdaLambda in Pristina, and galleries in London and Berlin. Alongside her exhibitions, she regularly organizes workshops, performances, and public readings. She lives and works between Brussels and Zagreb.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Nice (Alpes-Maritimes, France)
Biography:
Nivese Oscari (born 1944 in Labin, Croatia) is a Croatian-French visual artist associated with the School of Nice. After leaving Istria with her family in 1947, she grew up in Belgium, where her father worked as a miner in the Borinage coalfields. In 1973 she moved to Nice in search of what she described as a return to light after the darkness of her childhood. She studied as an independent student at Villa Arson, quickly developing a personal artistic practice that combined collage, assemblage, sculpture, and installation.

Oscari emerged within the predominantly male artistic milieu of the School of Nice, becoming one of its few prominent female figures. Early in her career she worked as an assistant to César, contributing to several of his projects, and later became closely connected to leading artists and critics of the movement, including Pierre Restany, Arman, Raymond Hains, Bernar Venet, and Sacha Sosno. Married to photographer and gallerist Frédéric Altmann, she played an important role in the artistic networks of Nice while maintaining an independent creative identity.

Her work explores the relationship between strength and fragility, often transforming industrial materials such as steel into delicate, lace-like forms. Beginning with collages and assemblages inspired by religious ex-votos and everyday objects, she later turned toward sculpture, developing a distinctive language based on folded, cut, and shaped metal. Throughout her career, Oscari has combined references to memory, femininity, spirituality, and personal history, creating works that balance monumentality with poetic sensitivity. Her sculptures and installations have been exhibited in France and internationally, establishing her as a singular voice within the legacy of the School of Nice.

Marija Novakovic (1885-1955) was a Croatian self-taught artist whose work emerged in the context of long-term psychiatric hospitalization. Born in Zagreb to an Austrian mother and an Austro-Hungarian military officer, she initially pursued a career in music, studying at the Vienna Conservatory and becoming a piano teacher, singer, and performer. After periods of hospitalization in Vienna and Berlin for mental illness, she was transferred to the Vrapče Psychiatric Hospital in Zagreb, where she spent the remainder of her life.

In 1936, at the age of fifty-one, Novaković began drawing and painting spontaneously without any formal artistic training. Art became her primary means of personal expression and psychological support, as she received neither medication nor other therapeutic treatments. Alongside her visual practice, she developed an extensive literary output, producing writings that, like her paintings, combined fantasy, humor, melancholy, and imaginative storytelling.

Her works are characterized by a highly personal visual language that moves between the fantastic and the everyday, revealing a rich imaginative world shaped by memory, emotion, and inner experience. Although her artistic production was first presented publicly in Zagreb in 1954, the exhibition was framed largely through a psychiatric perspective, emphasizing its clinical significance rather than its artistic originality and creative qualities.

Following her death, Novaković’s work gained wider recognition through exhibitions dedicated to art created outside conventional artistic institutions. In 1957, psychiatrist and art historian Robert Volmat included her works in the exhibition *Bosch, Goya et le Fantastique* in Bordeaux. Her paintings have since been exhibited in France and internationally, including presentations at the Franco-German Cultural Institute in Tübingen and the Galerie nationale du Jeu de Paume in Paris, contributing to her recognition as an important figure within the history of outsider and psychiatric art.

Nadezda Prvulovic (born 1930) is a Croatian-born painter known for her large-scale depictions of industrial landscapes and machinery. After leaving Yugoslavia and settling in the United States in 1984, she developed a body of work centered on steel mills, blast furnaces, and industrial structures, transforming these sites into powerful and often atmospheric pictorial environments. Her paintings draw inspiration from abandoned industrial facilities in Europe as well as photographs sourced from technical publications and trade magazines.

Working primarily in gouache and painting, Prvulovic combines documentary observation with a highly personal visual language. Although her subjects are rooted in the realities of heavy industry, her compositions often transcend straightforward representation through dramatic color, flattened perspectives, and an almost dreamlike treatment of space. Industrial machinery, furnaces, and factory interiors become monumental presences, stripped of human activity and imbued with a sense of mystery, memory, and solitude.

Her best-known series, developed during the 1980s and 1990s, explores the visual and symbolic legacy of the machine age. While critics have compared her industrial imagery to the documentary approach of Bernd and Hilla Becher, Prvulovic’s work is distinguished by its painterly sensibility and its transformation of industrial sites into evocative, almost theatrical landscapes. Rather than offering explicit social or political commentary, she focuses on the formal, emotional, and psychological dimensions of these environments.

Prvulovic’s works have been exhibited internationally and have appeared regularly at public auctions since the early 2010s. Through her monumental and atmospheric representations of industrial architecture, she has developed a distinctive artistic practice that bridges realism, memory, and poetic abstraction.

Nora Turato (born 1991 in Zagreb, Croatia) is a Croatian artist, performer, and graphic designer based in Amsterdam. Her multidisciplinary practice combines text, performance, graphic design, sound, installation, and publishing to examine contemporary language and modes of communication. Drawing material from social media, internet forums, advertising, literature, news media, and everyday conversations, she transforms fragments of collective speech into immersive visual and performative works that reflect the rhythms, anxieties, and contradictions of contemporary culture.

Turato moved to the Netherlands in 2009 and studied at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie in Amsterdam before completing the Typography Workshop at ArtEZ University of the Arts. She later participated in the prestigious residency program at the Rijksakademie van Beeldende Kunsten in Amsterdam. Her artistic practice is rooted in the collection, editing, and reconfiguration of language, which she treats as both a social archive and a performative medium.

Central to her work are scripts composed from appropriated texts gathered over time and organized into what she describes as annual “pools” of language. These scripts become the basis for live performances, publications, sound installations, and large-scale typographic interventions. Through changes in rhythm, tone, repetition, and visual presentation, Turato exposes the ways language shapes identity, power, desire, and collective behavior in the digital age.

Her performances and installations have been presented internationally at major institutions and exhibitions, including the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam, the Secession in Vienna, and the Museum of Modern Art in New York. By merging graphic design, spoken word, and conceptual art, Turato has established herself as one of the most distinctive voices of her generation, exploring how contemporary society produces, consumes, and recycles language.

Heba Y. Amin (born 1980 in Cairo, Egypt) is an Egyptian visual artist, researcher, and educator whose multidisciplinary practice explores the intersections of politics, technology, history, urbanism, and collective memory. Through installations, video, photography, research-based projects, and public interventions, she investigates systems of power, colonial legacies, surveillance, and the construction of political narratives. Her work is characterized by extensive archival and field research, often questioning dominant historical and geopolitical representations.

Raised in Cairo, Amin moved to the United States in 1998, where she studied Mathematics and Studio Art at Macalester College before completing postgraduate studies at the Minneapolis College of Art and Design and earning an MFA in Interactive Design from the University of Minnesota in 2009. She later received a DAAD fellowship in Berlin and pursued doctoral research at Freie Universität Berlin. Alongside her artistic practice, she has taught at institutions including the University of Minnesota, the American University in Cairo, the University of Applied Sciences in Berlin, and the State Academy of Fine Arts Stuttgart, where she serves as Professor of Digital and Time-Based Art.

Amin gained international attention in 2015 for her intervention on the set of the television series *Homeland*, where she and fellow artists inserted Arabic graffiti that subtly criticized the show's representation of the Middle East. Beyond this widely publicized project, her work consistently challenges cultural stereotypes, media narratives, and mechanisms of political control. She is also co-founder of the Black Athena Collective and has been active as a curator, researcher, and collaborator in international artistic and academic initiatives.

Her work has been exhibited worldwide at institutions and events including the Dak'Art Biennale, the Marrakech Biennale, the Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw, Kunstverein Hamburg, Camera Austria, Berlinale Forum Expanded, and numerous international museums and biennials. Currently based in Berlin, Amin is recognized as a leading contemporary artist whose practice combines critical inquiry, artistic experimentation, and political engagement.

Marianne Fahmy (born 1992) is an Egyptian artist based in Alexandria whose multidisciplinary practice spans film, installation, photography, sculpture, and mixed media. After earning a BA in Painting from Alexandria’s Faculty of Fine Arts, she joined the independent art program MASS Alexandria in 2016. Her work explores the intersections of history, memory, mythology, and speculative futures, using archival research and fictional narratives to examine questions of identity, place, and collective experience.

Fahmy’s artistic approach combines historical documents, found materials, personal imagery, and cinematic storytelling to construct parafictional narratives that blur the boundaries between reality and imagination. Drawing on marginalized histories, forgotten archives, and architectural remnants, she creates works in which cities, landscapes, and buildings become active participants in stories about displacement, desire, memory, and transformation. Recurring motifs such as deserts, coastlines, and abandoned urban spaces function as symbolic territories where alternative futures and identities can be imagined.

Influenced by concepts of fabulation and speculative history, Fahmy reinterprets historical and contemporary events through poetic and often ambiguous narratives. Her films and installations challenge dominant forms of knowledge and authority, questioning how science, geography, and political power have shaped landscapes and societies. By weaving together myth, prophecy, personal memory, and archival traces, she creates atemporal environments that invite viewers to reconsider established narratives of the past and present.

Her work has been exhibited internationally at institutions and events including the Sharjah Biennial, Manifesta 13, the Yokohama Triennale, the Havana Biennale, the Dak’Art Biennale, BOZAR in Brussels, MAXXI in Rome, and GAMeC in Bergamo. Fahmy’s films have also been screened at major international festivals and institutions, including the ICA Artists’ Film Programme in London. She received the Prince Claus Fund Seed Award in 2021, has participated in residencies in Morocco and Switzerland, and her works are held in the collections of Frac Bretagne and the Sharjah Art Foundation.

Daria Gamsaragan (1907-1986) was an Egyptian-born Armenian sculptor, medalist, and writer whose work bridged fine art, decorative arts, and literary production. Born in Alexandria to a prominent Armenian family originating from Constantinople, she grew up in a multilingual environment and received her early education at the Lycée Français d’Alexandrie. She later moved to Paris, where she studied sculpture at the Académie de la Grande Chaumière under artists including Antoine Bourdelle and Joseph Csaky, developing a refined sculptural practice rooted in both classical training and modernist influences.

Throughout her career, Gamsaragan worked across a variety of artistic fields, becoming particularly known for her miniature sculptures, medals, and jewelry designs. Between 1967 and 1982, she collaborated with the Monnaie de Paris, creating commemorative medals dedicated to notable historical and cultural figures. In the 1970s, she expanded her practice into luxury design, producing a series of zodiac motifs for Cartier and designing jewelry crosses for Chanel, demonstrating her ability to translate sculptural ideas into decorative and wearable forms.

Alongside her visual art, Gamsaragan was also active as a writer under the pseudonym Anne Sarag. Her artistic and literary work often reflected her Armenian heritage, memory, and cultural identity. One of her best-known sculptures, *Crucified*, was featured on the cover of the French-Armenian newspaper *Armenia* in 1977 as part of a commemoration of the Armenian genocide.

Her works were exhibited in France and internationally, culminating in a retrospective exhibition in Paris in 1984. Today, her sculptures and medals are held in collections including the Alexandria Museum of Fine Arts, the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Caen, and the Museum of Modern Egyptian Art. Gamsaragan spent most of her professional life in Paris, where she died in 1986, leaving a distinctive legacy that connected sculpture, design, and Armenian cultural history.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Le Caire (Egypt)
Biography:
Maha Maamoun (born 1972 in Oakland, California) is an Egyptian visual artist, curator, editor, and cultural organizer based in Cairo. Working primarily with photography, video, moving image, and archival materials, her practice explores the intersections of memory, representation, urban space, and collective perception. Through a critical examination of everyday images and dominant visual narratives, she investigates how political, historical, and cultural meanings are constructed and circulated within contemporary Egyptian society.

Raised in Cairo, Maamoun studied Economics and later earned a master’s degree in Middle Eastern History. Alongside her artistic practice, she has played a significant role in the development of independent cultural infrastructures in Egypt. In 2004, she co-founded the Contemporary Image Collective (CiC), a pioneering non-profit space dedicated to visual culture, artistic production, education, and critical discourse. She later co-founded Kayfa-ta, an independent Arabic-language publishing initiative focused on experimental approaches to publishing and knowledge production.

Maamoun gained international recognition for works that reinterpret familiar images, monuments, and urban landscapes to reveal overlooked political and social dimensions. Her videos and photographic projects often draw on archival research, popular culture, and everyday visual experience, creating subtle yet incisive reflections on history, ideology, and public memory. In 2009, she received the Jury Prize at the Sharjah Biennial for her film *Domestic Tourism II*, one of her most widely discussed works.

In addition to her artistic production, Maamoun has been active as a curator, editor, and researcher. She co-curated PhotoCairo3 in 2005, worked with the international platform Meeting Points, curated exhibitions and film programs across the Middle East and Europe, and joined the curatorial team of Forum Expanded at the Berlin International Film Festival in 2018. Her work has been exhibited internationally, and she is recognized as an influential figure in contemporary Arab visual culture whose practice bridges artistic creation, critical inquiry, and institutional engagement.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Paris (France) since 2002
Biography:
Estefanía Peñafiel Loaiza (born 1978 in Quito, Ecuador) is an Ecuadorian visual artist based in Paris. Working across drawing, installation, photography, video, and text-based practices, her work examines themes of memory, disappearance, migration, political violence, and the traces left by history. Through subtle and often ephemeral gestures, she explores the fragility of archives, the invisibility of marginalized narratives, and the ways personal and collective memories are constructed, erased, or transformed over time.

After studying in Ecuador, Peñafiel Loaiza continued her artistic training in France, graduating from the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts de Paris. She subsequently participated in postgraduate programs at the art schools of Paris and Lyon. Her practice has received significant recognition, including the Prix Ardoin from the Académie des Beaux-Arts in 2007 and the Mariano Aguilera Contemporary Art Prize in Quito in 2014. In 2019, she was nominated for the Fondation d’entreprise Ricard Prize.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Belgium since 2003
Biography:
Etiyé Dimma Poulsen (born 1968 in Ethiopia) is a Danish-Ethiopian sculptor renowned for her distinctive ceramic figures that combine fragility, spirituality, and expressive simplicity. Raised in Ethiopia, Tanzania, and Kenya before moving to Denmark with her adoptive Danish family at the age of fourteen, her multicultural background has deeply influenced her artistic vision. After studying art history and teaching art in Denmark, she relocated to France in her early twenties, where she began working with clay and developed the sculptural language for which she is now internationally recognized.

Poulsen’s practice centers on elongated, filiform ceramic sculptures characterized by their delicate silhouettes and weathered surfaces. Created by applying thin layers of clay onto metal mesh structures, her figures acquire cracks and fissures during firing that become integral expressive elements, suggesting facial features, emotions, and traces of lived experience. Inspired by African sculptural traditions, Oceanic art, and her own experiences across continents, she creates works that evoke both vulnerability and resilience, exploring the universal dimensions of human identity and presence.

Fire plays a central role in her artistic process, transforming the material and contributing to the organic, almost archaeological appearance of her sculptures. Through corrosion, fragmentation, and reduction of form, Poulsen seeks to reveal a profound sense of life and humanity. Her works balance strength and delicacy, creating contemplative figures that appear both timeless and deeply personal.

Since the early 1990s, Poulsen has exhibited extensively across Europe, Africa, and North America in both solo and group exhibitions. Her work was featured in the Smithsonian National Museum of African Art exhibition *Ethiopian Passages: Dialogues in the Diaspora* in 2003 and is held in numerous public and private collections, including the National Museum of African Art in Washington, D.C. She currently lives and works in Antwerp, Belgium.

Regina José Galindo (born 1974 in Guatemala City) is a Guatemalan performance artist and poet whose work confronts issues of violence, gender inequality, state repression, and social injustice. Emerging in the aftermath of Guatemala’s civil war, she uses her own body as a site of resistance and testimony, creating performances that expose the physical and psychological consequences of political violence. Through actions that are often intense, confrontational, and deeply personal, Galindo addresses themes such as femicide, abuse of power, colonial legacies, and the vulnerability of marginalized communities.

Initially active as a poet, Galindo entered the contemporary art scene in the late 1990s, developing a performance practice in which the body became both medium and message. Her early works responded directly to the pervasive violence affecting women in Guatemala, while later projects expanded to examine broader structures of oppression and social control. By placing herself in situations of physical endurance or symbolic risk, she transforms personal experience into a powerful form of political critique.

Among her most influential works is *¿Quién Puede Borrar las Huellas?* (2003), in which she walked from Guatemala’s Congress to the National Palace, leaving footprints of human blood in protest against the presidential candidacy of former dictator Efraín Ríos Montt. Other significant performances include *Perra* (2005), where she carved the word “perra” (“bitch”) into her skin to denounce violence against women, and *279 Golpes* (2005), a work commemorating women murdered in Guatemala through repeated blows inflicted upon her own body. These actions exemplify her commitment to making visible forms of violence that are often ignored or normalized.

Galindo gained international recognition after receiving the Golden Lion for Best Young Artist at the Venice Biennale in 2005 and was later awarded the Prince Claus Prize in 2011. Her performances, videos, and installations have been exhibited worldwide, establishing her as one of the most influential figures in contemporary Latin American performance art. Living and working in Guatemala City, she continues to create works that challenge systems of power and give visibility to experiences of injustice, trauma, and resistance.

Bhuri Bai (born in Pitol village, Madhya Pradesh, India) is a renowned Indian Bhil artist whose work played a pioneering role in bringing the traditional painting practices of the Bhil community into the contemporary art world. A member of the Bhil people, one of India’s largest Indigenous communities, she initially learned to create Pithora paintings on the walls of village homes, using natural pigments derived from plants, earth, and clay. Her artistic trajectory changed when she was encouraged by artist Jagdish Swaminathan at Bharat Bhavan in Bhopal to experiment with acrylic paints and paper, becoming one of the first Bhil women to adapt this traditionally mural-based art form to new media.

After moving to Bhopal, where she initially worked as a construction laborer at Bharat Bhavan, Bhuri Bai began developing a distinctive visual language rooted in Bhil traditions while incorporating personal memories, contemporary experiences, and elements of everyday life. Her paintings are characterized by vibrant colors, intricate patterns, and depictions of animals, forests, rituals, deities, and community life. Through this evolution, she helped establish contemporary Bhil painting as an internationally recognized artistic movement.

Beyond painting, Bhuri Bai is also skilled in traditional Bhil architecture and hut construction, knowledge she inherited from her mother. She contributed to the creation of a Bhil dwelling at the Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya (Museum of Man) in Bhopal, reflecting her commitment to preserving and transmitting Indigenous cultural knowledge.

Over the course of her career, Bhuri Bai has received numerous honors for her contributions to Indian art and culture, including the Shikhar Samman, one of the highest cultural awards of the Madhya Pradesh government. In 2021, she was awarded the Padma Shri, India’s fourth-highest civilian honor, recognizing her role in safeguarding and revitalizing Bhil artistic traditions while bringing Indigenous art to national and international audiences.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in New York (New York, United States)
Biography:
Rina Banerjee (born 1963 in Kolkata, India) is an Indian-American artist known for her intricate sculptures and installations that explore migration, identity, colonial histories, and cultural hybridity. Raised between India, the United Kingdom, and the United States, she draws upon her transnational experience to create richly layered works that combine found objects, organic materials, textiles, and manufactured goods from across the globe. Her practice examines the movement of people, commodities, and ideas, revealing the complex networks that connect personal histories to broader global narratives.

Banerjee studied Polymer Engineering at Case Western Reserve University before earning an MFA in Painting and Printmaking from Yale University in 1995. This unusual combination of scientific and artistic training informs her material experimentation and meticulous approach to construction. Her works often take the form of fantastical assemblages populated by hybrid figures and organic forms, blurring distinctions between nature and culture, past and present, reality and imagination.

Drawing inspiration from childhood memories, diasporic experiences, and histories of trade and empire, Banerjee creates visual worlds that challenge fixed notions of nationality, ethnicity, and belonging. Her sculptures frequently incorporate materials sourced from different continents, transforming everyday objects into poetic reflections on displacement, cultural exchange, and the legacy of colonialism. Through these complex assemblages, she investigates how identities are continuously shaped through movement, adaptation, and encounter.

Banerjee has exhibited widely in the United States and internationally, with her work presented at institutions including the Whitney Museum of American Art and the Bronx Museum of the Arts. In 2018, a major mid-career survey, *Make Me a Summary of the World*, was organized by the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and the San José Museum of Art before traveling to several major American museums. Based in New York City, she is regarded as one of the most significant contemporary artists addressing globalization, migration, and cross-cultural identity through sculpture and installation.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in New Delhi (India)
Biography:
Anindita Bhattacharya (born 1985) is an Indian contemporary artist based in New Delhi whose painting practice explores memory, loss, mythology, and the emotional dimensions of human experience. Working primarily through figurative and symbolic imagery, she creates layered visual narratives that draw upon personal recollections, cultural histories, and collective memory, producing works that balance intimacy with broader social and psychological themes.

Bhattacharya completed her MFA at the Faculty of Fine Arts, Maharaja Sayajirao University (MSU), Baroda, in 2009. Over the course of her career, she has received numerous distinctions, including the BW Art Excellence Award (2025), the Lt. Milind Madhukar Bhade Gold Medal, the Narendra Gajanan Bhatt Gold Medal, the Nasreen Mohammedi Award for Best Display, and awards from the Rajasthan Lalit Kala Akademi. In 2024, she became the first Indian artist invited to the Ashmolean Museum, University of Oxford, through the Freer Hall Artist-in-Residence programme.

Her work has been presented at major art fairs and exhibitions in India and internationally, including India Art Fair, Art Mumbai, Art Dubai, and Abu Dhabi Art Fair. Bhattacharya has also participated in numerous solo and group exhibitions, notably *Echoes of a Lingering Loss* (2025), *Lost in Translation* (2025), *Trans-Formative Vision* (2024), *Reflecting the Self* (2023), and *India Reflections* in Moscow (2022).

Recognized for her contribution to contemporary painting, Bhattacharya was featured in *Vitamin P4: New Perspectives in Painting*, Phaidon’s influential international survey of contemporary painters. Through her evocative compositions and nuanced visual language, she continues to investigate the relationship between memory, identity, and the passage of time.

Suruchi Chand is an Indian contemporary artist whose career remains relatively undocumented in publicly available sources. Although biographical information about her life and education is scarce, her work has appeared on the secondary art market and has been included in auctions of modern and contemporary South Asian art. Her artistic practice is associated with painting and drawing, often featuring stylized figurative and anthropomorphic forms that combine elements of abstraction and symbolism.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Paris (France) and in Amsterdam (Netherlands)
Biography:
Anju Chaudhuri (born 1944 in Kolkata, India) is an Indian painter and printmaker whose work brings together Indian cultural traditions and European artistic practices. Raised in a Bengali family of intellectuals deeply connected to Indian heritage, she was influenced from an early age by Hindu mythology, the diverse landscapes of India, and the country's rich artistic traditions. Throughout her career, she has developed a visual language that reflects a continuous dialogue between Eastern and Western cultures.

After studying painting in Kolkata and at the Faculty of Fine Arts of Maharaja Sayajirao University in Baroda, Chaudhuri continued her artistic education in Europe, attending Saint Martin's School of Art in London, the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, and later studying in Amsterdam. In Paris, she trained in printmaking under the renowned engraver Stanley William Hayter at Atelier 17, an experience that profoundly shaped her technical and artistic development.
