Her works entered important public collections, including the Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris, the French State, the Lebanese State, the Kingdom of Morocco, the Sursock Museum in Beirut, and the International Monetary Fund. Her paintings are also held in numerous private collections across Europe, North America, the Middle East, and Australia.

Tarazi's work was the subject of the monograph Visions d'Iran and was praised for its synthesis of Eastern spirituality and Western artistic language, establishing her as a distinctive voice within twentieth-century painting.

Paola Yacoub is an artist based between Berlin and Beirut.

She studied at the Lebanese Academy of Fine Arts and graduated from the Architectural Association School of Architecture in London in 1993. Between 1995 and 1999, she worked at the Institut Français d’Archéologie du Proche-Orient, producing excavation drawings for archaeological sites in downtown Beirut.

Yacoub presented her project Affects in 1998 at the University of Ljubljana Gallery. She developed her artistic practice in Beirut before beginning a collaboration with Michel Lasserre in 2000. Together they were invited to the Akademie Schloss Solitude in Stuttgart in 2001 and 2003, and received the DAAD Artists-in-Berlin fellowship in 2004–2005. Since then, she has lived and worked between Berlin and Beirut.

Marie Zolamian (born 1975, Beirut) is a Lebanese visual artist based in Belgium.

At the age of fifteen, she left Lebanon with her family and settled in Liège, where she continues to live and work. While studying marketing, she also pursued visual arts at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Liège and at La Cambre in Brussels. She later taught painting at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Liège.

Working across painting, drawing, writing, video, and installation, Zolamian develops a multidisciplinary practice that she describes as an experimental documentary of fictional ethnology. Her work explores themes of displacement, identity, and the coexistence of Eastern and Western histories, cultures, and ways of life.

In 2017, she created a monumental mosaic for the entrance of the Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp (KMSKA), composed of fragments inspired by works from the museum's collection and imaginary creatures. In 2022, a court recognized her exclusive copyright over the mosaic's design and execution. In 2023, she was awarded the Ianchelevici Prize for her contribution to public art and artistic integration within urban space.

Michel Lasserre (born 1947, Auch, France) studied architecture in Paris. Since 1996, he has collaborated with Paola Yacoub on projects exploring the expressiveness of territories and their aesthetic and political implications. Together they presented installations including Garden of Eden, Monument for Beirut at the 7th Venice Architecture Biennale (2000), Al Manazer at the Ayloul Festival in Beirut (2001), and Monuments of an Unfinished War at Galerie Claude Samuel in Paris. During their residency at the Akademie Schloss Solitude (2001–2002), they developed The Next Village, later exhibited in Stuttgart and Paris. Their collaborative work has also been presented in international exhibitions including the São Paulo Biennial, MACBA Barcelona, Media City Seoul, Witte de With Rotterdam, Kunstenfestivaldesarts Brussels, the Museum of Modern Art Ljubljana, and the International Biennial of Contemporary Art of Seville.

Karine Wehbé is an artist and graphic designer based in Lebanon. She obtained a diploma in Graphic Arts from the Paris School of Graphic Arts (Esag Penninghen) in 1996. She has exhibited her work at Espace SD, Beirut Art Center and BAR. She has published numerous publications including Music Fanzine and Stop Here for Happy Holiday. With Nadim Tabet, Wehbé co-directed “Eté 91” (2014), winning the Pavilion Award and Sacem Prize; and “It’s the war in Syria that killed her” (2016) that screened at Videoworks and Pantin Festival. Through photography, cinema, archival footage, geographic maps, her work embeds intimate and public chronicles, drawing on adolescent experiences, cinematographic and musical influences, and the mechanisms of memory and nostalgia.

Nadim Tabet (born 1982, Beirut) is a Lebanese filmmaker.

He began making films at a young age, directing his first short videos, Caravane (1997) and Kodak Color (1998). In 1999, he moved to France to study human sciences and cinema at the Sorbonne University. During this period, he directed a series of short films including Histoires extraordinaires du cinématographe (1999), Martine et Alia (2001), Passé présent futur (2002), L’Arche de Noé (2003), Violante (2005), Le Liban en automne (2006), Jeunes et innocents (2007), Spring 75 (2008), Souvenirs d’un été (2011), and Eté 91 (2014).

In 2001, Tabet co-founded the Lebanese Film Festival. Since 2011, he has been a member of the selection committee of the Oberhausen International Short Film Festival. In 2017, he directed his first feature film, One of These Days, which received critical acclaim and won the Best Debut Feature award at the 22nd Arab Film Festival. In 2019, he co-directed the television series Faraya with Lebanese filmmaker Mounia Akl.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in London (United Kingdom) and in Johannesburg (South Africa)
Biography:
Billie Zangewa (born 1973, Blantyre, Malawi) is a Malawian artist based in Johannesburg. She is known for her hand-stitched silk collage tapestries that explore Black femininity, motherhood, and everyday domestic life.

Zangewa studied printmaking and received a Bachelor of Fine Arts from Rhodes University in South Africa. Influenced by her mother's work in the textile industry, she developed a practice centered on raw silk, drawn to its luminosity and reflective qualities. After working in Gaborone, Botswana, and later in Johannesburg and London, she began creating textile collages that combined personal narratives with urban environments.

Her work is deeply autobiographical and reflects what she describes as 'daily feminism,' using self-love as a form of resistance to oppression. Through figurative silk compositions, she examines identity, domesticity, and the experiences of contemporary Black women. Her works often feature the artist herself as the central figure, transforming everyday moments into intimate and universal narratives.

Since 2004, Zangewa has exhibited internationally, including at the Paris Art Fair, the National Museum of African Art in Washington, D.C., and the Museum of the African Diaspora in San Francisco. Her solo exhibition Soldier of Love was presented by Templon in Paris in 2020, and her work is included in the publication Vitamin T: Threads and Textiles in Contemporary Art (2019).

Mariam Abouzid Souali (born 1989, Targuist, Morocco) is a Moroccan artist who lives and works in Tétouan, Morocco.

She graduated from the National Institute of Fine Arts in Tétouan in 2012. She continued her studies in French literature and art history at Mohammed V University in Rabat and Abdelmalek Essaâdi University in Martil. In 2014, she began her doctoral research and was awarded a Fulbright Scholarship to continue her studies at Bryn Mawr College in Pennsylvania, United States.

Her recent exhibitions include Des exploits, des chefs-d'œuvre at MAC Marseille (2024), Stardust at Galerie Cécile Fakhoury in Paris (2023), Zone Franche at the Institut des Cultures d’Islam in Paris (2021), I Have This Memory, It Is Not My Own at Galerie Cécile Fakhoury in Dakar (2020), Distance Ardente at MRAC Occitanie in Sérignan (2020), Mare Nostrum at Galerie Comptoir des Mines in Marrakech (2018), Silence at Villa des Arts in Rabat (2017), and Nilwood Melody, Qu’avons-nous fait de nos rêves? at the Fondation Abderrahman Slaoui Museum in Casablanca (2017).

Amina Agueznay (born 1963, Casablanca, Morocco) is a Moroccan visual artist and trained architect. Her contemporary practice includes jewellery design, art installations, and site-specific works. Using materials such as textiles, paper, rose petals, and burned plastic bags, she incorporates elements of Moroccan cultural heritage into her work.

Agueznay is the daughter of Moroccan painter and engraver Malika Agueznay. In 2018, they collaborated on the site-specific exhibition Metamorphosis at the Attijariwafa Bank Foundation in Rabat. After graduating from secondary school in Casablanca, she studied architecture in the United States and received a Bachelor's Degree in Architecture from the Catholic University of America in Washington, D.C., in 1989. She worked as an architect in the United States for fifteen years before returning to Morocco in 1997, where she has since lived and worked in Marrakesh.

Her work has been presented in art and fashion exhibitions in Morocco and Europe, featured in art catalogues, magazines, and the Financial Times, and documented by Moroccan photographer Leila Alaoui. She has also created site-specific installations for several exhibitions, including the 2026 Venice Biennale.

Malika Agueznay (born 1934, Marrakesh, Morocco) is a Moroccan visual artist and a member of the experimental Casablanca Art School. She is recognized as Morocco’s first woman Modernist artist and is known for her contributions to modern art and abstraction in Moroccan visual art.

From 1966 to 1970, she studied at the École des Beaux-Arts of Casablanca under Farid Belkahia, Mohammed Melehi, and Mohamed Chabâa. The school's experimental approach emphasized abstract art, geometric forms, and collaborative public projects. While still a student, Agueznay developed her signature biomorphic seaweed motif, which became a recurring element throughout her career. She explored this form through painting, printmaking, sculpture, woodwork, and calligraphic compositions, creating an abstract language informed by her own perspective.

In 1978, she became the first woman printmaker to participate in the Cultural Moussem of Asilah. She later continued her printmaking studies in New York with Mohammad Omar Khalil and Robert Blackburn and regularly exhibited her prints in group exhibitions. Agueznay also created large-scale public murals, including works at the psychiatric hospital of Berrechid in 1981 and at the Asilah Festival in 1985. She participated in the Asilah International Art Festival for more than twenty years as both an artist and art teacher. She is the mother of visual artist Amina Agueznay, with whom she collaborated on the site-specific exhibition Metamorphosis in Rabat in 2018.

Wafae Ahalouch El Keriasti (Tanger, Morocco, 1978) lives and works in Amsterdam, the Netherlands. She graduated from HKU University of the Arts Utrecht in 2001, followed by residencies at De Ateliers and later Rijksakademie van beeldende kunsten, Amsterdam (among others). She has received national and international recognition in the form of various fellowships, stipends, and awards, including, in 2003, the Koninklijke Prijs voor Vrije Schilderkunst (the Dutch Royal Prize for Modern Painting). Over the course of her career, her work has been shown in solo and group exhibitions at venues inside and outside the Netherlands, such as Künstlerhaus Bethanien, Berlin; Wiels, Brussels; EKWC, Den Bosch; De Nederlandsche Bank, Amsterdam; Club Solo, Breda; Billboard Festival, Istanbul and Casablanca; Museum Arnhem; Framer Framed, Amsterdam; Marrakech Biennale 5; FIAC, Paris; Stedelijk Museum Zwolle; Musée de Marrakech; Schloss Marquardt, Potsdam; Young Artists Biennale, Bucharest; W139, Amsterdam; and Centraal Museum, Utrecht. Her work is held in public and private collections in the Netherlands, Belgium, and France.

Aassmaa Akhannouch (born 1973, Meknes, Morocco) is a Moroccan artist and photographer. After earning an engineering degree in France and an MBA in the United States, she worked in marketing for fifteen years before turning to photography. In 2013, she studied digital photography at the Photo Academy Casablanca and decided to pursue photography full-time in 2016.

Akhannouch works primarily with the cyanotype process, an early monochrome photographic printing technique, which she combines with methods such as tea baths and watercolor highlights. Her practice explores memory through intimate and lyrical images that evoke emotions rather than document the past. Between 2016 and 2018, she collaborated with photographer FLORE at the L'Œil de l'Esprit studio in Paris.

In 2021, she received the 26th Prix HSBC pour la photographie for her series The House That Still Lives Within Me.... The award supported the publication of her photobook La maison qui m'habite encore, released by Atelier Xavier Barral in French and English in 2021. She lives and works between Casablanca, Morocco, and the Lot Valley in Occitania, France.

Meriem Bennani (born 1988, Rabat, Morocco) is a Moroccan artist based in New York City. She studied at the École Nationale Supérieure des Arts Décoratifs in Paris and later received a BFA from The Cooper Union in New York in 2012.

Bennani works across video, sculpture, multimedia installation, drawing, and social media. Her practice is known for its playful use of digital technologies, including 3D animation, projection mapping, and motion capture. She frequently publishes work on Instagram and Snapchat. In 2019, she was one of four artists in the Whitney Biennial who requested the removal of their work through a collective letter published in Artforum. The same year, she received the Eye Art & Film Prize. Her works are included in the collections of the Guggenheim Museum, the Kadist Foundation, and the Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris.

Orian Barki (born 1985, Tel Aviv) is a filmmaker based in New York. She has directed short documentaries and commercial films for platforms and publications including ESPN, PBS, Fader, Vogue, Nowness, Le Cinema Club, and Dazed Magazine.

Since 2020, Barki has collaborated with Meriem Bennani on the animated series 2 Lizards, which premiered on Instagram. The series was described by The New York Times as blending documentary structure with surreal animation and was praised for being both grounded in real events and imaginative. 2 Lizards was later acquired by the permanent collections of the Museum of Modern Art and the Whitney Museum.

Chaïbia Talal (1929–2004) was a Moroccan self-taught painter born in the village of Chtouka near El Jadida. At the age of 13, she was sent to Casablanca to marry a man much older than herself. By the age of 15, she had become a widow and worked as a maid to support herself and her son, Hocein. Although she remained illiterate throughout her life, she was determined to provide her son with an education.

Inspired by a dream in which strangers gave her art supplies, Talal began painting without formal training. Her work was initially rejected by the Moroccan art world, but in 1965 her son introduced her to Pierre Gaudibert, director of the Musée d'Art Moderne de Paris, who recognized the originality of her paintings. This led to exhibitions at the Goethe-Institut in Casablanca and the Museum of Modern Art in Paris in 1966. Known for breaking traditional artistic boundaries, her work has been associated with outsider art and was influenced by artists of the CoBrA movement. Chaïbia Talal died of a heart attack in Casablanca in 2004. Her work continues to be exhibited internationally, including in the Qatar–Morocco 2024 Year of Culture.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Paris (France) and in Martigny (Switzerland)
Biography:
Latifa Echakhch (born 1974, El-Khnansa, Morocco) is a Moroccan-French visual artist who creates installation-based works. She moved to France with her family at the age of three and studied at the École supérieure d'Art de Grenoble, the National School of Arts Cergy-Pontoise, and the Lyon National School of Fine Arts.

Echakhch began her artistic career in 2002. In 2008, she was invited to exhibit her work at Tate Modern in London, and in 2011 she participated in the Venice Biennale. In 2013, she was awarded the Marcel Duchamp Prize for her practice, which has been described as combining surrealist and conceptual approaches while exploring the meaning of symbols and the fragility of modernism. In 2015, she became the first woman to serve as guest curator of the annual GET OUT exhibition at the Haute École d'Art et de Design Genève.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Strasbourg (Bas-Rhin, France) and in Fes (Morocco)
Biography:
Souad El Maysour is a French-Moroccan artist based between Fez and Strasbourg. Working across sculpture, installation, and material-based practices, she develops works through processes of erosion, inscription, and transformation.

Her practice explores the ways in which forms circulate between use, ritual, archive, and sculpture. Through processes of erosion and transformation, her works preserve traces without fixing their meaning, allowing materials to carry multiple histories and interpretations. Matter becomes a space where systems of inscription continue to exist and evolve. Her work has been presented at Mucem in Marseille, the Dakar Biennale, Alliance Française Strasbourg, and Apollonia.

Safaa Erruas (born 1976, Tétouan, Morocco) is a Moroccan artist known for her abstract and minimalist practice. After studying science for one year at the Faculty of Sciences in Tétouan, she turned to art and graduated from the Institut National des Beaux-Arts de Tétouan in 1998.

Her work is often dominated by the color white, which she associates with immateriality, silence, and fragility. Using materials such as thread, needles, razor blades, knives, and seams, she creates works that evoke wounds, vulnerability, and healing. Based in Tétouan, Erruas has exhibited internationally since 1998. Following her graduation, she participated in the exhibition Morocco Time and completed a six-month residency at the Cité Internationale des Arts in Paris.

She participated in the Dakar Biennale in 2002 and again in 2006, where she received an award. In 2009, she was selected as one of five significant artists of a new generation of women artists from the Muslim world for an exhibition organized by MoCADA in New York. Her work has also been presented at AKAA in Paris, contemporary African art fairs in London, and the exhibition African Voices in Milan in 2022. Her works are held in collections including the Moroccan Royal Palace, Société Générale Morocco, the Caisse de Dépôt et de Gestion, the ONA Foundation, the Jean Paul Blachère Foundation, and the Centre for Contemporary Art in Lagos.

Majida Khattari (born 1966, Erfoud, Morocco) is a Moroccan-born French multidisciplinary contemporary artist. She studied at the School of Fine Arts of Casablanca, graduating in 1988, before moving to Paris to continue her education at the Beaux-Arts de Paris, where she received her national higher diploma in plastic arts in 1995.

Shortly after arriving in France, the 1989 Islamic headscarf controversy became a defining influence on her artistic practice. Working across photography, performance, sculpture, video, installation, and fashion-based performances, Khattari explores themes of fashion, women's bodies, and contemporary Islam. She is particularly known for staged fashion shows that connect the format of Western fashion presentations with Islamic dress and cultural identity. Her work has been exhibited internationally, including in Paris, London, New York, Québec, and Montreal.

Batoul S'Himi (born 1974 in Asilah, Morocco) is a sculptor whose work often comments on gender inequality and the global struggle for social change. She is best known for her series World Under Pressure in which she created sculptures from pressure cookers and other domestic tools and appliances. These works comment on international concerns such as growing environmental pressures. S'Himi's work is included in the Smithsonian permanent collection.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Tanger (Morocco) and in Paris (France)
Biography:
Randa Maroufi (born 1987, Morocco) is a visual artist and filmmaker whose practice spans photography, video, and installation. She graduated from the Institut National des Beaux-Arts de Tétouan, the École Supérieure des Beaux-Arts d'Angers, and Le Fresnoy – Studio National des Arts Contemporains.

Her work explores the staging of bodies in public and intimate spaces. Through carefully constructed images, she examines the status of representation and embraces ambiguity as a way to question political, social, and visual narratives. Her practice often investigates the boundaries between reality and fiction.

Her residency project focuses on a film exploring labor practices in anchovy canning factories across the Mediterranean. Through research and formal experimentation, the project examines the relationships between ecofeminism, colonialism, and social struggles, while considering how both the creative process and the finished work can support collective resistance.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Montpellier (Hérault, France)
Biography:
Sanaa Mejjadi is a French-Moroccan visual artist born in Casablanca. She lives and works in France. After studying visual arts and spatial design, she worked for several years as a 3D artist creating environments for the video game industry, an experience that shaped her interest in structure, space, and the immersive qualities of form.

Working across weaving, painting, ceramics, and installation, Mejjadi explores matter as a site of memory, transmission, and material heritage. Rooted in personal and cultural histories, her practice examines how gestures and fibers reactivate forms shaped by displacement, movement, and family traditions. Drawing on vernacular knowledge and nomadic textile traditions, she approaches shelter as a living, temporary structure that protects, adapts, and evolves. By bringing weaving from the domestic sphere into contemporary art, she reinterprets a practice passed down through the women in her family. Through repetition, layering, and tension, her works create abstract compositions where threads and suspended elements evoke spaces in which memory, time, and the body are inscribed into matter.

These works comment on international concerns such as growing environmental pressures. S'Himi's work is included in the Smithsonian permanent collection.

Ghita Skali (born 1992, Casablanca) is an artist based in Amsterdam. She studied at Villa Arson in Nice, completed the postgraduate program at the École des Beaux-Arts de Lyon, and participated in De Ateliers in Amsterdam between 2018 and 2020.

Skali uses curious news stories, rumors, and propaganda to disrupt institutional power structures. Her practice is both critical and engaged, often operating outside traditional art spaces through informal exchanges of goods, (il)legal documents, and everyday objects. Through subtle interventions, she questions perceptions of reality both inside and outside the museum.

Her work has recently been exhibited at Kunsthal Extra City in Antwerp, 1646 in The Hague, the Karachi Biennale, Cube Independent Art Room in Rabat, and the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam.

Yolanda Andrade (born May 22, 1950, in Villahermosa, Tabasco) is a Mexican photographer based in Mexico City. She studied at the Visual Studies Workshop in Rochester, New York, from 1976 to 1977 and has worked as a photographer since 1977.

She has taught photography at the Centro de la Imagen, Tecnológico de Monterrey, and the Escuela de Fotografía Nacho López. While living in Rochester, she received a Guggenheim Fellowship to develop a photographic project about Mexico City, later known as Mexican Passion. She also worked as a still photographer for a Mexican film production company before becoming an independent photographer.

Andrade initially specialized in black-and-white street photography focused on Mexican culture and everyday life. In 2003, she transitioned to digital color photography, shifting her attention toward composition, symbolism, and themes of cities, travel, memory, and pop culture. Her work explores the relationship between people and the city, documenting everyday life, celebration, tradition, and protest.

She is best known for Mexican Passion, a body of work capturing the culture and daily life of Mexico, including public celebrations, LGBTQ parades, and urban life. In addition to photography, Andrade is the author of several visual books and regularly participates in conferences on Latin American photography. She is a member of the Sistema Nacional de Creadores de Arte del FONCA, and her work has been exhibited extensively in Mexico, the United States, and Europe.

Tania Barajas Apocada (born 1984, Mexico) is a Mexican artist.

In 2006, she created Architecture corporelle, a color photograph printed on canvas, as part of the series 'Je n'ai pas dansé depuis si longtemps'. The work was produced within the Mission photographique Paris 8 and measures 68 x 90 cm. It was acquired by commission from the artist in 2007.

Artist: Tatiana BILBAO, Derek DELLEKAMP, Rozana MONTIEL
Biography:
Tatiana Bilbao Spamer is a Mexican architect born in 1972 in Mexico City. She studied Architecture and Urbanism at Universidad Iberoamericana, graduating in 1996. In 2004, she founded Tatiana Bilbao ESTUDIO, completing projects in Mexico, China, France, the United States, Guatemala, and other countries. Her practice focuses on sustainable design, museum design, and social housing, often combining geometry with nature. Among her notable projects are the Botanical Garden of Culiacán, an exhibition hall in Jinhua, China, and a prototype for sustainable social housing presented at the Chicago Architecture Biennial in 2015. Her work has received numerous international awards, including the Berliner Kunstpreis (2012), the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture (2014), the Architizer A+ Impact Award (2017), the Marcus Prize (2019), and the Tau Sigma Delta Gold Medal (2020).

Derek Dellekamp is a Mexican architect born in 1971 in Mexico City. He lives and works in Mexico.

Rozana Montiel is a Mexican architect and the founder and director of Rozana Montiel Estudio de Arquitectura, an interdisciplinary architecture studio based in Mexico City. She studied Architecture and Urban Planning at Universidad Iberoamericana, graduating with honors in 1998, and completed a Master's degree in Architectural Theory and Criticism at the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya in 2000. After working with architect Diego Villaseñor, she founded her own practice in 2009. Her work focuses on socially conscious, community-oriented, and sustainable design, ranging from small-scale objects to urban interventions. Her projects have been exhibited internationally, including in Mexico, Spain, France, the United States, England, China, and at the Venice, São Paulo, Rotterdam, Lima, and Chile Biennials. She has received several international awards, including the Emerging Voices Award (2016), the Moira Gemmill Award (2017), and the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture (2019).

Wendy Cabrera Rubio was born in 1993 in Mexico City, Mexico. She holds an undergraduate degree from the Escuela Nacional de Pintura, Escultura y Grabado “La Esmeralda” in Mexico City. After earning her degree, she studied at the Programa Educativo SOMA in Mexico City. Solo and two-person exhibitions of Cabrera Rubio's work have taken place at the Museo Jumex in Mexico City; Kurimanzutto in Mexico City; PEANA in Monterrey, Mexico; anonymous gallery in New York City; Biquini Wax EPS, in Mexico City; QUEENS in Los Angeles, California; and Nordenhake Gallery in Mexico City.

Pia Camil is a Mexican contemporary artist born in 1980 in Mexico City, where she was also raised. She studied painting and earned a B.F.A. in Painting from the Rhode Island School of Design in 2003, followed by an M.F.A. from the Slade School of Fine Art in London in 2008. Working across painting, sculpture, installation, and performance, her practice is closely connected to the Mexican urban landscape, the visual language of modernism, and its relationship to retail and advertising. More recently, she has incorporated public participation into her work to engage with the politics of consumerism. Her work is included in the collections of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, Centre Pompidou, and the Blanton Museum of Art.

Tania Candiani is a Mexican artist born in 1974 in Mexico City. She is known for her interdisciplinary practice, creating large-scale multimedia installations. Her work has been exhibited internationally, including at Meno Parkas Galerija in Lithuania, Kunsthaus Miami, the Museum of Contemporary Art San Diego, and the Museum of Contemporary Art Denver. Her first solo museum exhibition, Cinco variaciones sobre circunstancias fónicas y una pausa, was presented at the Laboratorio de Arte Alameda in Mexico City in 2012. Candiani represented Mexico at the 2015 Venice Biennale and participated in the Armory Show in 2019. She was an International Studio & Curatorial Program resident in 2010 and received a Guggenheim Fellowship in Fine Arts in 2011. In 2022, her solo exhibition For the Animals was presented at the Museum of Contemporary Art Denver, followed by Waterbirds: Migratory Sound Flow in Miami. In 2024, the Pérez Art Museum Miami presented Pulso, a solo exhibition centered on her three-channel video installation Pulse (2016–2018).

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Berlin (Germany) and in Amsterdam (Netherlands)
Biography: Mariana Castillo Deball is a Mexican visual artist born in 1975 in Mexico City and based in Berlin. She studied at the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México in Mexico City and the Jan Van Eyck Academie in Maastricht. Working across installation, sculpture, photography, and drawing, her practice explores the role of objects in shaping identity and history. Through extensive research and fieldwork, she assembles found materials to reveal new connections and meanings. Her projects often draw on archaeology and scientific display systems to examine the relationship between time, place, and history. Notable works include Stelae Storage (2013), Lost Magic Kingdoms Paolozzi (2013), and the works presented in her 2019 solo exhibition Replaying Life's Tape, inspired by the Ediacaran fossils of South Australia.

Paloma Contreras Lomas is a Mexican artist and writer born in 1991 who lives and works in Mexico City. Her practice combines literature, fiction, film, performance, drawing, sculpture, and narrative to explore issues of race, class, nationalism, territory, and global extractive economies. Positioning her work from a feminine rather than a feminist perspective, she addresses political and social issues that are rarely discussed in traditional Mexican society. Her work often takes a personal and autobiographical approach to themes of gender violence and social urgency. Since 2011, she has also been a member of the Mexican artist collective Bikini Wax, which founded an artist-run space characterized by a multidisciplinary and pedagogical approach to art.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Mexico (Mexico) and in Paris (France)
Biography: Ximena Cuevas is a Mexican video performance artist born in 1963 in Mexico City. She is one of the first video artists in Mexico to gain recognition from cultural institutions. After working in cinema and at the Cineteca Nacional restoring films censored by the government, she developed an interest in experimental film and video. In the 1990s, she co-founded the collective Cosa Nostra, which explored experimental interventions through film. Her work uses irony to comment on culture, politics, social issues, feminism, gender identity, and lesbian experience in contemporary Mexico. Her videos and films have been presented at festivals including Sundance and the New York Film Festival, as well as institutions such as the Museum of Modern Art, the Guggenheim Museum, the Berkeley Art Museum, the Contemporary Art Museum of San Diego, and the Museo Universitario de Arte Contemporáneo in Mexico City. Since 2011, she has lived part-time in Guerrero, where she has also been involved in sea turtle conservation efforts.

Pía Elizondo is a Mexican photographer who has lived in France since 2003. After studying philosophy and developing a self-taught approach to photography, she earned a Master's degree from the École Nationale Supérieure de Photographie in Arles in 2012. Since beginning her photographic practice in 1993, she has participated in numerous solo and group exhibitions in France, Spain, Mexico, the United States, Brazil, Colombia, and Puerto Rico. She has published the books Primer cuadro and Entre deux, contributed to collective publications, and received the Sistema Nacional de Creadores grant in Mexico twice. Elizondo has also worked as a photography teacher in Mexico and France, leading workshops in Arles and at ENS Louis-Lumière. Her work is included in the collection of the Fonds National d’Art Contemporain in Paris and has been exhibited at Flaere Gallery in London, Galeria LMI in Mexico City, and Neg-Pos in Nîmes.

Frida Escobedo is a Mexican architect born in 1979. She studied architecture at Universidad Iberoamericana and earned a master's degree in Art, Design and the Public Domain from Harvard Graduate School of Design. In 2006, she founded her own architecture and design studio in Mexico City. Her practice focuses on housing, community centers, art venues, hotels, and public spaces, with an emphasis on sustainable design and the social experience of architecture. She is known for creating temporary and interactive works, often exploring the concept of time in a social rather than historical context. Her notable projects include the courtyard at La Tallera in Cuernavaca, installations at Museo Experimental el Eco and the Victoria & Albert Museum, and the 2018 Serpentine Pavilion in London, where she became the youngest architect and the second woman invited to design the pavilion. In 2022, she was selected to renovate the Oscar L. Tang and H.M. Agnes Hsu-Tang Wing at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, becoming the first woman to design a wing for the museum.

Alejandra Figueroa is a Mexican photographer born and raised in Mexico who has lived in Paris since 1992. Passionate about photography, she focuses on sculpture while also photographing stained glass, paintings, textures, and architecture. Her first major exhibition took place at the Grand Louvre in Paris in 1997, followed by an exhibition at the Musée d'Orsay in 1998 commissioned by the French Ministry of Culture. In 2001, she exhibited at the Vatican with a book of photographs of sculptures from St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. She represented Mexico at Expo 2000 in Hannover and photographed the collection of the Museo Nacional del Virreinato in Mexico, later participating in the exhibition D'après l'Antique at the Musée du Louvre. In 2002, she was invited by the AFAA and the City of Paris to an artist residency in China and participated in the Mois de la Photo exhibition in Singapore. Her work is included in the collections of the Louvre, the French National Fund for Contemporary Art, the Bibliothèque Nationale de France, and the Maison Européenne de la Photographie. In 2004, she was commissioned to produce a book documenting the architecture and altars of the Museo Nacional del Virreinato in Mexico.

Meta (Mari Carmen Hernández Álvarez) is a Mexican artist and architect based between Paris and Troncones, Mexico. She studied architecture at university, where Luis Barragán was one of her mentors. Since the early 1990s, she has lived and worked between France and Mexico, developing her artistic practice while creating most of her paintings in her studio in Troncones. She works primarily in oil, producing portraits, seascapes, and abstract paintings. Her work reflects a close connection to nature, everyday life, and the dialogue between Mexican and French culture.

Her best-known series include Acaba de Pasar, inspired by the horizon and the sea, Faces, a collection of portraits, Xochitl, dedicated to flowers, and In-Adaptés, created during the pandemic. Her portraits have been exhibited in Paris, Madrid, Washington, San Antonio, São Paulo, and San Miguel de Allende. In 1995, they were published in the book Faces by Franco Maria Ricci. Alongside her artistic practice, Meta has supported educational initiatives in Troncones through the organization Las Hermanas and has contributed artworks to projects benefiting the local community.

Iracema Arditi (1 February 1924 - 4 October 2006) was a Brazilian painter born in São Paulo, where she also died. In 1972, she founded the Museu do Sol, a museum dedicated to naïve art, originally established in São Paulo and now located in Penápolis.

In 1985, Arditi was awarded the title of Chevalier of the Order of Arts and Letters in recognition of her contribution to the arts.

Graciela Iturbide (born 1942) is a Mexican photographer whose work has been exhibited internationally and is included in major museum collections, including the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and The J. Paul Getty Museum. Born in Mexico City, she grew up in a traditional Catholic family as the eldest of thirteen children. She became interested in photography at an early age after receiving her first camera when she was eleven. In 1970, following the death of her daughter Claudia, she decided to study photography at the Centro Universitario de Estudios Cinematográficos at the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, where she was mentored by photographer Manuel Álvarez Bravo. She traveled with Bravo between 1970 and 1971 and was awarded the W. Eugene Smith Grant in 1971.

Working almost exclusively in black and white, Iturbide photographs everyday life, focusing on identity, rituals, festivals, daily life, death, and the role of women. She has documented indigenous communities including the Zapotec, Mixtec, and Seri peoples, as well as life in Mexico City, Oaxaca, and along the Mexican-American border. Among her best-known projects are the Seri People series, the decade-long Juchitán de las Mujeres, and iconic photographs such as Mujer Ángel and Nuestra Señora de Las Iguanas. Her work has also explored communities in Argentina, India, and the United States. A founding member of the Mexican Council of Photography, she continues to live and work in Coyoacán, Mexico.

Frida Kahlo (1907 - 1954) was a Mexican painter best known for her portraits, self-portraits, and works inspired by the nature, culture, and traditions of Mexico. Born in Coyoacán, Mexico City, she grew up in a traditional Catholic family and developed an interest in art from an early age. After a severe bus accident at the age of eighteen left her with lifelong pain and medical complications, she began painting during her recovery. She studied at the Centro Universitario de Estudios Cinematográficos at the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, where photographer Manuel Álvarez Bravo became her mentor. In 1927, she joined the Mexican Communist Party and married muralist Diego Rivera in 1929. Together they traveled throughout Mexico and the United States, while Kahlo developed her distinctive artistic style inspired by Mexican folk culture and autobiographical experience.

Kahlo's work explores identity, gender, class, race, pain, and Mexican cultural traditions, combining realism with fantasy and symbolic imagery. She became known for her self-portraits and for documenting her own physical and emotional experiences. Among her best-known works are The Dream (The Bed), The Two Fridas, The Broken Column, and Viva La Vida. During her career, she exhibited in New York, Paris, Mexico, and the United States, becoming the first Mexican artist whose work entered the Louvre collection. She also taught at the Escuela Nacional de Pintura, Escultura y Grabado 'La Esmeralda' and was a founding member of the Seminario de Cultura Mexicana. Although her work remained relatively little known during her lifetime, it gained international recognition from the late 1970s onward and today is regarded as a major contribution to modern art and Mexican cultural identity.

Águeda Lozano (born 1944, Cuauhtémoc, Chihuahua, Mexico) is a Mexican visual artist specializing in abstract painting and sculpture. She studied at the Taller de Artes Plásticas of the Universidad Autónoma de Nuevo León between 1960 and 1964. Since 1971, she has lived and worked in Paris, where she developed her career after receiving a studio at the Cité Internationale des Arts and presenting her first solo exhibition at Galerie du Haut Pavé.

Throughout her career, Lozano has exhibited extensively in international biennials, salons, and galleries in Mexico and France. In 1975, she was invited by Fernando Gamboa to exhibit at the Museo de Arte Moderno in Mexico City. In 2006, she became the first Mexican artist to install a permanent sculpture in a Parisian public square with Tierra de México en Tierra de Francia at Place du Mexique. She received the Médaille Haute Assemblée from the French Senate in 2013. Since 2014, she has directed the Espacio Cultural Águeda Lozano in Mexico. Her sculptures and paintings have also been presented in major public exhibitions in Mexico, including at the Palacio de Bellas Artes and the Universidad Autónoma de Chihuahua.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Mexico (Mexico) and in Madrid (Spain)
Biography:
Teresa Margolles (born 1963 in Culiacán) is a Mexican conceptual artist, photographer, videographer, and performance artist. As an artist she researches the social causes and consequences of death.

Margolles communicates observations from the morgue in her home city, Mexico City, and other morgues located in Latin America, as well as the extended emotional distress and social consequences that occur as product of death by murder. While working around the topic of the body, her work extends to the families of the victims, the remaining living bodies that witness the death of a loved one.

The main medium of her work comes from the morgues themselves, which she transforms into sensory experiences that provoke a feeling of memory to the audience. Margolles finds particularly remarkable how the activity inside the morgues reflects the truth from the outside. In the case of Mexico City, she observes that the majority of victims belong to the lower classes. 'Looking at the dead you see society'.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in London (United Kingdom)
Biography:
Alicia Paz (born 1967, Mexico City) is a Mexican artist based in London. Raised in Mexico, she graduated from the University of California, Berkeley in 1989 before continuing her studies at the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris, Goldsmiths College in London, and the Royal College of Art, where she received an MA in Painting in 2008.

Paz's practice explores the relationship between illusion and representation through painting, focusing on hybridity, metamorphosis, and the female figure. Her works combine references to art history, advertising, and comics, creating portraits and landscapes in which human, animal, and plant forms merge into fluid, fantastical compositions. In 2017, she unveiled her first public sculpture, *Insel der Puppen (Island of Dolls)*, at the Kunstmuseum Kloster Unser Lieben Frauen in Magdeburg.

Supported by Arts Council England, Paz developed a research project exploring networks of women in her personal and professional life, resulting in the exhibitions *Río y Mar* (2021), *River Makers* (2021), and *Juntas* (2022). In 2024, her solo exhibition *Explorations au féminin* was presented at the Château de Haroué in France. In 2026, she presented *Odisea* at Drexel Gallery in Monterrey, featuring works that explore water and ceramic traditions from a hybrid and feminist perspective.

Tania Pérez Córdova (b. 1979) is a Mexican artist born in Mexico City where she lives and works. After studying at the school of Fine Arts in Mexico City, she went on to get a BA in Fine Art at Goldsmiths College in London.

Tania Pérez Córdova uses a large range of media, namely sculpture, found objects and installation, but also photography and performance, through which she explores the contextual relationship between everyday objects. The visual elements she presents are meant to be understood in the context of a larger narrative to which the titles give the keys - the artist likes to refer to her works as 'situations'.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Mexico (Mexico) and in Oaxaca (Mexico)
Biography: Naomi Rincón Gallardo is a visual artist. Her work constructs imaginary narratives, often inspired by Mesoamerican myths, stories and accounts of resistance against heteropatriarchal and colonial dispossession. In her stories, ancestral beliefs combine with contemporary aesthetic references, such as DIY and queer aesthetics, creating a universe that is visually saturated and abundant, but also familiar in its almost handcrafted construction. Some of her notorious works include Sangre pesada (2018), Resiliencia Tlacuache (2019). Her exhibitions include the Berlin Biennial (2020) and the Venice Biennial (2022).

Betsabeé Romero (born 1963) is a Mexican visual artist whose practice spans sculpture, installation, printmaking, perforated paper, photography, and video. She has presented more than forty solo exhibitions across the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Europe. Romero describes herself as a 'mechanic artist', working with everyday materials such as used tires, automobile parts, and chewing gum.

Combining these industrial materials with traditional Mexican symbols and imagery, Romero explores the intersections of history, culture, and the contradictions of modernity. Her work reflects on themes including migration, gender roles, cultural traditions, religiosity, and cultural hybridity, connecting the history and identity of Mexico with broader contemporary and global contexts.

Mariana Yampolsky (1925 - 2002) was a Mexican-American photographer known for documenting everyday life in rural Mexico. Born in Chicago, Illinois, she studied social sciences at the University of Chicago before moving to Mexico in 1945 to study art. She joined the Taller de Gráfica Popular and became a Mexican citizen in 1958, remaining in the country for the rest of her life.

Yampolsky began using photography to document her travels and artistic work before establishing it as the focus of her practice in the 1960s. Her photographs captured ordinary people and rural communities throughout Mexico, becoming a significant contribution to twentieth-century Mexican photography. Her work was widely exhibited internationally and received numerous awards and recognitions during her lifetime and after her death in 2002.

Derek Dellekamp is a Mexican architect born in 1971 in Mexico City. He lives and works in Mexico.

Rozana Montiel is a Mexican architect and the founder and director of Rozana Montiel Estudio de Arquitectura, an interdisciplinary architecture studio based in Mexico City. She studied Architecture and Urban Planning at Universidad Iberoamericana, graduating with honors in 1998, and completed a Master's degree in Architectural Theory and Criticism at the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya in 2000. After working with architect Diego Villaseñor, she founded her own practice in 2009. Her work focuses on socially conscious, community-oriented, and sustainable design, ranging from small-scale objects to urban interventions. Her projects have been exhibited internationally, including in Mexico, Spain, France, the United States, England, China, and at the Venice, São Paulo, Rotterdam, Lima, and Chile Biennials. She has received several international awards, including the Emerging Voices Award (2016), the Moira Gemmill Award (2017), and the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture (2019).

Euridice Zaituna Kala graduated in Experimental Photography at Market Photo Workshop, Johannesburg, South Africa in 2012. Euridice Zaituna Kala is the laureate of the research residencies with the Villa Albertine season 2022/2023 in New York and was also laureate of the Bourse Villa Vassilieff/ ADAGP (2019/2020). She has presented numerous performances, including Sea(E)scapes: Séance d'écoute at the Jeu de Paume, Paris in 2022. Her work will also be included in the 5th edition of the Casablanca Biennale (2022-2023). She is also founder and co-organizer of e.a.s.t. (Ephemeral Archival Station), a laboratory and platform for artistic research projects, established in 2017.

Tuli Mekondjo (b. 1982) is a self-taught Namibian artist whose work explores the construction of identity in the shadow of Namibia's violent past as both a German and later South African colony. She uses a variety of media including natural silks, embroidery, photo-transfer, soil, paint, resin and mahangu (millet) grain, a staple food in Namibia, to reframe imagery from historical photographs from both the German colonial period (1884-1919) and subsequent occupation by South Africa. Mekondjo’s multilayered works result from a process of both literal and figurative burial and retrieval, and draw heavily on photographic representations of indigenous Namibian people from multiple ethnic groups.

Mekondjo also has a performance practice which extends the her archival research and interventions, and locates her personally in the context of Namibian history. The presence of female ancestors is particularly important for Mekondjo, whose connection to her mother and grandmother are the beginning of a cycle of connections to female ancestors stretching back in time. This ties her performances to her two-dimensional works, which often have images of wombs and foetuses embroidered onto them, metaphorically connecting the beginnings of life to the soil and to women.

Mekondjo, whose name means “we are in the struggle”, was born in Angola to Namibian parents who joined SWAPO (South West Africa Peoples' Organisation) in exile in the early 1980s. She has exhibited widely in Namibia, South Africa, France, the United States, Hong Kong and Germany. In 2022 she became the first black Namibian woman ever to exhibit in the United States, where she is co-represented by Hales. In 2023, her work was shown at Frieze London, Art Central Hong Kong, EXPO Chicago, ARCO Lisboa and Art Joburg. She is represented in multiple international collections.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in New York (New York, United States) and in Lagos (Nigeria)
Biography:
Oroma Elewa is a Nigerian visual and performance artist, writer, and creative director. Her multidisciplinary practice examines the impact of social constructs on identity, behavior, and self-expression, exploring themes of contemporary womanhood, Black identity, the African diaspora, and the experience of inhabiting a Black body. She first gained international recognition as the founder, editor-in-chief, and publisher of *Pop’Africana*, a magazine launched in 2009 that presented contemporary African fashion, style, and culture to a global audience. The publication ran until 2014.

Since 2017, Elewa has expanded her practice through writing and performance. Her book *Crushed Guava Leaves* brings together poems and stories conceived as texts for performance, while her ongoing project *Area Babes & Ashawo Superstars*, launched in 2019, uses the language of internet memes and Nollywood imagery to examine class, power, sexuality, and African feminism. Through these projects, Elewa continues to explore cultural narratives and create spaces for dialogue around identity, gender, and representation.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in London (United Kingdom) since 2015
Biography:
Rahima Gambo is a multidisciplinary artist based between London, UK, and Abuja, Nigeria. Working across photography, moving image, and installation, her practice explores the intersections of documentary, biography, memory, and place. Her process is shaped by repetition and long-term engagement, with recurring visits to sites that become central to her work. She graduated from the Columbia Graduate School of Journalism and was a Magnum Foundation Fellow in 2014.

Gambo's ongoing project *Tatsuniya* (2017-present), developed in collaboration with students at Shehu Sanda Kyarimi School in Maiduguri, Nigeria, brought international recognition to her practice. Her work has been presented at major international exhibitions, including the Diriyah Biennale (2026), Gasworks London (2024), Liverpool Biennial (2023), Kunsthalle Bern (2022), Rencontres d'Arles (2022), the Mercosur Biennial (2020), the Yokohama Triennale (2020), the Lagos Biennale (2019), and the Rencontres de Bamako (2017-2019).

Adéọlá Ọlágúnjú is a Nigerian visual artist working with photography, video, sound, and installation. Growing up in Nigeria during the period of military dictatorship, her experiences have shaped a practice that reflects on transformation, memory, and the idea that 'rebirth comes with chaos, confusion, and destruction'. She received a bachelor's degree in Fine and Applied Arts from Ladoke Akintola University of Technology in 2009 and completed a master's degree in Photography Studies and Practice at the Folkwang University of the Arts in Essen, Germany, in 2021.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Princeton (New Jersey, United States)
Biography:
Marcia Kure (born 1970, Kano State, Nigeria) is a Nigerian visual artist known for her mixed-media paintings and drawings exploring identity, history, gender, and the legacy of colonialism. She studied painting at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, graduating in 1994 under the guidance of Obiora Udechukwu. She currently lives and works between Princeton, New Jersey, and Abuja and Kaduna, Nigeria.

Kure's practice combines painting, drawing, textiles, and traditional African pigments such as kola nut and coffee. Her work is deeply influenced by the contemporary uli tradition and is characterized by linear forms, bold shapes, and symbolic motifs. Recurring images of veiled women, first introduced in *Purdah* (1992), examine the relationships between gender, power, motherhood, fashion, and political identity. Her later works also reflect on expatriation and cultural hybridity, bringing together African visual traditions with Western artistic references.

Her work has been exhibited internationally in museums and galleries across Africa, Europe, and the United States. She is represented by Susan Inglett Gallery in New York, Purdy Hicks Gallery in London, and Officine Dell'Immagine in Milan.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in New York (New York, United States)
Biography:
Emily Jacir (born 1970) is a Palestinian artist and filmmaker based in Bethlehem, Palestine. Raised in Saudi Arabia, she attended high school in Italy before studying art at the University of Dallas and earning an MFA from the Memphis College of Art. In 1998, she attended the Whitney Independent Study Program in New York. She divides her time between Bethlehem and New York City.

Jacir's multidisciplinary practice spans film, photography, installation, performance, video, writing, and sound. Her work explores transformation, resistance, displacement, exile, and silenced historical narratives, with a particular focus on the Palestinian experience. Since 1994, she has exhibited internationally across the Americas, Europe, and the Middle East, presenting solo exhibitions in cities including New York, Los Angeles, Ramallah, Beirut, London, and Linz.

Alongside her artistic practice, Jacir has played an active role in developing Palestine's contemporary art scene. She founded the International Video Festival in Ramallah in 2002, taught at the International Academy of Art Palestine, and established Dar Yusuf Nasri Jacir for Art and Research in Bethlehem, a community and contemporary art space. In 2023, she collaborated with artist Baha Hilo on *Preserve*, a project dedicated to the restoration of the olive terraces at Dar Jacir.

Jumana Manna (born 1987) is a Palestinian visual artist working across installation, film, and sculpture. Born in Princeton, New Jersey, she lived in Jerusalem and Oslo before settling in Berlin. She studied at the Oslo National Academy of the Arts and completed a Master's degree in Aesthetics and Politics at the California Institute of the Arts.

Manna's multidisciplinary practice explores preservation, agriculture, science, law, and the political implications of cultural and environmental heritage. Her films and installations investigate the relationships between memory, land, identity, and systems of control. Notable works include *A Magical Substance Flows Into Me* (2015), *Wild Relatives* (2017), and *Foragers* (2022), which examines the impact of restrictions on the gathering of wild plants in Palestine.

Her work has been exhibited internationally at institutions including the Museum of Modern Art, MoMA PS1, the Museum van Hedendaagse Kunst Antwerpen, and the Wexner Center for the Arts. In 2021, she presented the exhibition *Thirty Plumbers in the Belly* in Antwerp, followed by her first major U.S. museum exhibition, *Break, Take, Erase, Tally*, at MoMA PS1 (2022–2023). In 2024, *Foragers* was exhibited at the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art in Seoul.

Raeda Saadeh (born 1977) is a Palestinian artist working across photography, installation, and performance. Born in Umm al-Fahm, she studied at the Bezalel Academy of Arts and Design in Jerusalem, where she received both her BFA and MFA, and later continued her studies at the School of Visual Arts. She lives and works in Jerusalem.

Saadeh's practice explores themes of identity and the Palestinian experience through staged photographs, installations, and performances. In 2000, she received the Young Artist of the Year Award from the A. M. Qattan Foundation. A monograph of her work, *Raeda Saadeh: Reframing Palestine*, edited by Rose Issa, was published in 2012.

Her work is included in the collections of the Victoria and Albert Museum, the Fonds régional d'art contemporain de Lorraine, and Le Magasin.

Sandra Eleta (born 1942) is a Panamanian artist and photographer. Born in Panama City as Sandra Eleta Boyd, she studied Fine Arts at Finch College in New York before continuing her education in Social Investigation at The New School for Social Research. In the 1970s, she studied photography at the International Center of Photography (ICP) under Ken Heyman and George Tice, later teaching at the Universidad Nacional de Costa Rica. Since the mid-1970s, she has lived and worked in Portobelo, Panama.

Eleta is recognized for her socially engaged documentary photography, which explores the lives of people from different social backgrounds across Latin America. Her long-term photographic practice is rooted in close observation and human relationships. One of her best-known works, *The One with the Feather Duster* (1977), was featured in the exhibition *Radical Women: Latin American Art, 1960-1985* at the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles in 2017.

Elsa Cayo (also known as Elsa Cayo Cordova; born 1951 in Lima, Peru) is a Peruvian-born filmmaker, and photographer.Her work is included in the collections of the Museum of Modern Art, New York, the Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec, Centre Pompidou, and the National Gallery of Canada.

Lives / Works: Lives in Lima (Peru) and in Mexico (Mexico)
Biography: XIMENA GARRIDO-LECCA (b. Lima, 1980) lives and works between Mexico City and Lima. Recent solo exhibitions include Reverse Engineering at CAN Centre d’art Neuchâtel, Switzerland (2023), and Inflorescence at Portikus, Frankfurt (2022). Her works have also been featured in major international exhibitions such as the 2025 Sharjah Biennial; the 5th Kochi-Muziris Biennale, India, and the 34th Bienal de São Paulo, and are included in public collections such as Tate Modern, London; Boros Collection, Berlin, Germany; Kadist Foundation, Paris/ San Francisco; The Staatsgalerie, Stuttgart; the Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires (MALBA), Argentina; and Museo de Arte de Lima, among others.

Daniela Ortiz (born 1986, Peru) is a Peruvian artist based in Cuzco. Her multidisciplinary practice explores the intersections of nationality, race, class, and gender, critically examining colonial, patriarchal, and capitalist systems of power. Her work investigates European migration policies, colonial legacies, and institutional violence against racialized and migrant communities, while also addressing labor exploitation and class relations in Peru. Working across ceramics, collage, publications, and children's books, Ortiz has increasingly shifted toward manual and material-based practices that challenge the aesthetics of Eurocentric conceptual art.

Alongside her artistic practice, Ortiz is a researcher, educator, and activist who regularly participates in public talks, workshops, and discussions on migration, coloniality, and anti-racism. She received the Barcelona Producció grant and the Grupo Investigación Península grant from Museo Reina Sofía in 2013, and completed a residency at Darat al Funun in Jordan the same year. In 2017, she published the anti-racist children's book *ABC of Racist Europe*, made freely available online.

Her recent solo exhibitions include *The Children of the Communists* at Kunstverein Wiesbaden (2022–2023), *And We Will Grasp the Knowledge of Our Resistances* at Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo (2022–2023), *Nurtured by the Defeat of the Colonizers Our Seeds Will Raise* at Kölnischer Kunstverein (2021), and *This Land Jamás Será Fértil por Haber Parido Colonos* at La Virreina Centre de la Imatge, Barcelona (2019). Her work has also been presented in group exhibitions at Palais de Tokyo, EMST National Museum of Contemporary Art Athens, Ludwig Museum Cologne, Arnhem Museum, and CIVA Brussels, among others.

Ortiz's works are held in major public collections, including Museo Reina Sofía (Madrid), MACBA (Barcelona), Museo de Arte de Lima (MALI), CNAP - Centre national des arts plastiques (Paris), Cisneros Fontanals Art Foundation (Miami), and CA2M (Madrid).

Xosé Quiroga (born 1979, Ourense, Spain) is a Spanish artist, photographer, and researcher. He holds a degree in Law and a qualification in Artistic Photography. His work has been presented in exhibitions across Spain, the United States, Peru, Sweden, Italy, England, France, and Australia.

Quiroga is co-director of the Institute for the Community Monitoring of Contaminated Areas, a founding member of the photographic collective Groundpress, coordinator of the Voizes Archive, and a member of the cooperative Càmeres i Acció. His interdisciplinary practice creates spaces of tension that examine race, class, nationality, and gender, focusing on the mechanisms of inclusion and exclusion that shape contemporary societies.

In recent years, his research has centered on international migration control systems and the policies implemented by receiving states, investigating how borders, surveillance, and institutional frameworks reinforce inequality and exclusion.

She received the Barcelona Producció grant and the Grupo Investigación Península grant from Museo Reina Sofía in 2013, and completed a residency at Darat al Funun in Jordan the same year. In 2017, she published the anti-racist children's book *ABC of Racist Europe*, made freely available online.

Her recent solo exhibitions include *The Children of the Communists* at Kunstverein Wiesbaden (2022–2023), *And We Will Grasp the Knowledge of Our Resistances* at Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo (2022–2023), *Nurtured by the Defeat of the Colonizers Our Seeds Will Raise* at Kölnischer Kunstverein (2021), and *This Land Jamás Será Fértil por Haber Parido Colonos* at La Virreina Centre de la Imatge, Barcelona (2019). Her work has also been presented in group exhibitions at Palais de Tokyo, EMST National Museum of Contemporary Art Athens, Ludwig Museum Cologne, Arnhem Museum, and CIVA Brussels, among others.

Ortiz's works are held in major public collections, including Museo Reina Sofía (Madrid), MACBA (Barcelona), Museo de Arte de Lima (MALI), CNAP - Centre national des arts plastiques (Paris), Cisneros Fontanals Art Foundation (Miami), and CA2M (Madrid).

Milagros de la Torre is a Peruvian artist based in New York. Since the 1990s, her practice has explored photography as a conceptual medium, examining systems of representation, identity, power, and cultural memory. After leaving Peru early in her career, she lived and worked in London, Paris, and Mexico City before settling in New York.

De la Torre's work has been widely exhibited internationally and is held in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York. She received a Guggenheim Fellowship in Creative Arts - Photography in 2011 and a Smithsonian Artist Research Fellowship in 2021. She also serves on the Advisory Board of the Penumbra Foundation in New York.

Alongside her artistic practice, De la Torre has been active as an educator and lecturer. In 2023, she was appointed Wolf Chair in Photography at The Cooper Union. She has delivered lectures and artist talks at institutions including New York University, Columbia University, Parsons School of Design, the International Center of Photography, Pratt Institute, the School of the Museum of Fine Arts at Tufts University, Artpace, Americas Society, Museo de Arte de Lima (MALI), MALBA, and the School of Visual Arts.

Maya Watanabe (b.1983 in Lima, Peru) is known for her multi-channel video installations in which the unspeakable becomes present, not by being voiced, but by its effect being made tangible. She makes tangible the tension and the ongoing process of creeping violence that is characteristic of the internal conflict in her home country Peru, which gradually but persistently changes everyday life and produces gaps in the emotional landscapes of the people affected by it.

Watanabe work has been exhibited in numerous solo and group exhibitions at Asian Art Biennial, National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts, Taichung (2019); Coimbra Biennial of Contemporary Art, Coimbra (2019); 13th Havana Biennial (2019); MAXXI, Rome (2019); Art Museum of Lima (2019); Palais de Tokyo, Paris (2019); 13th Media Arts Biennial, National Museum of Fine Arts, Santiago (2017); Kyoto Art Center (2017); Fridericianum, Kassel (2016); Kadist Foundation, San Francisco (2016); Matadero, Madrid (2014); Frestas: Art Triennial, São Paulo (2014); Lima Photography Biennial (2014); Pantallas del Video Arte Peruano, Fundación Telefónica, Lima (2010); V Marmara Triennial, Istanbul (2010); Beijing Biennale, (2009); Amsterdam Mediamatic Biennale (2009); and Contemporary Art Festival FAC, Básico Art Collective, Lima (2006). In 2021 she participated in Genealogies in the Middle East and Latin America (Sharjah Art Foundation).

Among Watanabe's awards are ARCOmadrid Award, Hans Nefkens Foundation, Madrid (2018); DAFO Peruvian National Competition of Experimental Films, Lima (2016); 19th Festival Internacional SESC_VIDEOBRASIL, Res Artis residency prize, Kyoto Art Center; (2015); Videoakt, International Videoart Biennial, LOOP Fair, Barcelona (2011); and FIVA, Festival Internacional de Videoarte Almirante Brown, Buenos Aires (2011). She has participated in residencies at The Watermill Center, New York (2019); Kyoto Art Center (2016); Matadero Madrid, Spain (2012); and Cité Internationale des Arts, Paris (2010).

Eisa Jocson, born in 1986, is a contemporary choreographer and dancer from the Philippines with a background in ballet and trained in the visual arts. She has been commissioned by and toured extensively in major contemporary art festivals with her solo triptych: Death of the Pole Dancer (2011), Macho Dancer (2013) and Host (2015). She exposes body politics in the service and entertainment industry as seen through the unique socioeconomic lens of the Philippines. Jocson studies how the body moves and the conditions behind migrant workers' mobility across levels of society and international borders. In all her chosen subjects and mediums - from pole, macho dancing, hostessing to depictions of Disney princesses- capital is the driv- ing force of movement pushing the indentured body into spatial geographies.

Eisa Jocson is the winner of recent Hugo Boss Asia Art Award 2019; commissioned by Sharjah Biennale 2019; recipient of the 2018 Cultural Centre of the Philippines 13 Artists Award; elect- ed as one of the outstanding contemporary productions for the 2018 edition of Tanzplattform, Germany and clinched the Zurcher Kantonallbank Acknowledgement Prize at Zurich Theater Spektakel in 2013.

Nena Saguil (September 19, 1914 - February, 1994) was a Filipina artist of modernist and abstract paintings and ink drawings. She was most known for her cosmic, organic, and spiritual abstract works depicting internal landscapes of feeling and imagination. For these, Saguil is considered a pioneer of Filipino abstract art.

Elisa (Siau Hua) Y. Tan (January 8, 1937 - January 7, 2022) was a Filipino-Chinese conceptual artist who was born in a small village in Southern China and moved to Manila when she was only a year old. She grew up and was schooled in Manila and went to the University of the Philippines Diliman to earn a BA in Fine Arts in1963. She left for the US in 1964 for artist residencies in New York and Ohio including a National Endowment for the Arts fellowship from 1970 to 1974. She moved to Europe shortly after and started another string of residences beginning with one from the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam. She settled in Paris for the next two years, where her art career, now spanning five decades, floated in between obscurity and recognition, never completely breaking through, despite prestigious residencies, public acquisitions, and solo exhibits. Her early efforts as a painter of large-scale canvases garnered significant recognition in the middle to late '70s in New York, but it was not until she moved to Paris in the ‘70s that her intellectual efforts to merge word, image, and the everyday began to reach their most sustained following.

In 1995, Tan did her last public show at the Galerie Entre Temps at Espace Eiffel Braly in Paris. At this point, she underwent a spiritual crisis and did not create any form of public art for her remaining years in Paris. She left Europe and moved to her ancestral village in China for eight months, conversing with Buddhism and eastern mysticism until, she says in her memoir, she chanced upon a local evangelical Christian church and converted to Christianity. She moved on to Baguio to lead a largely solitary but highly spiritual life. Much of the art she had created was stored in her attic, still packed in the crates shipped from Paris in 1995.

For the next 27 years she lived a rather private life in Baguio, acquiring a three-story house where she lived by herself. She had become very involved in a local church and was a well-loved fixture in the community. When she had a mild heart attack in 2009, se began to think of revisiting her art, but this time, dedicating any future work or sales to raise money to fund her various humanitarian projects with the local church in Baguio. On January 6, 2022, she passed away at the age of 85, just a few days after she had expressed wanting to find a way to recreate some of her well-known art performances, or exhibit her art. Her entire oeuvre as well as her papers are now being catalogued and archived under the custodianship of her estate.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Riyad (Saudi Arabia) and in London (United Kingdom)
Biography:
Maha Malluh is a Saudi artist based in Riyadh. She works between London & Vienna. Malluh began exhibiting her art in 1976. Since then, she has become an internationally acclaimed artist, gaining recognition from important institutions.

She has a BA in English Literature from King Saud University in Riyadh and a certificate in Design and Photography from De Anza College in California. She has been exhibiting in Saudi Arabia and internationally while continuing to radically develop her practice. Malluh's more recent work is considered her most experimental.

Her artworks examine the emblematic and cultural symbols of Saudi Arabian civilization and hinge on globalization, as well as its effect on the urban population in Saudi Arabia, the rural environment, and material culture in the Kingdom.

Over the past years, she has explored, experimented with, and expanded the art of the photogram. This art form is an early turn-of-the-century technique invented by Fox Talbot, which captures a photographic image without a camera by exposing photosensitive paper directly to a light source. The arrangement of objects interrupting the passage of light determines the photogram's appearance. These photograms chronicle the great changes that have continued to occur in Saudi Arabia over recent decades, with the resulting clashes between tradition and modernity. Her most recent work includes mixed media installations, which use found objects that can be seen as historical symbols of collective Saudi identity. Among these items are massive enameled dishes, cassette tapes of religious lectures, discarded oil barrels, and metal doors typical of the region.

Marina Abramović (born 1946, Belgrade, Serbia) is a Serbian conceptual and performance artist whose work has fundamentally shaped the field of contemporary performance art. For more than five decades, her practice has explored endurance, the body, memory, vulnerability, and the relationship between performer and audience, often pushing physical and psychological limits. Abramović is widely regarded as one of the pioneers of performance art and has described herself as the 'grandmother of performance art'. In 2007, she founded the Marina Abramović Institute (MAI), dedicated to the preservation and development of long-duration performance.

Born in Belgrade, then part of Yugoslavia, Abramović studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Belgrade before beginning her groundbreaking performance practice in the early 1970s. Her early works established a new language of body art through acts of endurance, risk, and direct audience participation. Throughout her career, she has exhibited and performed internationally, becoming one of the most influential figures in contemporary art.

Abramović's work has been presented at major museums and biennials worldwide, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York, where her retrospective *The Artist Is Present* (2010) became one of the most significant performance art exhibitions in museum history. Her practice continues to investigate the transformative potential of performance, presence, and human connection.

Ulay (Frank Uwe Laysiepen, 1943-2020) was a German artist whose pioneering practice spanned photography, performance, and body art. Based for many years in Amsterdam and later in Ljubljana, he gained international recognition for his experimental Polaroid works and for the influential performances he created with Marina Abramović. His work explored identity, gender, relationships, and the limits of the body, making him a key figure in the development of performance art.

After moving to Amsterdam in the early 1970s, Ulay began experimenting with Polaroid photography, producing autobiographical and self-reflective works that challenged conventional ideas of gender and identity. His early series *Renais sense* (1974) featured constructed self-portraits that questioned fixed notions of masculinity and femininity, establishing themes that would continue throughout his career.

From 1976 to 1988, Ulay collaborated closely with Marina Abramović on a series of landmark performances that examined trust, endurance, and human relationships. Following their artistic partnership, he continued to develop an independent practice centered on photography, performance, and socially engaged projects, exhibiting internationally until his death in 2020.
