Birth / death: 1909, Serbie-Monténégro - 1945, New York (New York, United States)
Biography:
Milena Pavlović-Barili (1909 - 1945) was a Serbian painter, poet, and illustrator, and one of the leading figures of Serbian modernism. Born in Požarevac to an Italian father and a Serbian mother from the Karađorđević lineage, she studied at the Royal School of Arts in Belgrade before continuing her artistic education in Munich. During the 1930s, she lived and worked in Spain, Italy, France, and England, where she encountered the work of leading European modernists, including Giorgio de Chirico, Jean Cocteau, and André Breton, whose ideas influenced the dreamlike and symbolic character of her paintings.

In 1939, Pavlović-Barili moved to New York, where she established a successful career as an illustrator for magazines including *Vogue* and *Harper's Bazaar* through the J. Walter Thompson advertising agency. In 1943, her work was included in Peggy Guggenheim's landmark exhibition *Exhibition by 31 Women* at the Art of This Century gallery in New York. Alongside illustration, she continued to develop a distinctive artistic language combining surreal, metaphysical, and symbolic imagery.

Her paintings frequently feature portraits, biblical references, angels, classical sculptures, veils, and dreamlike figures arranged in enigmatic compositions. Pavlović-Barili died in New York in 1945 at the age of thirty-five. Today, her work is held in major collections, including the Museum of Contemporary Art in Belgrade, and the house where she was born in Požarevac has been transformed into a museum dedicated to her life and work.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Venice (Californie, United States) and in Singapore (Singapore)
Biography:
Ana Prvački (born 1976) is a Serbian-born interdisciplinary visual artist whose practice spans performance, video, film, sculpture, painting, augmented reality, and immersive installations. Born in the former Yugoslavia to a Romanian mother and a Serbian father, she later moved to Singapore, where she continued her artistic education alongside studies in classical flute, theatre, and beekeeping. Since 2002, she has developed a conceptual practice exploring themes of etiquette, hospitality, music, ritual, communication, and social behavior through humor and participation.

Prvački has presented her work internationally at institutions including Gropius Bau (Berlin), the de Young Museum (San Francisco), the Hammer Museum (Los Angeles), the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum (Boston), and through a commission by the Los Angeles Philharmonic. She has also participated in major international exhibitions such as documenta 13, the Gwangju Biennial, the Sydney Biennial, the Bangkok Art Biennale, the Chicago Architecture Biennial, and the Istanbul Biennial.

From 2018 to 2019, Prvački was artist-in-residence at the de Young Museum, culminating in the solo exhibition *Detour*. In 2023, Sternberg Press published her book of watercolors with an essay by Zadie Smith. Her works are held in the collections of the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles (MOCA), the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), Castello di Rivoli Museo d'Arte Contemporanea, and n.b.k. Artothek in Berlin, among others. In 2025, she was shortlisted for the Gabriele Münter Prize.

Katarina ZDJELAR (1979, Serbia) is an artist based in Rotterdam. She completed her MFA at the Piet Zwart Institute and makes videos, sound pieces, book projects and different platforms. Her work investigates subjectivity and communication in a foreign language when a mental and physical struggle with language occurs. She exhibits solo and in group shows and is selected regularly for international film festivals.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Amsterdam (Netherlands) and in Khartoum (Sudan)
Biography: Ola Hassanain (b. 1985, Khartoum) is an artist currently based in Amsterdam. Her work considers the politics of habitation, moving through architecture, film, performance and installation to reflect on how ecological and social systems shape one another across time, as well as on how power becomes visible and felt through built environments. Her solo exhibitions include The Watcher (Tell The Waters What The Clay Kept Secret III), Kunstinstitut Melly, Rotterdam (2025) and Whispers (Tell The Waters What The Clay Kept Secret II), Büro Stedelijk, Amsterdam (2024). Her group exhibitions include The Woman Who Thought She Was A Planet, Border Buda Project, Brussels (2025); All That We Have Built, Naughton Gallery, Queen's University, Belfast (2025); Triënnale van Beetsterzwaag,  Kunsthuis SYB (2024); the 3rd Chicago Architecture Biennial (2019).

Candice Breitz (born 1972) is a South African artist working primarily with video, photography, and multi-channel installations. Born in Johannesburg, she studied at the University of the Witwatersrand, the University of Chicago, and Columbia University. Her practice examines contemporary media culture, celebrity, identity, migration, and the politics of representation, often using appropriated footage from popular culture to explore how personal and collective narratives are shaped through mass media.

Breitz has exhibited extensively at leading museums and international biennials. In 2017, she represented South Africa at the 57th Venice Biennale. Her acclaimed installation *Love Story* (2016) juxtaposes the testimonies of refugees from Syria, Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, India, Venezuela, and Somalia with performances by well-known actors, questioning the role of celebrity in shaping public empathy. Her work also includes performance, photography, and large-scale video installations that investigate identity, spectatorship, and the global attention economy.

Breitz received the Prince Pierre of Monaco Prize in 2007 and has presented solo exhibitions internationally, including *Whiteface* at Fotografiska Berlin in 2023. Her work is represented by Goodman Gallery, KOW Berlin, and kaufmann repetto, and is held in major public and private collections worldwide.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Johannesburg (South Africa)
Biography: Gabrielle Goliath (born 1983 in Kimberley, South Africa) is a South African contemporary artist who lives and works in Johannesburg, South Africa. Goliath is recognized for her immersive installations and performances that confront themes of violence, memory, and identity. Her work often centers on the experiences of marginalized communities. She is a researcher at the Institute for Creative Arts at the University of Cape Town, where her research continues to explore ethical strategies for addressing violence and absence in contemporary art.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Kimberley (South Africa)
Biography:
Bronwyn Katz (born 1993) is a South African sculptor and visual artist whose interdisciplinary practice encompasses sculpture, installation, video, and performance. Born in Kimberley, South Africa, Katz graduated with a Bachelor of Fine Arts from the University of Cape Town in 2015, where they received the Simon Gerson Prize. They are a founding member of iQhiya, a collective of young Black womxn artists based in Cape Town and Johannesburg.

Katz's work explores the relationship between land, memory, and history, considering the landscape as a repository of lived experience and collective remembrance. Through the use of found and everyday materials, their installations and sculptures investigate themes of displacement, belonging, colonial histories, and the traces left by occupation. Their practice reflects on how places retain memory and how personal and political histories become embedded within the physical environment.

In 2016, Katz presented the solo exhibition *Groenpunt* at Blank Projects in Cape Town. Since then, their work has been exhibited internationally in museums, galleries, and biennials, establishing them as one of the leading voices in contemporary South African art.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Johannesburg (South Africa)
Biography:
Lebohang Kganye (born 1990) is a South African visual artist based in Johannesburg. Working across photography, installation, sculpture, collage, and moving image, she explores memory, family history, identity, and the construction of historical narratives. Born in Johannesburg and raised in Katlehong, she studied at the Market Photo Workshop, completing its Advanced Photography Programme in 2011, before earning a Fine Arts degree from the University of Johannesburg in 2016. She later pursued a Master's degree in Fine Arts at the University of the Witwatersrand.

Kganye's practice emerged from a personal exploration of family archives following the death of her mother. Using family photographs, oral histories, performance, and self-portraiture, she reconstructs scenes from the past to investigate the relationship between memory, fiction, and identity. Her works often combine photography with sculptural paper cut-outs, animation, and immersive installations, creating layered narratives that question the reliability of historical records and inherited memories.

As part of a generation of South African artists shaped by the legacy of apartheid, Kganye addresses the ways personal histories intersect with broader political and social histories. Her work has been exhibited internationally in museums, biennials, and major contemporary art institutions, and has established her as one of the leading voices in contemporary photography and installation art.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Johannesburg (South Africa)
Biography: Donna Kukama is a South African interdisciplinary artist whose practice merges various media by using performance as a tool for artistic research. Moving across performance, video, painting, and installation, her practice often presents socially engaged art through unconventional modes of storytelling in order to destabilize existing historical metanarratives and how we look at reality. Her work takes on an experimental and undisciplined form. With her practice, Kukama opens up multiple ways of inhabiting space, creating other worlds, and conceiving reality. To counter the predictable, she goes beyond the constraints of identity to uncover its complexities, layers, and contradictions while actively opening up possibilities for different narratives and less-told histories to exist. Whether written, drawn, performed, or sculptural, her work can be understood as gestures of poetry that speak about time and memory while presenting alternate realities where both the material and immaterial coexist to engage erasures within history.

Alice Mann is a South African photographic artist who's intimate portraiture essays explore notions of picture making as an act of collaboration. She aims to create images that empower her subjects and creates projects over extended periods, allowing for engaged and nuanced representations.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Soweto (South Africa)
Biography: Senzeni Marasela (born 11 February 1977) is a South African visual artist born in Thokoza who works across different media, combining performance, photography, video, prints, textiles, and embroidery in mixed-media installations. She obtained a BA in Fine Arts at the Wits School of Arts, University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg in 1998. Her work has been exhibited in South Africa, Europe, and the United States, and is part of local and international collections, including the Museum of Modern Art and the Newark Museum.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Cap (South Africa)
Biography: Jo Ractliffe (born 9 March 1961) is a South African photographer and teacher working in both Cape Town, where she was born, and Johannesburg, South Africa. She is the oldest of six sisters born to artist Barbara Fairhead and business leader Jeremy Ractliffe. Ractliffe is considered among the most influential South African 'social photographers.'

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Durban (South Africa)
Biography:
Tracey Rose (b. 1974, South Africa) is best-known for her revolutionary performative practice which often translates to and is accompanied by photography, video, installation, and digital prints. Often described as absurd, anarchic, slapdash and carnivalesque, Rose's work explores themes around post-coloniality, gender and sexuality, race and repatriation.

Rose was born in Durban, South Africa. In 1990 she joined the Johannesburg Art Foundation before obtaining a B.A. in Fine Art from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg in 1996. In 2004 Rose attended The South African School of Motion Picture Medium and Live Performance and later obtained her Master of Fine Arts, Goldsmiths College, University of London, UK in 2007. She currently lives and works in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Rose has taken part in several residencies including the WysingArts Centre, Cambridgeshire, UK (2014);   DAAD, Berlin, Germany (2012/13); Darb1718, Cairo, Egypt (2012);   Cruzes, Montevideo, Uruguay (2011);   KhojInternational Artists Workshop   Vasind, India (2005);   Africa 2005 Residency, The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, London, UK, (2004);   Hollywood Hills Horrorhouse, Los Angeles, CA, USA (2001);   Fresh, South African National Gallery, Cape Town, South Africa (2001) and OK Centrum, Linz, Austria (2000).

She has exhibited widely internationally, most notably, May You Live in Interesting Times South African National Pavilion,   58thLa Biennale di Venezia, Venice, Italy (2016);   Body Talk -Feminism, Sexuality & Body, 49 Nord 6 Est -Frac Lorraine, Metz, France (2016);   False Flag, Art Parcours, Art Basel, Basel, Switzerland (2016);   Toro Salvaje, Museum of Modern Art, Buenos Aires, Argentina (2016);   (x), Reina SofÃ­a Museum, Madrid, Spain (2014);   Waiting for God, Johannesburg Art Gallery, Johannesburg, South Africa and Bildmuseet, UmeÃ¥, Sweden (2011); Rose O’Grady (with Lorraine O’Grady), Goodman Gallery, Johannesburg, South Africa (2011);   Lubumbashi Biennial, Lubumbashi, Democratic Republic of Congo (2017); Performa 17, New York, USA (2017);   Documenta14, Athens, Greece and Kassel, Germany (2017);   11th Biennale de Lyon, Lyon, France (2011);   Afro Modern: Journeys through the Black Atlantic, Tate Liverpool, Liverpool, UK (2010);   StedelijkMuseum Amsterdam, Netherlands (2008);   Africa Remix, The Haywood Gallery, London, UK and Centre George Pompidou, Paris, France   (2005); and Africaine, The Studio Museum, New York, USA (2002) to name a few.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Cape Town (South Africa)
Biography: Lyndi Sales' artistic process is guided by her desire to explore the limits of human perception. She draws her inspiration from quantum physics as well as spiritual philosophy. Her aim is to achieve “looking with closed eyes”- to ignore what could obscure our vision and finally perceive our reality in its entirety. She seeks to state that the universe is a living organism, that each entity is a part of this whole and that – in the words of William Blake – “If the doors of perception were cleansed everything would appear to man as it is, Infinite.” Lyndi Sales’ artworks are influenced by scientific imagery, one can find structures that repeat themselves on a microscopic scale as well as in the immensity of space. These abstract motifs interweave to form symbols that can be found in multiple cultures. The artist explores different techniques - drawing, embroidery, laser cutting - to expose the spectator to artworks that may be openings towards new visions, towards a utopian world.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Johannesburg (South Africa)
Biography:
Mary Sibande (born 1982) is a South African artist based in Johannesburg whose multidisciplinary practice includes sculpture, photography, painting, installation, and design. Born in Barberton during apartheid, she was raised by her grandmother and draws extensively on her family's history, particularly the experiences of women who worked as domestic workers. She studied Fine Arts at Technikon Witwatersrand, receiving her diploma in 2004, and completed a B-Tech degree at the University of Johannesburg in 2007.

Sibande's work examines identity, race, gender, and social class in post-apartheid South Africa. Combining elements of fashion, sculpture, and staged photography, she creates powerful narratives that challenge historical stereotypes surrounding Black women while exploring personal and collective memory. Her iconic alter ego, Sophie, reimagines the domestic worker as a figure of empowerment, fantasy, and transformation, confronting the legacies of colonialism and apartheid through symbolic and theatrical imagery.

Representing South Africa at the 54th Venice Biennale in 2011, Sibande gained international recognition for her exploration of Black female identity and social history. Her works have been exhibited in major museums, biennials, and public institutions worldwide, establishing her as one of the leading contemporary artists from South Africa.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Cape Town (South Africa) and in Amsterdam (Netherlands)
Biography:
Buhlebezwe Siwani (born 1987) is a South African multidisciplinary artist whose practice spans performance, installation, photography, and video. Born and raised in Johannesburg, she has also lived in the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal. She studied at the Wits School of Arts, where she completed a BA in Fine Arts with Honours in 2011, and earned an MFA with distinction from the Michaelis School of Fine Art in 2015.

Siwani's practice explores spirituality, Black womanhood, ritual, healing, and the politics of the body. Drawing from her experience as a trained sangoma (traditional healer), she uses performance and installation to examine the intersections of African spiritual practices, colonial histories, gender, and systems of power. Documentation through photography and video often extends her live performances, allowing the body to remain present through its traces and representations.

Her work has been presented in major international exhibitions, biennials, and museums, where she has gained recognition for creating deeply personal yet politically charged works that challenge dominant narratives while foregrounding Indigenous knowledge, ancestral memory, and embodied forms of resistance.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Cape Town (South Africa)
Biography:
Sue Williamson (born 1941) is a South African artist, writer, and curator based in Cape Town. Born in Lichfield, England, she moved with her family to South Africa in 1948. She studied at the Art Students League of New York between 1963 and 1965 before earning an Advanced Diploma in Fine Art from the Michaelis School of Fine Art in Cape Town in 1983. Williamson has also received major international recognitions, including the Smithsonian Institution's Visual Arts Research Award (2007) and the Rockefeller Foundation Bellagio Creative Arts Fellowship (2011).

Working across printmaking, photography, installation, video, archival materials, and mixed media, Williamson explores themes of memory, identity, migration, colonialism, slavery, and apartheid. Her practice is grounded in extensive historical research, often combining archival documents, personal testimonies, and contemporary interventions to recover overlooked histories and examine the lasting impact of political violence and social injustice. Many of her installations address displacement, cultural memory, and the preservation of marginalized narratives.

Williamson is widely recognized for works investigating South Africa's apartheid history, including projects dedicated to District Six and the legacy of the slave trade. Alongside her artistic practice, she has contributed significantly to contemporary art discourse as the founding editor of *Artthrob*, one of South Africa's leading contemporary art publications. Her work has been exhibited internationally in major museums, biennials, and public institutions, establishing her as one of the most influential contemporary artists in South Africa.

Amel Alzakout, born in 1988 in Syria, is an artist and filmmaker based in Leipzig. Between 2010 and 2013 she studied journalism at Cairo University. In 2017 she participated with other artists in the video installation 'Trust Us' in the 3rd Herbstsalon at the Maxim Gorki Theater Berlin. Between 2017 and 2018 she studied art at the Weißensee Art Academy in Berlin, currently she is studying media art at the Academy of Visual Art (HGB) in Leipzig. 'Purple Sea' is her debut film.

Khaled Abdulwahed (born 1975, Syria) is a visual artist. He began his career in design, specializing in visual communication arts. His practice includes fine art photography, mixed-media works, and video art. His exhibitions and video art screenings have been presented in the Middle East, Europe, and the United States.

Pannaphan Yodmanee (born 1988 in Nakhon Si Thammarat, Thailand) is a contemporary artist whose practice fuses sacred tradition with experimental form. Trained from childhood in temple mural restoration and later at Silpakorn University in Bangkok, she built a foundation in Buddhist iconography before expanding into installation and mixed media.

Her large-scale works layer rocks, minerals, jute, cement, spray paint, and gold foil with painting, carving, and engraving, creating fresco-like surfaces that evoke both ruin and renewal. By bringing together the textures of archaeology with the language of sacred art, she produces environments where history and spirituality are reimagined through contemporary materiality.

Christelle Lheureux (born 1972) is a French artist and filmmaker who lives and works between Paris and Geneva. After studying at the Universities of Amiens and Paris VIII, she continued her education at the École des Beaux-Arts de Grenoble and Le Fresnoy - Studio national des arts contemporains. Since 1997, she has produced video installations presented in France and internationally. Her work is included in the collections of the Centre Pompidou, the Centre national des arts plastiques, and the Fonds national d'art contemporain. She has completed several residencies in Asia and has collaborated with artists, filmmakers, architects, and writers, including Apichatpong Weerasethakul, Philippe Rahm, and Sébastien Betbeder. Alongside her artistic practice, she directs short and feature films, including *Un sourire malicieux éclaire son visage* (2009), and has taught cinema at the Geneva University of Art and Design (HEAD Genève) since 2006.

Apichatpong Weerasethakul (born 16 July 1970) is a Thai independent film director, screenwriter, film producer, and professor at Tama Art University in Tokyo. Working outside the Thai studio system, he has directed numerous feature films and short films. His internationally acclaimed films include *Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives*, winner of the Palme d'Or at the 2010 Cannes Film Festival; *Tropical Malady*, winner of the Jury Prize at Cannes in 2004; *Blissfully Yours*, which received the top prize in the Un Certain Regard section in 2002; *Syndromes and a Century*; *Cemetery of Splendour*; and *Memoria* (2021), his first English-language feature.

His films explore themes such as dreams, nature, sexuality, and Western perceptions of Thailand and Asia, often employing unconventional narrative structures and non-professional actors. Alongside his filmmaking, Weerasethakul has exhibited extensively in international galleries and museums, including FACT Liverpool and the BFI Gallery in London.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Paris (France) since 1970
Lives and works in Roubaix (Nord, France)

Biography:
Mouna Jemal Siala (born 1973 in Paris) is a Tunisian multidisciplinary artist who lives and works in Tunis. She holds a Ph.D. from Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne University and has taught visual arts at the Higher Institute of Fine Arts of Tunis since 1998.

Her practice brings together digital media, photography, video, textile, and installation, exploring the relationships between the virtual and the real. Concerned with preserving the memory of actions, events, and lived experiences, she intertwines her personal history with her artistic practice. Themes such as motherhood, the female body, and the social and political realities of Tunisia are central to her work. Projects including *Non à la division* (2014) and *Union* combine photography, digital processes, and textile techniques to address questions of identity, unity, and collective memory.

Since 1993, Jemal Siala has exhibited internationally in France, Germany, Spain, Belgium, Algeria, Mali, Senegal, Switzerland, Morocco, India, the United States, and Tunisia. She has participated in the Instants Vidéo festival in Marseille, represented Tunisia in *Lumières d'Afrique* during COP21, and taken part in major international events including the Cairo Biennale, the Marrakech Biennale Off, Dak'Art Biennale, Casablanca Biennale, and Addis Foto Fest.

Nadia Kaabi-Linke (born 1978) is a Tunisian-born visual artist based in Berlin. Raised between Tunis, Kyiv, Dubai, and Paris, she studied at the Tunis Institute of Fine Arts before earning a Ph.D. in aesthetics and the philosophy of art from the Sorbonne in 2008. Her work explores themes of geopolitics, migration, identity, memory, and borders through conceptual installations, sculpture, and mixed media.

Kaabi-Linke gained international recognition after receiving the 2011 Abraaj Group Art Prize, which commissioned her installation *Flying Carpets*. The work was presented at the 54th Venice Biennale and later acquired by the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum as part of the Guggenheim UBS MAP Global Art Initiative. She also received the Discoveries Prize at Art Basel Hong Kong in 2014 and the Ithra Art Prize in 2021.

Her practice combines autobiographical experiences with historical and political narratives, often using architectural surfaces, found materials, prints, thread, and delicate sculptural interventions to examine displacement, violence, migration, and collective memory. Her works are included in the collections of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, the Museum of Modern Art, the Dallas Museum of Art, the Burger Collection, the Samdani Art Foundation, and M+, among others, and have been exhibited internationally in major museums, biennials, and galleries.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Paris (France) and in Sfax (Tunisia)
Biography:
Mouna Karray (born 1970) is a Tunisian photographer and video artist born in Sfax, Tunisia. She studied cinema and photography at the Institut Supérieur d’Animation Culturelle in Tunis before earning a Master's degree in Photography from Tokyo Polytechnic University in Japan in 2001. She has completed residencies at the Centre d’Art Vivant de Radès (Tunisia), the Cité internationale des arts (Paris), and the Civitella Ranieri Foundation (Italy), and currently lives and works between Sfax and Paris.

Working primarily with photography and video, Karray explores themes of identity, gender, poverty, political transformation, and the social realities of contemporary Tunisia. Her projects often combine documentary and staged approaches, reflecting on personal experience alongside broader political and cultural contexts. Series such as *Self Circumstances*, *Identity at Stake*, *Murmurer*, *Live*, and *Nobody Will Talk About Us* examine questions of belonging, memory, neglected landscapes, and the aftermath of the Tunisian Revolution through photography, performance, and moving image.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Paris (France) and in Tunis (Tunisia)
Biography: Farah Khelil (1980) studied at the Tunis Institute of Fine Arts and holds a PhD in arts and art sciences from the Ecole des arts de la Sorbonne. Her work combines artist's books, videos, archives, and displays with writing and theoretical research. She has participated in many international group exhibitions, such as at the Undercurrent Projects artspace (New York, 2014), the Es Baluard museum (Palma, 2015), the Officine dell'Immagine Gallery (Milan, 2017), the Handel Street Projects Gallery (London, 2017), the Institut français de Saint-Louis/Galerie du Fleuve (Saint-Louis, Senegal, 2018), and the Institut français de Tunisie (Sousse, 2018). She has also had several solo exhibitions, including at the International Cultural Centre in Cerisy-la-Salle (Normandy, 2013), Appartement (Paris, 2017), and the Selma Feriani Gallery (Tunis, 2018). Her work is part of the FRAC Normandie collection.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Tunis (Tunisia) and in Paris (France)
Biography:
Nicène Kossentini (born 1976) is a Tunisian visual artist. She graduated from the Higher Institute of Fine Arts of Tunis and the University Marc Bloch in Strasbourg, and also trained at Le Fresnoy - Studio national des arts contemporains in Tourcoing and at Les Gobelins in Paris.

Kossentini has participated in international residency programs, including the Artist Residency in Algiers, and took part in the DJART Biennale in Algiers in 2014. Alongside her artistic practice, she is an assistant professor of experimental cinema at the University of Tunis.

Diana Blok (born 1952 in Uruguay) and Marlo Broekmans (born 1953 in the Netherlands) are a photographic artist duo who collaborated between 1979 and 1981 before continuing their careers independently. They first met through their shared passion for photography, initially by chance at the Rencontres d'Arles in 1977 and later in Amsterdam in 1979, where they formed both a personal and artistic partnership. Their collaboration was marked by an intense period of experimentation, resulting in projects such as the series *Invisible Forces*, which includes the photograph *Horses* (1979).

Both artists developed their photographic practice outside formal academic training. After spending her early life across several Latin American countries, Diana Blok moved to the Netherlands in the 1970s, where she chose to learn photography through professional practice rather than attending the Gerrit Rietveld Academie. Marlo Broekmans studied pedagogy and psychology before turning to photography in the late 1970s. Their collaborative work marked the beginning of their professional artistic careers, establishing a foundation that each would later continue to develop independently.

Alicia Mihai Gazcue (Montevideo, Uruguay 1949, lives in Bucarest, Romania) was an early practitioner of the politically loaded and playful conceptualism which several pioneering Latin American artists became engaged with in the late 60s and 70s. During the violent military dictatorship in Uruguay Alicia went into exile in Romania, and silently continued her art practice for many years, always emphasizing the conceptual slant in her approach. In 1990 artists Liliana Porter and Ana Tiscornia met Alicia Mihai Gazcue in Cuba, while being jurors for an art award. They continued to be in touch throughout the years and for the past decade they have been promoting Mihai Gazcue's work in the West, helping her reach new audiences. Several prominent curators specializing in Latin American art have exhibited her work or written about it.

While already living in exile, Alicia Mihai Gazcue made several small paintings reproducing the patterns of traditional sidewalk and floor tiles common in Uruguay. Some have stains of red paint ('Blood', 'Blood Again') some have objects that appear to have been dropped or lost in a hurry. They are meant as reflections on political persecution and exile, while conveying a sense of nostalgia for the textures of her home country.

One of Mihai Gazcue's earliest works is a performance in which two actors dressed as soldiers stood at the sides of the narrow entrance to an art gallery. Visitors needed to squeeze through their menacing and physically close presence in order to enter the space. This piece was made when there was already a strong threat of military violence against the civil population in the region. The work was recorded in 16 mm film and it is shown as a film installation.

Alicia Mihai Gazcue has participated in the 12th Shangai Biennial, 2018; the Second Performance Biennial, Buenos Aires, 2017. Her work has been exhibited at the Boston Center for the Arts; MAK Center for Art and Architecture, Los Angeles; and galleries worlwide.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Los Angeles (Californie, United States)
Biography:
Jill Mulleady is a Uruguayan-born artist who grew up in Buenos Aires, Argentina. She studied at Chelsea College of Art and Design in London, where she completed a Master of Fine Arts degree, and is currently based in Los Angeles. Working primarily in painting, her practice also incorporates sculpture, architectural interventions, and readymade objects, creating immersive installations that explore memory, history, transformation, and the relationship between reality and imagination.

Mulleady's paintings bring together references to historical art, popular culture, and personal experience, producing layered narratives in which different temporalities coexist. Her work investigates the contemporary image as both representation and interface, reflecting on how images shape perception, attention, and social experience. She has exhibited internationally at institutions including the Whitney Museum of American Art, Hammer Museum, Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Kunsthalle Bern, Le Consortium, the 58th Venice Biennale, and the Swiss Institute in New York. Her works are held in the collections of the Whitney Museum of American Art, Musée d'Art Moderne de Paris, Hammer Museum, Los Angeles County Museum of Art, Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, and Le Consortium.

Magda Andrade was a post-war artist. Magda Andrade was a venezuelan female artist born in Maracaibo (VE) in 1912.

Magda Andrade's first verified exhibition was III Bienal Do Museu De Arte Moderna De São Paulo at Bienal de Sao Paulo in São Paulo in 1955, and the most recent exhibition was 6th Ljubljana Biennale of Graphic Arts at Ljubljana Biennial of Graphic Arts in Ljubljana in 1965. Magda Andrade is most frequently exhibited in Brazil, but also had exhibitions in Slovenia. Andrade has also been in no less than no art fairs but in two biennials. A notable show was III Bienal Do Museu De Arte Moderna De São Paulo at Bienal de Sao Paulo in São Paulo in 1955. Another notable show was at Ljubljana Biennial of Graphic Arts in Ljubljana. Magda Andrade's art is in at least one museum collection, at Galería de Arte Nacional in Caracas.

Andrade's best rank was in 1955, with the most dramatic change in 1976. For a complete illustration of the artist's career since 1955, please see the career chart on the analytics page.

Carla Arocha is a Venezuelan artist based in Antwerp, internationally recognized for her work in Minimalism, geometric abstraction, and design. Originally trained as a biologist, she later studied fine arts at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago and completed an MFA at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Since the mid-1990s, her work has been exhibited internationally, and since 2006 she has collaborated with Stéphane Schraenen as the artist duo Arocha & Schraenen.

Arocha's practice explores the relationships between geometry, ornament, the body, and perception through painting, installation, sculpture, and mirrored structures. Drawing inspiration from art, fashion, biology, and Venezuelan visual culture, she combines minimalist forms with intricate patterns and reflective materials. Her works often investigate themes of identity, transformation, and surface, creating immersive spatial experiences that shift according to their surroundings while balancing visual precision with decorative complexity.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Paris (France) since 1974
Biography:
María Eugenia Arria (born 1951, Caracas) is a Venezuelan painter, draftswoman, printmaker, and educator. She studied literature at the Central University of Venezuela before continuing her artistic education at the École Nationale Supérieure des Arts Décoratifs in Paris and the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales. Since the late 1970s, she has exhibited extensively in Venezuela and internationally, including in France, Switzerland, Argentina, Chile, China, Colombia, and the Dominican Republic. She currently teaches at the National Experimental University of the Arts (UNEARTE).

Arria's artistic practice has evolved through two distinct periods, moving from a darker, more restrained visual language in the early 1980s toward a body of work characterized by light, color, and abstraction from the late 1980s onward. Influenced by American Abstract Expressionism and Informalism, her work centers on the exploration of line, light, and color, reducing sensory perception to its essential visual elements. Although associated with the Latin American avant-garde, she remained independent from the Venezuelan artistic groups of the 1970s, developing a highly personal abstract language.

Sol Calero (born 1982, Caracas) is a Venezuelan visual artist based in Berlin. She studied at the Complutense University of Madrid and the University of La Laguna in Tenerife. Her practice draws on Latin American culture, visual stereotypes, and the ambiguity of cultural symbols in the context of globalization.

Through immersive installations, painting, and participatory environments, Calero examines the tension between lived reality and exoticized perceptions of Latin America. Works such as *El Autobús* (2019) and *El barco de barro* (2020) invite audiences to engage directly with spaces inspired by everyday Latin American life, while her colorful *Fruitas* series reflects on political and social issues through references to Carmen Miranda and the idealized images of Latin America constructed by popular culture. Her work challenges cultural clichés and questions how identity is represented across global contexts.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Guadalajara (Mexico) and in New York (New York, United States)
Biography:
Patricia Esquivias (born 1979, Caracas) is a Venezuelan-born Spanish artist who works primarily with video. She studied at Central Saint Martins College of Art and Design in London and later completed an MFA at the California College of the Arts in San Francisco. Based on storytelling, her practice often features her own voice as narrator, weaving together personal anecdotes, historical references, and cultural memory.

Esquivias' work explores the relationships between history, memory, and everyday narratives through essayistic videos that combine research with subjective interpretation. Her work has been exhibited internationally, including in Madrid, Los Angeles, New York, and Marrakesh, and is part of the collection of the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid.

Cristina Merchán (1927 - 1987) was a Venezuelan artist who began her career as a painter before becoming known for her ceramic sculpture. She studied at the Universidad de Guadalajara in Mexico and later trained in ceramics at the School of Fine and Applied Arts in Caracas under Miguel Arroyo. After receiving the National Award for Applied Arts in 1957, she continued her studies in Barcelona with Francesc Albors and Josep Llorens Artigas, specializing in high-fired stoneware.

From the late 1950s onward, Merchán lived and worked between Barcelona, Paris, and Caracas, exhibiting widely in Venezuela, France, and Spain. Her early works evolved from functional ceramics into sculptural forms, notably with the *Los Bichos* series of fantastical animal figures. Her later practice focused on sculptural vessels and ovoid forms distinguished by refined glazes, subtle tonal variations, and textured or incised geometric surfaces. Her work is represented in major collections, including the Musée des Arts Décoratifs at the Louvre in Paris.

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Paris (France) since 1969
Lives and works in Aurillac (Cantal, France)
Biography:
Anhar Salem is a multidisciplinary artist with a multi-ethnic background (Yemeni and Indonesian). Salem studied Information Technology at the Arab Open University in Jeddah, then completed a postgraduate degree at Le Fresnoy - Studio national des arts contemporains in Tourcoing. Her artistic practice explores, documents, and reveals private spaces to the public realm through themes of everyday life, the body, and social media. Working primarily with video, Salem draws an emphasis on new forms of communication that critique video as a medium. She often improvises with her iPhone camera, working collaboratively with her subjects and characters as a means to foreground processes around the marginalization of people and their images.

Salem's work has been recognized with several awards, including the Reiffers Art Initiatives Prize (2025), Révélation Art Numérique – Art Vidéo / ADAGP Prize (2021, France), the Prix Around Video Art Fair / Renato et Catherine Casciani (2021, France), the Radar Award at Curtocircuíto International Film Festival (2022, Spain), and the Prix Analix Forever / Galerie Analix (2021, France).

She has participated in several artist residencies, including the Pickle Bar Residency with Slavs and Tatars (Berlin, 2022), the Almansouria Residency at Cité Internationale des Arts (Paris, 2023–2024), the Heretige and Innovation Residency (AlUla, 2024), and the Pinault Collection Artist Residency (Lens, 2025-2026).

Her solo exhibition “Mashallah. Why Did You Wander Out?” was presented at the Cité internationale des arts in Paris (2023). She has also participated in prominent group exhibitions, including “THE FUTURE IS UNMANNED” at La HEAD (2024, Switzerland), “I Took a Screenshot of the Whole World” at POUSH (2023, France).

Lives / Works: Lives and works in Harare (Zimbabwe) and in Tripoli (Libya)
Biography:
Virginia Chihota was born in 1983 in Chitungwiza, Zimbabwe and currently lives and works in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. In 2004 she graduated in Fine Arts at the National Gallery BAT Workshop School (now the National Gallery School of Visual Art and Design) and in 2006 she obtained a Diploma in Visual Arts from Harare Polytechnic. Chihota represented Zimbabwe at the 55th Venice Biennale in 2013 and was awarded the Prix Canson in the same year.

Over the past fifteen years, Virginia Chihota's introspective work has been influenced by personal experiences - landmark and every day. In a reflection on intimacy and the human figure, she has addressed themes such as childbearing, childrearing, marriage, kinship, bereavement and faith. At once mundane and transcendental, rife with allusions to everyday life, and religious and folkloric symbolism, her large works on paper display a raw, expressionist verve and a striking grace in the elaborate use of patterns, textures and layers.

Having trained as a printmaker, Chihota's use of screen-printing is as confident as it is original. She mixes printing techniques with drawing to produce unique works of striking formal complexity. They often depict the female form blending into near abstraction, and bodies caught in strange embraces evoking a figural union; along with an iconographic repertoire which points towards the domestic whilst emphasising connectedness and collectivity. Chihota's work highlights the ways in which the female agency disrupts borders and activates concerns around different forms of belonging. Subjectivity emerges as a concept embedded in notions of interrelatedness.

She is represented in collections including Deutsche Bank Collection, Frankfurt; FRAC Picardie, Amiens; National Gallery of Zimbabwe, Harare, Saatchi Gallery, London; Tate, London; U.S. Department of State; J.P. Morgan Chase. She has shown internationally including National Gallery of Zimbabwe, Harare (2019), SAVVY Contemporary, Berlin (2019), solo at The Armory Show (2019) The Drawing Room, London (2018), Academy of Fine Arts, Vienna (2017), Muséum d'histoire naturelle, Le Havre, France (2016), Saatchi Gallery, London, UK (2015), Kunsthalle Faust, Hannover (2014), Neuer Berliner Kunstverein, Berlin (2014), Musée des Beaux-Arts de la Ville de Paris (2013), Fundación Proa, Buenos Aires (2012), Korea Foundation Cultural Center, Seoul (2010).

Georgina Maxim (born 1980) is a Zimbabwean artist and curator who lives and works in Harare and Mutare, Zimbabwe and studied at University of Bayreuth, Germany (MA/AVVA) and Chinhoyi University in Zimbabwe. She develops here artistic practice around textiles, using techniques as varied as sewing, weaving, embroidery and crochet to (re)bring used clothes to life. Maxim is also the co-founder and co-director of Village Unhu, an arts space offering residency programs, exhibitions, workshops, and studio spaces in Milton Park, Harare, and Mutare, Zimbabwe. Her recent exhibitions include the 61st Venice Biennale, In minor Keys curated by the late Koyo Kouoh (2026); solo exhibitions at Button Gallery Nordenhake (Mexico City, 2025), and Winter Wonders Goodman Gallery (London, 2024). Group exhibitions include: Kaaraalines Vers, Muset for Samtidskunst (Roskilde, Denmark, 2025): Femmes curated by Pharrel Williams Perrotin Gallery, (Paris, 2024), group exhibitions and art fairs with 31 Project (Paris, 2020-25); Memoria: récits d’une autre histoire, National Museum of Yaoundé (Yaounde, 2023) and Fondation H, Antananarivo (2024), O Quilombismso, O Quilombismo: Of Resisting and Insisting. Of Flight as Fight. Of Other Democratic Egalitarian Political Philosophies (Quilombism, 2023); Unravel: The power and politics of textiles in art, Barbican Centre, (London, 2024) and Stedelijk Museum (Amsterdam, 2024); A Different Now is Close Enough to Enhale, Goodman Gallery (Cape Town and Johannesburg, 2022); Eternally Yours, Somerset House (London, 2022); 58th Venice Biennale, Zimbabwe Pavillion (Venice, 2019). Residencies include Fondation H (Antananarivo 2023), Bag Factory (Johannesburg 2019), Goethe Institut (Salvador de Bahia 2018), Embassy of Foreign Artists (Geneva 2017). Maxim has curated group exhibitions at Village Unhu and art fairs including Kuvhunura/Kupinda ne mwenje mudziva, Fondation Blachere, Bonniuex 2024.

Kresiah Mukwazhi was born in Harare, Zimbabwe, in 1992. She studied visual arts and photography at the National Gallery School of Visual Art in Harare and design at the Market Photo Workshop in Johannesburg. Recently she was a guest at the Nefasi Art Space residency that was concluded in 2019 at Dar es Salaam, in Tanzania, with different workshops and a conference by the artist. Among personal exhibitions we can mention: in 2016, In My Private Moments at the National Gallery of Zimbabwe in Bulayano, in 2018 Bedroom Interview at SMAC Gallery, Cape Town and the most recent one, the collective Five Bhobh: Panting at the End of an Era at the ZEITZ Museum of Contemporary Art Africa (MOCAA) a Cape Town. Currently she lives and works in Harare, Zimbabwe.

Priyageetha Dia is an interdisciplinary artist based in Singapore. She works at the intersections of the biographical and cultural production of the Tamizh identity. Nurturing  speculative fiction and decolonial feminist thought, she works across digital animation, installation, and performance. Combining personal narratives and national histories to re-present the notion of the ‘future-past’, her practice unfolds the complexities of identity politics and spatial relations of the Tamizh diasporic experience in Singapore and Southeast Asia. Dia’s work offers speculative narratives on Southeast Asian plantations, which she views as sites for recovering stories of resistance. Her research interests also include building nonlinear narratives through digital semiotics, migrant histories, and our relationship with the non-human. Her practice represents an important voice from a new generation of Singaporean artists, and their unique position to discuss ecological issues through the lens of decolonization and technologically mediated reality.

Simryn Gill (born 1959) is a Singapore-born artist who lives and works between Sydney, Australia, and Port Dickson, Malaysia. Working across sculpture, photography, drawing, printmaking, writing, and publishing, her practice reflects a life shaped by movement between Singapore, Malaysia, India, the United Kingdom, and Australia. After settling in Australia in 1987, she briefly studied at the South Australian School of Art before leaving to focus on her artistic practice and family.

Gill's work explores themes of place, migration, language, memory, and transformation through a wide range of materials and processes. She has participated in major international exhibitions, including Documenta in Kassel (2007 and 2012) and the 55th Venice Biennale, where she represented Australia in 2013. Her work has also been exhibited internationally at institutions including the Museum of Modern Art and the Guggenheim Museum in New York, and in 2015 she presented her first major solo exhibition, *Hugging the Shore*, at the Centre of Contemporary Art in Gillman Barracks, Singapore.
